Title: Remarks of all members of the Lee Il-hyung Committee "Press Conference Organized by the Gold Barrel Committee"
text: Financial and Monetary Commission Press Conference 2018.3.19.( Mon) Efficient operation of macroeconomic policies Efficient operation of macroeconomic policies Financial and Monetary Commissioner Lee Il-hyung * This document is not an official opinion of the Bank of Korea or the Financial and Monetary Commission, but the personal opinion of the Gold Barrel Commissioner. At last year's press conference, we asked the question of whether monetary policy should also consider growth, the link between the policy of the ROK and financial stability, and how the Korean economy will be affected by the global situation. This year, we will look at the usefulness and interconnectedness of the harmonization of monetary and fiscal policy that form the two pillars of macroeconomic policy, as well as the considerations to be taken into account when operating these policies. Specifically, the main points of the remarks and the implications for the Korean economy are as follows: Because the pathways in which monetary and fiscal policies affect economic activity are different, the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies can be increased through appropriate harmony, depending on the cause of economic volatility. From this point of view, if it is determined that there is a need to continue to maintain a fiscal policy framework in a relaxed manner, then expansionary fiscal policy is desirable and if targeting in the right sectors is done well, it is thought that it will also be beneficial from the standpoint of macroeconomic balance. Next, macroeconomic policies cannot replace structural reforms, and since they may be more costly than the benefits of policies (e.g., accumulating financial imbalances can hinder growth in the medium term), an accurate understanding of the economic situation and structure is needed. Financial imbalances can be amplified through deregulation along with monetary policy. The cumulative accumulation of financial imbalances through the recent tightening of wealth regulations has shown some degree of control, but it is already showing a high level. If you are more cautious or change the policy keynote, you will have to consider the trade-offs of what the price to pay and the benefits you can get are in the short and medium term. Finally, since it is a non-reserve currency and the small open economy is fully exposed to the global economy , it is also necessary to consider how relative competitiveness and structural differences can affect our economy when implementing macroeconomic policies. Since the prices and wages of the non-traded sector are relatively low compared to developed countries, we recommend policies that have comparatively high benefits for workers in the non-traded sector, such as raising the minimum wage. In addition, the solution to achieving sustainable results is market-driven regulation through increased productivity.  Goals of macroeconomic policy The macroeconomic objectives, represented by monetary policy (including exchange rate policy) and fiscal policy, are to maximize social welfare by reducing economic uncertainty and risk to increase the efficiency of the judgment and allocation of resources necessary to run the market. Monetary policy adjusts the financial markets and the incentives for consumption and investment through interest rates, which will affect growth and prices. Fiscal policy, on the other hand, refers to the role of government policy in coordinating the economy through the tools of macroscopic operations, such as tax rates, government spending , and fiscal surpluses/deficits. In the latter case, targeting to specific sectors is also possible, which in some cases can be more effective than monetary policy. Such a macroeconomic policy, in its very nature, is useful for minimizing economic volatility, but it cannot replace the role of structural reform. However, caution is required as it may have semi-perpetual consequences that have affected resource allocation behavior. The effectiveness of monetary and fiscal policy needs to be looked at separately from theory and practice. In principle, an independent monetary policy is possible if a non-reserve currency country introduces a floating exchange rate system. In practice, however, small open economies find it difficult to implement their own monetary policy, regardless of the exchange rate system. 1) On the other hand, in the case of a re-political policy, theoretically the effect may be weak as the effect of the policy is spill-over to other countries under a small open economy, but empirical analysis shows that the impact on the country is not small . . 2) Because the delivery paths of the two policies are different, it is important to make the most of this when formulating policies. Theoretically , a rate cut would boost domestic demand and at the same time contribute to exports, accompanied by a devaluation of the yuan. On the other hand, in the case of a long-term fiscal policy, the associated costs have to be financed by the market, which will cause interest rates to rise and the yuan will rise. This can result in a contraction in exports, which can be said to be effective in adjusting the relative share of exports to domestic demand in addition to the recovery of the domestic economy. However, because reducing economic volatility soon contributes to price stability, and price stability reduces economic volatility, when the two policies are harmonized together, they can more effectively achieve their respective goals. The direct link between fiscal and monetary policy is also determined by how the cost of the deficit is financed and where the government's net savings are stored. In other words, the transfer of government savings from commercial banks to central banks itself has a tightening effect on the financial markets. On the other hand, if you finance the cost by issuing bonds outside the country, it will also affect the foreign exchange market depending on the purpose of the expulsion. As such, fiscal and monetary policy are inextricably linked, as the effect is directly transferred not only to the macroeconomy but also to the financial markets according to fiscal operations. As an example, if you look at the case of the United States, this connection has been working well since the financial crisis. The United States continued to maintain a relaxed monetary policy in the 2000s, except for the short period prior to the global financial crisis. Especially after the crisis, the central government further implemented an unconventional monetary policy in which the row bought Treasury bonds and MBS and lowered long-term interest rates. In the case of fiscal policy, on the other hand, although the role of automatic stabilizer was relatively large due to the fact that fluctuations in tax revenues were sensitive to the economy, even in the meantime, large shocks such as the global financial crisis required additional discretionary measures. In other words, during the global financial crisis, the deficit was widened due to a lack of tax revenue, but the rise in unemployment was excessive, requiring additional fiscal spending. The gradual reduction in the size of the fiscal deficit in preparation for the subsequent falling unemployment rate has resulted in an expansion of the contribution of fiscal policy. Thus, in response to the shock of the financial crisis, macroeconomic policies moved in the same direction , maximizing each other's effectiveness. In particular, a significant portion of the bonds issued to finance fiscal expenditure can be seen in the fact that the U.S. Federal Reserve has mitigated the impact on the market by its purchases. During the course of deleveraging, the demand for safe assets surged both internally and externally, but the purchase of bonds by Ang Bank also contributed to the decline in long-term interest rates. The additional contribution of the Fed intervention can also be seen in the expansion of the short-term liquid funds held by financial institutions at the Fed at the time.  The Cost of Macroeconomic Policy (COST) and the Importance of Efficient Operation As mentioned earlier, the purpose of macroeconomic policy is to maximize the aftermath by minimizing economic volatility. However, it should not be overlooked that the process of running macroeconomic policy involves not only benefits but also costs. However, it should be noted that in the case of monetary policy, the benefits and costs will be greatly affected by changes in financial regulations , so it is difficult to distinguish the contributions of the two. In the event of a recession caused by factors of ordinary economic fluctuations, including a contraction in consumer sentiment , it is expected that expansionary macroeconomic policies will not lead to inefficient allocation of resources. However, after a financial crisis or in the case of a long-term recession accompanied by structural changes, macroeconomic policies can be costly. The best illustration of the cost of expansionary macroeconomic policy is the surge in private or government debt. 3) In the case of developed countries, the deregulation in addition to easing monetary policy prior to the financial crisis has led to a rapid growth in private sector financial debt and an overboost to the economy. 4) Eventually, the financial crisis broke out, and the intervention of the government to promote stability again led to a significant increase in government debt, which in particular enabled the deleveraging of the private sector. In emerging countries, on the other hand, since the global financial crisis, the liquidity of the dollar has helped the private sector expand rapidly and boost the economy. Of course, the phenomenon of increasing debt is not a problem in itself. If a policy accompanied by debt growth drives higher growth in the medium term, causing prices to reach their target and the ratio of debt to GDP to fall, the policy goal is achieved. However, this is only possible if the allocation of resources under the expansionary policy is efficiently achieved. If the rebound is temporary and unsustainable, it will put a strain on the economy. For example, if the normalization of policy has become a greater burden when the economy recovers as a result of monetary policy accompanied by an increase in debt , then the effectiveness of the policy needs to be reconsidered. In this case, an unconditional delay in the normalization of the policy will not solve the problem. In addition, even during the implementation of the policy, its effectiveness will have to be constantly checked. Economic Growth, Financial Development and Financial Stability  From now on, I would like to expand the discussion of the issue of financial stability at the level of monetary policy and talk about the issue of financial stability at the level of economic growth and financial development. (Economic Growth and Financial Development)  There are many analyses that financial development has a positive effect on economic growth Economists have pointed to human resources, R&D, etc. as factors for economic growth. Some scholars believe that financial development is positive for economic growth. Claimed to be an influencing factor (King and Levine, etc.)  However, the view of the relationship between financial development and economic growth has been highly debated among scholars. Robinson argues that "corporations are ahead, gold financing follows"* and interpreted as a reduction in the role of finance * It seems to be the case that where enterprise leads finance follows.( J. Robinson, The Generalization of the G eneral Theory, 1952) However, Goldsmith, McKinnon, Shaw, and others argued in the early 1970s that there was a positive relationship between financial development and the economic arena.  In particular, McKinnon and Shaw argue that financial repression policies that control interest rates and credit supply by the government are detrimental to economic growth.  According to the traditional view, financial development is the activation of financial intermediation skills, facilitating the supply of funds to productive sectors . For the smoothness of this function of financial intermediary, it is essential to have sound operating financial institutions and an efficient financial market .  When finance develops and the financial intermediary function is activated, the ability to mobilize funds through savings, etc. is enhanced, and risk management and monitoring functions for financial institutions and financial markets become more efficient. It will also perform the function of producing and providing necessary information to financial entities (money consumers and donors, financial institutions that perform financial intermediary functions, and supervisory bodies such as governments) 9.  In the meantime, in the quantitative analysis of the relationship between financial development and economic growth, there have been studies in which the indicator such as "Gold Loan Floating Bond / GDP Ratio" has been used as a surrogate variable for financial development. In particular, after the so-called Cross Country Regression Analysis, which is based on cross-sectional data from countries made famous by the ship, scholars including King and Levin10 have concluded through quantitative analysis that financial development has a positive impact on economic growth.  However, it has also been argued that this defined financial development can have a negative effect on economic growth. In the early 1980s, many Latin American countries, including Mexico, experienced a financial crisis following policies of rapid financial liberalization of the gold market. Words to enter As is well known, our country's monetary policy operates on the basis of inflation targets. Currently, the target is 2.0% of the consumer inflation rate, which is temporary, rather than the price level at a particular point in time. Considering price fluctuations due to irregular factors and the ripple lag in monetary policy, this is the target level that we want to achieve on the medium-term clock. Accordingly, from a medium-term perspective, the analysis and forecasting of sustainable underlying price flows is indispensable for ensuring the credibility of monetary policy. However, estimating the underlying price trend is not as easy as it seems. As the economic landscape continues to change, movements that were considered temporary last longer than expected, affecting medium-term price flows and even settling for structural factors. On the other hand, in many cases, the movement that was supposed to be a structural change was only a game phenomenon if you look at it after a certain period of time. Accordingly, various studies have been carried out to analyze and predict price trends. A concept commonly used in these studies is the Augmented Phillips Curve, in which prices are influenced by economic and supply factors. Studies of policy effects tend to focus more on analyzing the link between prices and economic factors, but estimating the underlying price trend on the medium-term clock To make predictions, the analysis of supply factors is also quite important. In today's conference, I would like to focus on the exchange rate among the many factors that affect prices. Normally, the exchange rate is considered a supply factor in the price path, but despite its short-term volatility, it has a significant impact on the underlying price flow in the medium-term clock. To this end, we will continue the discussion on the relationship between domestic prices and exchange rates, the main factors influencing the exchange rate, and the order of the city's four points on monetary policy.  Relationship between domestic prices and exchange rates Our country is a so-called small, open economy. There are a lot of exports , but the imports are also substantial. With more than 70% of raw materials and about 20% of intermediate goods being sourced by import, overseas prices are ultimately driven through multiple production and distribution processes. This will affect domestic consumer prices. The direct impact of importing consumer goods cannot be ignored either. There is also an indirect impact through price expectations. However, since the global price flow affects domestic prices through imports, the price variable that is an important conduit is the Barro exchange rate. In general, when the yuan/daler exchange rate rises (depreciates the yuan), there is a light direction that acts as an upward pressure on domestic prices (Figure 1). Many empirical studies also estimate that the impact of the exchange rate on domestic consumer prices is statistically significant (1). The relationship between exchange rates and inflation is not limited to our country, but it is usually known that its influence is relatively large and the time difference is shorter in emerging countries than in developed countries (2).  The main factors that affect the exchange rate (Exchange Rate Determination Theory and Application in Financial Markets) So how is the exchange rate determined? The theory about this has a very long history and has developed in various ways with the changes in the economic situation. If we only outline the theory from a macroeconomic point of view, we can broadly distinguish between the current account approach, which focuses on the supply and demand of foreign exchange according to ordinary transactions, and the asset market approach, which places more emphasis on capital transaction flows. In the current account approach, as the model is constructed around macrovariables that affect current transactions, the volume of currency, inflation expectations, and the gap in the rate of real income growth are considered to be the main factors in the determination of the exchange rate, whereas in the asset market approach, the investment target We believe that expectations of the return of an asset play a more important role in determining the exchange rate. The asset market approach is again divided into a monetary approach and a portfolio balance approach, depending on assumptions about substitution between assets. The problem is that it is not easy to actually use the above theories to predict exchange rate fluctuations in the financial markets. This is because most exchange rate determination theories are based on assumptions that differ in degree, but are somewhat at odds with reality, and need to be verified. The numbers are obviously very low, but this is somewhat explainable given the situation 7 years ago and the fact that the potential growth rate itself has fallen in the meantime. more worrisome is the acceleration of the downward trend in inflation rates. What is more worrisome about the economic situation in 2019 compared to 2012 is the trend in inflation. After the plunge in growth in 2012, our economy grew by an average of 3.1% in the five years from 2013 to 2017. It grew by 2.7% last year, so it seems that by the time this slowdown began , our economy had returned to its path of potential growth. Consumer inflation, on the other hand , has fallen from 2.2% in 2012 to a six-year average of 1.3% from 2013 to 2018. It has been falling below the target of 2% for a considerable long time, and has fallen further to 0% this year. It is known that the expected inflation of economic actors is shaped by past experience. The low inflation rate, which has been going on for 6 years already, is likely to have caused some degree of decline in the expected inflation of the Korean economic actors. A further decline in inflation to a record low this year risks adhering to or worsening this expected downward trend in inflation. In fact , according to the trends shown in the Bank of Korea survey, the general public's expected inflation has fallen from 2.9% at the end of 2013 to 2.0% as of August 2019. It is customary for the average person expected inflation to appear in any country survey to be exaggerated over the actual realization inflation. It is a widely known fact in the academic community. Therefore, it is thought that the large inflation manifested by the actions of real economic actors is likely to fall below the monetary policy target of 2%. It is a risk that cannot be ignored as a person in charge of the policy of tonghua. * Materials 2. See "Expected Inflation Trend in Korea" Risk of Falling Expected Inflation "Isn't the lower the inflation rate, the better", or "What's wrong with an inflation rate of 1%, or even 0%, which is lower than the target of 2%? If the prices don't rise, it's not better" - a story you often hear. If it does not affect the expected rate of inflation, a temporary low rate of inflation is not a big problem. For example, the inflation rate of around 1% will last for 1-2 years and then recover. However, the low rate of inflation over the long term, which risks falling expected inflation below 2%, is a problem. Let me introduce two reasons: First, if expected inflation falls below the target to a level close to 0%, there is a risk of dampening the consumer sentiment of economic actors. For example, let's say that expected inflation has fallen to the level of 1%. In order for prices to be expected to rise by an 'average' 1%, a significant number of items should be expected to fall in price. 1) The consumption of these items is no reason to rush, and the economic sentiment of consumers and producers is more likely to shrink than before. This risk of economic psychological contraction is mainly cited against the backdrop of a deflationary situation in which expected inflation is negative. However, even if it is not theoretically deflationary, it is a risk that arises if expected inflation deviates from the target and falls close to 0%. Second, a drop in expected inflation is the door when there is a risk of crippled the monetary authorities' interest rate policies. This is why it is even more important than the first reason before. 2) As you know, the formula of the central bank's interest rate policy today is as follows: "During a recession, we cut the benchmark interest rate to boost aggregate demand to promote inflation and recovery, and in times of economic upheaval we respond in reverse." Against the backdrop of achieving price stability and economic stability with the formula of this interest rate policy, the premise is that neutral interest rates must remain unchanged. Let me illustrate with an example. Let's say an economy is in equilibrium, with a real neutral rate of 1% and expected inflation of 2%. In other words, the nominal neutral rate is 3%. The central bank was keeping the benchmark interest rate at 3% at the level of the nominal neutral rate because the economy was in equilibrium. Now, suddenly, a recession has arrived with a negative shock , and the central bank is attempting a softer monetary policy. To do this , we cut the base rate from 3 % to 2%. For this rate cut to have the effect of a softening monetary policy, the reference rate of 2% must be lower than the nominal neutral rate. However, if the nominal neutral rate does not remain at the previous 3% and has fallen to 2% or less, then the rate cut will of course have no effect.  The trend of the source price of our country during this year is an example of this. During January to August of this year, source prices rose 0.8%. In the same period, 84 of the total 317 items saw a drop in price.  To explain this risk, a somewhat economic-theoretical discussion is inevitable and a bit reluctant, but it is so important that it now seems necessary to learn from the general public. This is where the decline in expected inflation comes into play. This is because if expected inflation falls, the effect of a decline in nominal neutral interest rates occurs. Today, many economists cite deflation as the greatest risk because if expected inflation falls to a negative rather than deflation itself , the likelihood of incapacitating interest rate policy is very high. In the preceding example, if the real neutral rate is 1% (or less than 1%) and the expected inflation is -1%, the nominal neutral rate will be 0% (or less than 0%). There is no way for the monetary bureau to pursue a policy of easing tariffs unless it deviates from traditional interest rate policy and opts for negative interest rates. In fact, this "risk of crippled monetary policy" is something economists have learned about the gravity of the Japanese economy, which has been mired in a long-term recession for the past 20 years. This was recently discussed by the Governor of the Central Bank of Japan, Kuroda, not anyone else, in a special lecture 3) of the IMF. In Kang's Righteousness, he asks why the Japanese economy fell into deflation and a long-term recession in the late '90s. Then we analyze it as follows: Inflation rates fall amid environmental changes in which real neutral interest rates fall rapidly; The Bank of Japan attempted to respond in 1999 with a zero interest rate (0%) policy, but the nominal neutral rate had already reached zero interest rate, so the easing effect of monetary policy was minimal; In the end, economic actors doubt the monetary authorities' policy commitment to maintaining adequate inflation and adhere to low expected inflation; Continuing a vicious cycle  etc. is the goal. In general, in an economy where real neutral interest rates are falling, when expected inflation falls to excessively low levels, interest rate policy becomes crippled, making it difficult to bring the economy back to equilibrium with a policy of conciliation when the economy is in a temporary recession. As such, the risk of enteric cough increases. When reweighting policy objectives As is well known, over the past few years, the Treasury has emphasized financial stability along with price stability. The two policy objectives are frequently in conflict. When you use the term in economics, it's in a 'trade-off'. When pursuing two goals in an alternative relationship at the same time, the optimal weight for each goal must be found in order to implement the optimal policy. The long-term persistence of low inflation rates below the target of 2% is not just a problem for our country. After the 2008 global financial crisis, many countries have a common experience  Haruhiko Kuroda (2019), Overcoming Def lation: Japans Experience and Challenges Ahead, Speech at the 2019 Michel Camdessus Central Banking Lecture, International Monetary Fund. is a global phenomenon. Therefore, preventing a fall in expected inflation is a challenge and a challenge that the central of the major countries has faced in common in recent years. Monetary policymakers in each country may have been enforcing interest rate policy in pursuit of the common goal of managing expected inflation, taking into account the peculiar circumstances of each country and finding weights that are believed to be optimal for their country. * Resources 3. See "Macroeconomic Conditions and Base Rates in Major Countries" Looking back, it is my personal assessment that the weight that our monetary commission has given to financial stability, represented by household debt, has been a little higher than that of other countries. So were the social demands, and so were the intentions of the gold barrel expressed in the resolutions, etc., so it would not be the prejudice of that individual. Naturally, the optimal weight in monetary policy depends on the situation. If not only is the risk of financial instability high, but financial health policies, which are more effective and preferential policy instruments, are not only difficult to prevent instability from rising to the level of risk, the relative weight of financial stability should increase. On the other hand, if there is a different situation than that, there will have to be a corresponding change in the policy posture. I think our economy is now in a time when we need a new situational awareness. Conclusion Let's wrap it up. I will conclude with the same conclusion as the last two conferences. The ultimate challenge of the inflation target system is to maintain confidence in monetary policy. It is the responsibility of the monetary policymaker under the inflation target to give the economic actor the belief that even if there is a divergence from a temporary shock, eventually the inflation rate will stabilize near the target of 2%. Even under the economic environment of high uncertainty, we will always ask ourselves whether the Financial and Monetary Commission is fulfilling its responsibilities and will work on the operation of policy. Thanks.
