Title: New Year Speech
text: Governor's New Year Speech January 3, 2011 Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea The following is an unofficial English translation of the Governor's New Year speech. Governors New Year Speech My dear friends and colleagues of the Bank of Korea, The past year in retrospect To all of us at the Bank of Korea, 2010 was the year when we resolved to open the next 60 years of our Banks history, upholding the first 60 years of tradition since its foundation. It was the year in which we united our efforts to establish a new profile for our central bank, reaching out to the world under the banner of a Global BOK on the basis of our time-honored history and culture. This last year, the whole world participated actively in the drive to overcome the global financial crisis, and we may interpret the worlds response to our achievements as the equivalent to giving us top class honors. 2010 was the year when we also elevated our nations prestige by successful staging of the historic G20 meetings. In bringing about all these achievements, I believe that the Bank of Korea faithfully performed the mission entrusted to it, and I should first like to compliment all members of the staff for their painstaking endeavors exerted over the course of the 1 year just gone by. Looking back on economic conditions at home and abroad over the past year, it was in short a year during which uncertainty ruled. We may well speak of the years most distinguishing feature as having been the great uncertainties surrounding us, more so than in other years, in carrying out policy and forecasting the future; for the post-crisis state of the economy constitutes a stride forward to a new economic paradigm, and not a return to the pre-crisis status quo. A recognition of this as the greatest economic crisis since the 1930s Great Depression has prevailed, and this sense of crisis was what has facilitated real-world accomplishment of a mission that had only been discussed in text books and never realistically achieved before, i.e. policy cooperation among countries worldwide. This may be taken as an extremely significant and historic development. In an economic environment exposed to the possibility of sudden changes both domestically and externally, such as a double dip recession in advanced economies starting with the United States, debt problems in the euro area and geopolitical risk 2 surrounding the Korean Peninsula following North Korean provocations, we cannot relax for even a moment. Nor can we be at all sure that the uncertainty shrouding the future environment will recede significantly from its present level. Our economy was the fastest in the world to recover from the crisis, and entered onto a normal track relatively early. This was ascribable to the harmonious cooperation achieved between economic agents and our policy authorities. I dont believe there is room for disagreement about the effectiveness of our epochal fiscal and financial policies, while we also had in place a national-level institutional setup in the form of the Emergency Economic Council. And on the external front, meanwhile, Korea, as the G20 Summit chair country, took the lead in ushering in a framework for cooperation among not just member countries but also international financial institutions (IFIs), a feat that we may regard as truly significant. And I take this as having constituted an invaluable opportunity for us to experience global trends first hand. 3 As the central bank established with the purpose of maintaining price stability through inflation targeting, the Bank of Korea has also devoted efforts to steps in the process of defusing inflationary pressures and normalizing interest rates  by raising the Base Rate, which had been held at 2% for 16 months, by a quarter of a percentage point in July and again in November, under the judgment that the trend of economic recovery had become more tangible and that inflationary pressures have been rising from the beginning of the second half of last year. As a result of our economic management, consumer price inflation last year exhibited a rate of 2.9%, below the 3% midpoint of our inflation target. Dear members of the Bank of Korea, Changes in the Domestic and External Environments this Year and the Banks New Roles It is said that the reason for reflecting on the past is to prepare for the future. Well, what changes do we expect to see unfolding before us? Amid greater intensification of global trends, Korea, having such a high degree of external 4 dependence, has no option but to scrutinize the external environment as its first priority. We have currently begun to hear various new expressions emerging, including talk of a two-speed global recovery, which sees the gap in recoveries between the advanced and emerging economies continuing or widening, and of a three-way split, envisioning divergent patterns of economic growth in the US, Europe and emerging markets including China. Without doubt we will see a range of situations different from the present developing before our eyes. When we were still dealing with the crisis, identifying the tasks required to overcome it, and the future course of action, was relatively simple. It would be fair to say that such a state of affairs was what made activation of a system of international cooperation possible. In a new environment, however, in which various new developments will arise, a corresponding set of new and appropriate plans will be called for. Our policy responses will therefore also have to be drawn from new plans, differing from those in the past. I would therefore say that swiftly seeking out a well-reasoned strategy that we may opt for is the first duty that this new age has imposed upon us. 5 Rectifying the imbalances in the global economy is a sine qua non for eliminating the causes behind the current global financial crisis, and at the same time for establishing in a stable manner the international economic order in the future. The key will be how effective a set of indicative guidelines for global rebalancing we may draw up in the next few months. Contributing to this process through active and enthusiastic participation is the second task laid upon us. Now, there is no doubt that exports contributed decisively in the course of our recovery from the economic crisis. At the same time, however, balanced development of all sectors of the economy, through the parallel growth of domestic demand and exports, is a medium- and long-term goal that we must pursue. We must concern ourselves with what kind of development model we need to design. It is no easy matter to bring about balanced growth, sustained among all sectors, under the precondition of maintenance of external equilibrium. And it is also time to deeply consider what role the central bank could play in this, which I believe constitutes the third of the tasks assigned to us. 6 Given the changes in both the domestic and the external environments, I would say that the challenges lying before us are so many that we can scarcely count them. It goes without saying that, as the central bank, we must conduct monetary policy with the Base Rate while placing our main focus on maintaining a sound trend of growth and on firmly anchoring the basis for price stability. Some examples of the tasks requiring action that now face us are as follow: analyzing various macroeconomic policy instruments for maintaining a balance between domestic demand and exports  narrow though the range is that we, as a small open economy, have to choose from; looking into the household debt issue, and devising plans for enhancing the competitiveness of our small and medium-sized enterprises, both of which issues must be resolved if we are to achieve sustained growth; scrutinizing the impacts that realignment of the international financial order may have on our financial structure and our capital and financial markets; and preparing suitable policy options in response, including macro-prudential policies. Since in reality none of the departments at our Bank are free from responsibilities in carrying out these tasks, I should say that 7 the situation calls for dedicated efforts from each and every member of our organization, in developing new duties in line with this transformation in our environment. It is clear that competitiveness in each department can be upgraded only if we seriously ponder the raison detre of each element of our organizational structure suitable to the changing tide, and respond appropriately to what we find. How long of an institutional memory do we have? Economic crises have generally led to crises in the field of economics as well. Economists and economic institutions have proven limited in their abilities recently, in that they failed to predict this unprecedented crisis, and were hard put to readily come up with policy options for dealing with it. And although central banks too are unable to escape this criticism, it is by no means an exaggeration to say that the biggest change since the global financial crisis has been in the central banks role and position. As the lender of last resort, the central bank could not but play a vital role in overcoming the crisis, and it is now called upon by society to continue in the future also to bear responsibility for the task of analyzing and 8 examining macro-prudential regulations and the policies associated with this role. Dear fellow members of the Bank of Korea, Restructuring our Organization and Changing our Ways of Thinking A new development plan for the Bank of Korea, worked on by our own task force on organizational restructuring over the last few months, will soon be presented to you for your opinions. diversity, flexibility and openness are the three fundamental pillars underpinning our organizational restructuring. We, who in fact are responsible for a variety of operations, cannot all uniformly work on the same things; nor should we be rigid. If we do so, and are closed-minded, is it not clear that there are limits on us in enhancing our competitiveness? I am convinced that it is the responsibility of the organization to recruit outstanding and talented individuals, and to continue to make them even more so, in such a way that the social demand for them is maintained. This I say in the same vein as the commitment I have already made to you 9 all, to pursue the objective of capacity building. To this end we will continue to promote on-the-job training with other central banks and IFIs, and expand opportunities for specialized in-house training by establishing our own Human Resources Development Institute. Our current human resource structure is a far departure from the common pyramidal form based on rank or seniority observed in most organizations, and in view of this it would be difficult to assign each member to the right post as desired. Under the constraints imposed by such a structural mismatch, however, I think it necessary that we seriously review which proposal among those for the deployment of human resources is most optimal. For example, being assigned to a managerial post implies assumption of administrative responsibilities; in my judgment, however, there are cases in which members of our staff do not wish to take on administrative burdens, but aspire rather to contribute as specialists. I believe it possible to design for staff, regardless of rank, various responsibilities that will contribute to boosting the reputation of our Bank while earning our societys respect. Would it not be at times 10 when our Bank retains many knowledgeable and experienced individuals, in terms of academic qualifications or experience, to advise on socially difficult issues that have emerged, that its social value is truly upheld? I look forward to all of your participation in finding such alternatives. One point that I should like to emphasize, with regard to the methodology for drawing up plans to meet these targets, is that in an organization such as our Bank, where working practices are established, there is a higher probability of success in opting for sequential and progressive change rather than change which is short-term and drastic. I hope that the abolishment of rigid job groups for starters, to thereby further extend the boundaries of our staffs thinking and action, will serve as a trigger for our reform efforts. It is also my judgment that true organizational change is brought about by placing greater emphasis on reform of the software than the hardware aspects. I would therefore like to try to maximize the effects of organizational change by making it our first priority to undertake various measures that can stir changes in our ways of thinking. And by granting each department autonomy and 11 freedom, so that it can select at will from among a wide range of systems befitting it, I anticipate that this organization will become even more dynamic and competitive. I am sorry to harp on this point, but we shall concentrate on putting into practice the principle that reforms are successful only to the extent that the initiative comes from within, i.e. on the parts of the members of the organization to be reformed. We shall continually proceed to embrace consistent change in a dignified manner. We shall also state clearly in advance what it is that we need to do this year, next year and the following year, and then see these objectives through in the order in which they are prioritized. Dear friends and colleagues of the Bank of Korea, Vision of the Bank of Korea as a Locus of Knowledge and Experience It bears repeating that the Bank of Korea played an important role, of which we may all be very proud, in overcoming the global financial crisis. In actual fact, the roles of central banks around the world are growing. Last year IFIs 12 including the Bank for International Settlements, the G20, the International Monetary Fund, the Financial Stability Board and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision all strove to draw up new international standards in a range of areas. And the reality is that the only organizations participating in all of the related meetings are the central banks. What other evidence speaks so clearly of the importance of central banks role in establishing international standards for overcoming the global financial crisis? When I said to you before that my dream is a Bank of Korea that never closes, I hope you took it, as an expression of my resolve to combine all of our efforts, because our Banks contribution in the current external environment is of monumental importance. It is said that the future belongs to those who dream it, but in order to dream we must have a vision that we may refer to as our dream. Hoisting a Global BOK as our banner, we have embarked on elevating the stature of our central bank  as one that measures up to the changes in the international order, that meets the calls upon it made by all economic agents, and at which all of our Bank staff can take pride in 13 working  and on formulating a vision befitting it. Since this is not a matter for any one individual, the opinions of many staff members are being sought in the course of our reorganization. I have at one point stressed the importance of the concept of glocalization, to imply that it is not just the staff at our headquarters but those posted in other areas of the country and abroad alike who must contribute to our Banks development. We must also appreciate that realizing this vision will entail a considerable degree of hardship; it is of course a law of nature that you can only put out as much as you put in. Over the past few months, desirable organizational changes have been observed on several fronts. Above all, since the on-the-job training of our Bank staff in foreign institutions was begun the spirit of our younger staff has risen considerably, and their efforts to join IFIs have been stepped up; I find these and other tangible results very gratifying to witness. In the treasure trove of human resource excellence that is the Bank of Korea, I look forward eagerly to a continual arrival of young professionals aspiring to 14 demonstrate their individual excellence. Another good example of this change I have found was in the reports completed last week by all departments on their operational plans for the coming year. Specifically, I believe it constitutes a giant step forward that each of the department heads voluntarily invited relevant counterparts from other departments to exchange opinions with them, marking a break from the silo thinking that characterized our previous organizational structure based on job groups, and to share information; that almost all departments were planning joint research work with IFIs; and that our Banks executives spontaneously presented their views on matters of concern to the bank as a whole. It certainly was not an occasion for reporting on everyday operations as had been the case in previous years, and I know great efforts must thus have been exerted, to develop and report on new operations. Competition is admittedly necessary for organizational development. But at the same time it is important to build a pleasant organizational culture, in which members encourage and lead one another so that no one gets left behind in this 15 rapidly changing world. And in order to not lag behind, from an individual standpoint we need to constantly reflect on whether our ways of thinking and behavior differ from in the past. We now live in an era that demands the wisdom to flexibly deal with changes in the external and domestic environments by steadily accumulating at all times new knowledge and experience, rather than thinking that there are eternal principles and theories while remaining trapped in the past. I believe the time has come for us to take to heart the intent of Keynes in his famous remarks such as Practical men, who believe themselves to be quite exempt from any intellectual influences, are usually the slaves of some defunct economist, and The difficulty lies not in the new ideas but in escaping from the old ones. For persons who settle for a familiar pattern of life, there are probably not all that many opportunities to grow. We must bear in mind that a new environment always makes things uncomfortable. A sixty-year cycle has passed since our Banks foundation, and a new cycle has already begun. I hope that the days ahead of us in this New Year will be full of hope. Let us 16 all step forward hand in hand so that this, the Year of the Rabbit, will go down in history as the year in which we drew together through sweat and effort to create a Global BOK, reaching far out to the world and into the future. I would like to wish to all fellow members of our Bank, working not only at our headquarters but also in our sixteen regional branches, five overseas representative offices and other locations, the very best of health, and to your families the greatest of happiness and good fortune at all times. Thank you. January 3, 2011 Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea 17

Title: New Year Speech
Subtitle: The following is an unofficial English translation of the Governors New Year Speech
text: Embargo: 15:00 December 30 New Year Speech January 2, 2012 Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea The following is an unofficial English translation of the Governors New Year Speech. Governors New Year Speech The first working day of the New Year has dawned, on which we take up our duties for 2012, the Year of the Dragon. We are gathered here together to look back over the year that has just passed, and to dedicate ourselves to what we must do in the year ahead. On this same day last year I unfurled the banner of a Global BOK, as the Bank of Koreas vision for its new leap forward from the foundation laid during the first 60 years of its proud history and tradition, and I presented to you three tasks that we had to tackle: overcoming the global financial crisis, participating actively in international policy coordination by way of bodies such as the G20 and the Basel Committee, and framing a stable development strategy for our national economy. I also recall anew emphasizing three principles for the future operation of our organizationdiversity, flexibility and openness. This last year has seen a host of changes both large and small, no whit less than any past years. I should like to first compliment all members of our staff for your painstaking endeavors in faithfully carrying out your responsibilities, even in the midst of a rapidly changing environment. A look at the international economic environment shows the global financial crisis to have become an obstacle to sustained growth and stability of the entire world economy, with the crisis spreading out across the euro area in the form of sovereign debt problems, and these global conditions pose a grave threat to stable growth of the Korean economy, whose external dependency has intensified further. On the domestic economic front, we now expect the GDP growth rate to remain in the upper 3% level in 2012, slightly below our original forecast. Inflation has in contrast hit the 4% upper bound tolerated by our inflation target, and so price stability has emerged more than ever before as an important matter of general public concern. Coupled with this, fresh geopolitical risks potentially harmful to our economy have emerged additionally, including those related to the recent crucial changes in the North Korean political situation. Within the Bank of Korea itself, meanwhile, as you all know well, we have experienced historic changes with the revision of the Bank of Korea Act. I venture to use the term historic not because it is essential to capture the emotions of all of us working in the central bank, but rather in the sense that the central banks contribution to the running of our economy could differ in the future from what it was in the past. To put it briefly, I would say that these changes were made possible by the demands of public expectations of a greater role of the central bank in overcoming the still-ongoing global financial crisis and in preventing future crises. Honoring the high aims of the public and holding to heart a resolve to carry out our greater responsibilities, I would like now to reflect on the past year and unveil our aspirations for the New Year while taking time to share with you my thoughts on how we should understand the economic realities confronting us at home and abroad, the profile that our central bank must cultivate to be able to contribute to the national economy, how our organization including not just the Head Office in Seoul but also our regional branches and 2 overseas representative offices must change to achieve these objectives, and what our staffs way of thinking and manner of activity should be. Looking back on the past year: broadening the scope of our work and fostering an active and progressive spirit Firstly, I encouraged you last year to pull together to qualitatively advance our work to a higher standard even as we diversify it. I said that only when we set ourselves lofty ideals, turning our sights outward and seeing the larger world, can we find the right vision, and I sought to repay the public trust by pressing for a Bank of Korea where the lights never go out (i.e. which is ever on the alert) so that we would be noted as the first country in the world to overcome the global financial crisis. I stressed in addition that we must not become buried under particular dogmas established by others in the past, in disregard of the distinctive characteristics of Korea, nor ever fall behind in understanding the changing global currents of the world today. I would say that the greatest change for us, above everything else that happened this past year, was the previously mentioned revision of the Bank of Korea Act that entered into force from December 17. The role of the Bank of Korea and the scope of its responsibilities have now been widened. This revision is in keeping with the global current and trend toward changing the functions of central banks around the globe, and its key feature is that going forward our central bank may also now play an active part in the search for measures to prevent financial crisis being discussed on the international stage, and in the efforts to reform financial regulations. We must now conduct our monetary policy while paying attention as well to financial stability, and periodically submit to the National Assembly the Financial Stability Report as a statutory report along with the Annual Report and the Monetary Policy Report. I expect these responsibilities to bring revolutionary changes in the Bank of Koreas discharge of its duties. One thing that I would like to emphasize in this regard is that the central bank must perform its duties while maintaining even closer mutual cooperation with the relevant government agencies and related financial authorities, as the responsibility for financial stability is a task that cannot be assumed by the central bank alone. Secondly, we have dispatched some ten or so members of our staff for medium- to longterm training at multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the BIS, and at prominent central banks with which we have close relationships, thereby nurturing experts competitive at the global level. At the same time, in efforts to keep pace with these overseas secondments on the home front as well, we have been regularly operating very intensive two-week global human resource development programs such as our Global Initiative Program, to which we invite world-renowned academics and staff from various central banks around the world. Apart from this, we are providing other training programs in a diverse range of fields, and I believe such endeavors to be contributing positively to the heightening of our staffs competitiveness 3 and cultivation of their overall capacity for analysis. Furthermore, the fact that we are now well equipped with the foundation for deep and wide ranging analysis of regional economic developments of the world economys G2thanks to the opening of our Shanghai Representative Office, which as a result gives us footholds now in Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong and enables us to closely analyze the economy of Greater Chinais a result of our attempts to achieve the objective of contributing through operation of the central bank to development of the national economy. Thirdly, it is my judgment that the productivity of our entire organization has been heightened with the renewal of the profiles and positioning of our regional branches and overseas representative offices, so that the entire staff is now mutually interlinked and conducts business in an organic manner. To meet the demands of the regions, which expect the central bank to contribute to development of their regional economies, our regional branches are becoming their mainstays in carrying out policy tasks under the joint responsibility of economic experts in each region, the officials in charge of the economic policy in the regional governments, and the related policy departments of our Banks Head Office, and are thereby presenting practicable alternatives. The fact that the heads of policy at some regional governments have already begun adopting policies suggested by the Bank of Korea is a very encouraging outcome. Our overseas representative offices, too, are in contrast with the past selecting tasks that are timely, and conducting more in-depth analysis. Apart from these outcomes, I would cite the introduction of the Macro-prudential Stability Levy on non-core foreign exchange liabilities, the expansion of the global financial safety net through our rapid conclusion of currency swap agreements with Japan and China, the Bank of Koreas assumption of the post of first member country chair of the Financial Stability Board (FSB) Regional Consultative Group for Asia, comprising 16 FSB member and non-member countries in the Asia Pacific region, and our simultaneous chairmanships of international consultative bodies such as the Executives Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks (EMEAP) and South East Asian Central Banks (SEACEN), as achievements that have made no small contribution to boosting not only our central banks own but also our nations prestige. But despite these many achievements and changes, the burden besieging our minds as a central bank employing inflation targeting is rooted in the fact that the rate of increase in the CPI last year reached the upper bound of the tolerance range. As a central bank, whose highest value is price stability, we are obliged at this time to analyze and assess again in great detail the various tools at our disposal and our efforts toward it. Surely, we have all seriously felt the importance of communicative efforts, to explain transparently and in detail to all economic agents the things which the central bank can and cannot do, and also about the policy instruments that monetary policy can mobilize in a rapidly changing global financial environment and their effects. I would say that, in managing the rise in the price level, even if monetary policy cannot realistically serve as a panacea, and even if we evaluate ourselves as 4 having done our best in our own way, we must with humble minds and attitudes engage in earnest examination as to what part of the criticism of us voiced by society we should embrace, make efforts to thoroughly check whether there were loose ends left undone, and determine in what areas we could do a little better after building on our skills. Understanding of the current economic situation: peak uncertainty due to confusion of the past, present and the future I should next like to stress the urgency of building a consensus on economic trends and our perception of reality to understand the external and domestic environment that we now confront. It is by no means an exaggeration to say that finding another time when the past, present and the future coexisted as they do right now is difficult. The insistence on solving problems relying on past knowledge and experience, the short-term remedies for the issues now being newly raised, and the efforts to establish a vision for the future and to present long-run solutions to the conflicts of interests we see between various classes are all entangled together, resulting in a state in which uncertainties concerning economic activities are at a maximum. When compared with this international economic and financial environment, our domestic situation is also not so very different. It has gotten to the point where we cannot even avoid outcomes where the various solutions to problems we attempt depending upon the angle from which the economic realities are viewedare in conflict. The fact of the matter is that, while global economic crises had previously followed a 10-year cycle, we now again see a crisis looming before us just three years after the last one, in the form of the euro area sovereign debt problems. It has reached the point where the expression we must learn the wisdom to live with crises does not sound awkward at all. Churchill left us the epigram If we open a quarrel between the past and the present, we shall find that we have lost the future. With the anxiety that knowledge and experience we possess could possibly have become useless, it is high time to place our priority on seeking forward-looking solutions. There are no differences in views on the point that the present crisis had its origin in systemic risk arising from the rapid progress of global trends. The fact that the financial regulatory reform being discussed under Basel III assumes interconnectedness and pro-cyclicality as the two key concepts for problem resolution going forward for the purpose of the stable management and soothing of systemic risk, proves that the global situation is actually the fundamental cause of the problems concerned. But more importantly, we must recognize that the absence of a global jurisdiction capable of responsibly handling global economic problems, despite the world economys having already become globalized, is acting as a decisive stumbling block to our devising of solutions to problems. The emphasis placed on international policy coordination through international consultative groups such as the G20 may also be interpreted as part of the drive to make up for this very lack of a global jurisdiction. The implication of all this for Korea, as an economy with an extremely high degree of external dependency, is that we cannot neglect for 5 even one moment efforts to understand the developments in international finance and economy, and that we must at the same time face squarely up to the reality that policies which do not properly take international trends into account will necessarily be very limited in their effectiveness. Taking into account the limitations for decision-making of a global environment in which a strong propensity for pursuit of local equilibria rather than a global equilibrium exists, what we should now be concerned about is, for the reasons I have just mentioned, appropriate establishment of proactive counter plans embracing our own position and strategy befitting the situation. The characteristics of local equilibria are that they are not stable, as they have tendencies toward being knife edge equilibria whereby in the event of even a weak external shock their resilience for returning to their original state will weaken, and a sustainable equilibrium can consequently not be maintained. The probability of experiencing an unpredictable state, shifting easily from one local equilibrium to another, becomes higher. It is also possible to have a state in which the coexistence of various types of multiple local equilibria persists. Rather than groping toward resolution of the euro areas economic problems by way of the local equilibria of member states, it would therefore be preferable to seek a global equilibrium on the back of worldwide efforts. Despite this, the current situation is one in which the tendency to discuss advanced economy-centered efforts to seek local equilibria as the major agenda for international cooperation still predominates. To cite a typical example, while it is the global liquidity and capital flows generated as a result of advanced economies pursuit of quantitative easing in the course of overcoming the financial crisis that is exercising such an enormous influence on the world economy, the discussions nowadays lean in reality toward analysis of uni-directional influencesarising from advanced economies mainly, and affecting the emerging ones. In fact, however, rather than analysis of such uni-directional influences I would say that analysis of their bi-directional influences, including the knock-on effects from emerging to advanced economies, is what is more important. Although global issues are in the current environment discussed in international fora under advanced economy leadership, we must see to it that the focus of future discussions is concentrated on seeking ways to achieve an overreaching global balance encompassing both advanced and emerging economies, participate more actively to this end in international policy cooperation and look for response strategies, and also take note of how decisively important it is to arm ourselves with the ability to develop and persuade others of the value of ideas that can produce outcomes coinciding with our own national interest. We must bear in mind that having a critical view of the current state of affairs amounts merely to identifying what the problems are, and that only when we possess the ability to present and to put forward alternative proposals in response, based on fresh ideas, will we be able to contribute to problem resolution. We must face up to the fact that, in the international arena, there is nobody to work for our interests but we ourselves. Because the responsibility for financial stability has now been conferred upon us, we must strive to identify and ward off systemic risks at the right moment, and to this end build a 6 model that can detect a looming crisis beforehand. And it goes without saying that if changes in international conditions or predictions of future shifts are not appropriately taken into account in our model analysis, it is then highly likely that the model we have constructed will end up being good for explaining past crises only. I have always stressed that a crisis foreseen is unlikely to materialize into a crisis, and even from this perspective there are concerns that models explaining past crises will be of little use in foretelling future ones. I would like to emphasize that if we are to forecast and prevent future crises our views cannot remain mired in the past or at home. Understanding the agenda being discussed internationally is just a necessary precondition, not a sufficient one, and only when a correct recognition of our unique situation is established will we be able to develop effective models. We must keep in mind that our countrys systems and policies that have brought us such spectacular development by way of condensed growth, unparalleled in the world, may be quite different from the universal types adopted in advanced and emerging economies. What kind of relationship would you think should exist between our economys distinctive economic legacy and environment and the role of the Bank of Korea? It is self-evident that carrying out the role of a central bank based on the experiences of other countries, while having overlooked the factors unique to us, will be of little effect. A New Profile for the Bank of Korea: the role of representing the nations economic attributes, and leading its stable development Based upon this perception of the realities of the domestic and international economic environment that I have explained so far, what kind of central bank must we move ahead to create? Only when we adopt universally-accepted values as our fundamental principles and operate based on them will we be recognized on the international stage, and only then will these efforts lay the foundation enabling Korea to leap forward and join the ranks of the advanced economies. What we must at the same time bear in mind, however, is that the central bank must be representative of our economy, and in a broader sense serve as a microcosm of our economy. Given the relatively small size of our economy our achievement of a one-trillion dollar trade volume this year is unprecedented in the world economy, and Koreas being the only country in Asia to have signed FTAs with both the EU and the US is also a characteristic unique to Korea. Considering how our economy enjoys such active exchanges with the world, it will only be when our central bank plays a commensurate role as well that it will be able to contribute to the setting of a harmonious balance between our real and financial sectors. And this point has many implications for the establishment of the future development strategy for our central bank, which we must put our heads together to formulate. The first challenge that we must figure out together is defining at manageable levels the details and scope of the policies for financial stability entrusted to us as our new responsibilities. To live up to this challenge, we must first restructure our organization swiftly 7 and appropriately. We all know there are many discussions now underway, in multilateral institutions and international fora, on systemic risk and on the details and instruments of macro-prudential policies, and that there are many related proposals under review. Over the several years ahead, during the transition from Basel II to Basel III, various policy tools for financial stability will be continuously developed. What is important in this regard is moving to create a highly flexible organization, capable of keeping a hand on the pulse of global trends and of adopting them. Instead of nurturing an organization based on conventional knowledge and outlook, which is therefore rigid, I believe managing that organization flexibly, so as to remain receptive to new changes, is desirable. Given its vast coverage, for example, and the judgment that it would be inappropriate for any one department alone to be in charge of publishing it, the Financial Stability Reportnow a focus of attention, and to which new responsibilities as a legally-mandated report have been assignedwill henceforth be published under the joint responsibility of several relevant departments, coordinated by a committee charged with organizing an inter-departmental network. The second task before us is that we should pay even closer attention to achieving our inflation target in 2012. More than half the rate of price increase last year was attributable to supply-side factors, and their pressures on prices are expected to weaken this year. Inflation expectations do remain high, however, and in this regard we must be sure we devise measures to anchor the basis for price stability. With the recent revision of the Bank of Korea Act, the monetary policy instruments available to us have now become more diverse, and we must solidify the theoretical groundwork for such new instruments, and strive to analyze their effects empirically. We must meanwhile take extra care to avoid stirring concerns about a neglect of price stability due to our newly-added responsibility for financial stability. But it would of course be unrealistic to seek measures to stabilize prices when financial stability is not achieved. Essentially, we must strive to find an effective policy mix, that will enable financial stability and price stability to complement each other. This explains why the central bank must play a central role in the conduct of macro-prudential policies. It is also the reason why, in most countries of the world, central banks cannot but assume responsibility for financial stability, even if only in part. It is needless to say that the independence of and confidence in the central bank are essential prerequisites if monetary policy is to be effective in securing price stability. I should say, however, that these two prerequisites are not numerical goals that can be presented in quantitative terms, but rather qualitative values that we must safeguard. The authority of the central bank is built on these two pillars of its independence and credibility, as I have mentioned, but we can also never forget that the essential condition for all of this is the recognition and respect of our competence that we must earn from the global community and domestic economic agents. And so I would like to stress once more that building up our capacities is the very first step toward fulfilling all of our objectives, and that nothing else can take its place. Lastly, the third task confronting us is the need to consistently and resolutely pursue internal restructuring of our central bank, to enable us to meet the growing expectations of us 8 by the public. It is by no means an easy feat to transform, in a short period of time, an organization with such a long history. For while organizational structures themselves can be changed quite easily, it takes a long time for the organizations staff to change. Last year, during my first year in office, I strove to expand the boundaries of our staffs thinking and action by abolishing job groups, and by setting up the Bank of Korea Academy, to nurture our human resource potential and improve the efficiency of our personnel management, and the Reserve Management Group, to provide the impetus for autonomous organizational management. While establishing this year a unit in charge of financial stability, I will at the same time focus on the setting up and reform of units comprising our banks infrastructure. The existence of a strong infrastructure leads to maximum work efficiency in any organization. This follows the same logic applicable to cars and paved roads, whereby even if everyone buys a car to reach his/her destination more quickly, unless others also pave the roads these purchases will be ineffective. Without roads, these cars will be not only useless, but more importantly a nuisance. In order for an organization to develop, the treatment and recognition of its staff working in road paving sections must be placed on a proper footing. And in my judgment we have been very negligent in this regard up until now. Infrastructure plays positive roles like a public good that generates externalities. How to measure and compensate for externalities has long been a difficult task for organization managers. However, we will all agree on thisthat if those driving the cars are in the organizations upper echelons, and those paving the roads in the lower ones, in other words if the staff who generate externalities are not treated appropriately, the organization can obviously not develop. Looked at in relative terms, the country is richer than the individual in advanced countries, while the reverse is true in underdeveloped countries. I believe that only when the Bank of Korea is modeled after its peers in advanced countries will its organization be long lasting and its members ultimately benefit. My focus of organizational management on capacity building, including the education and training of staff, is directly related to the generation of externalities. Investing steadily in education and training, and rewarding those with a dedication to developing the organization should be what personnel management and evaluation are based upon. If there are many people reaping benefits from an organization in excess of their own individual contributions to it, this indicates the prevalence of rent-seeking activities and that externalities are not appropriately rewarded. I hope you will all understand in this vein my efforts to establish a department in charge of communications, and to introduce a function for formulating strategies for the future vision of our entire bank. In order for an organization to develop, there must be an overflowing of new ideas within it, gushing out like a spring. Who are the ideas men and women in our organization? Where are the thinkers? The world is changing rapidly, and we must not be bound to our past. There is no hope when the young only follow in the footsteps of their seniors. Living on others ideas will lead to a life subordinate to others, one that can never be first class. We cannot expect those buried in collective thinking and behavior, rather than individual excellence, to ever come up with new ideas. Those who can create their own added value must comprise the majority. And you can never create your own value by just following 9 others orders. You should realize that only when the endless acquisition of knowledge, contemplation and agony become a way of life will you be superior to others and will you yourself as a result become the beneficiary of your efforts, because society will ultimately recognize their value. I hope that the year 2012 will be remembered as the first year we all began moving ahead with great devoted efforts till such time as society recognizes the value of your work at the central bank and your services come to be in demand in various walks of society even after your retirement from the BOK. From a historical perspective, I would like to remind you that in many organizations innovation has always been led by those on the periphery, and not at the center. I sincerely look forward to the nurturing of leadership that can drive our organizational change, and to the emergence of leaders in our regional branches and our departments that make up our foundation. Hoping that my next years New Year speech will be one of greater hope and more encouraging content, let us all during 2012the year of the Black Dragon that comes but once every 60 yearscarry in our hearts the magnificent spirit of a dragon soaring to the skies, and begin writing the new history of a resurgent Bank of Korea. I hope each of you will achieve great feats during the coming year, and wish the very best of fortune and happiness to all of you and your families. January 2, 2012 Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea 10

Title: 2022 Pan-Finance New Year's Greetings New Year's Address
text: 2022 Pan-Finance New Year's Greetings New Year's Address 2022, 1. 4, Bank of Korea Governor Lee Ju-yeol Dear financiers, Another year has come to an end amid the corona pandemic, and a new year has dawned. In 2022, I sincerely hope that we will all be able to restore our precious daily lives and that all our wishes will come true smoothly. Looking back, the past year has been a year of both hope and regret. As vaccinations began around the world and economies resumed, we were hopeful that we would be able to return to normal life. However, with the repeated emergence of new variants of the virus, we have not been able to get out of the long tunnel of COVID-19. Despite these difficult conditions, our economy has recovered faster than expected, but at the same time, concerns about polarization and inequality have increased. In the new year, I look forward to a year in which our economy will be completely free from the risks of the coronavirus and make further progress. However, there are many challenges and dangers to overcome. First of all, the spread of COVID variants is the biggest threat to economic recovery. In addition, there are growing concerns about external risks, such as increasing global inflationary pressures, the consequent normalization of monetary policy in major economies, and the possibility of slowing economic growth in People's Republic of China. After the pandemic, the structural weaknesses of our economy, such as debt accumulation and asset inequality, have intensified. The transition to the digital economy is difficult to fathom its direction and speed. In order for our economy to overcome these difficulties and move towards the 'next normal' ([approximation 0111131)' in the post-pandemic era, the role of finance is more important than ever. First of all, you need to make a thorough effort to manage risk. As the economic recovery continues, borrowers' ability to repay their debts will improve, but credit risks may widen in the process of monetary easing, especially for some households and the self-employed, who are facing excessive leverage and sluggish business conditions. In particular, in a situation of high external uncertainty, such internal vulnerabilities can act as a weak link in the financial system, so we need to keep a close eye on them and prepare for potential risks. Finance should also play a leading role in creating and developing new growth engines for our economy. Joseph Schumpeter emphasized that the dynamism of capitalism comes from the technological innovation of entrepreneurs, but for this to be realized, there must be an active supply of capital through finance. Finance as a catalyst for innovation and greenness in the post-pandemic era. We should take the lead in enhancing investment vitality in the high-tech industry that will lead the transition to a digital economy. In addition, along with the rapid progress of technological innovation, the convergence of digital technology is actively taking place in the financial industry. Ministry of Finance Inquiries It should be borne in mind that securing digital competitiveness is a prerequisite for future finance and an important task that is directly related to the establishment of a stable financial system. Dear financiers! The changes caused by Corona are unimaginably great, as the post-war period can be compared to a year (he (6 Nan 016 (G 01X) 113) and 'Show 1' (Se 61 0136336)', and the post-pandemic era will be a way to find a new balance, not a return to the past. 2022 is expected to be an important milestone year in the journey, and I hope that by preemptively responding to risk factors while constantly striving for financial innovation, we will be a reliable guide for our financiers on the unknown voyage towards the new era. The Bank of Korea will also do its best to create a stable macroeconomic environment so that your dedicated efforts can shine brighter. May 2022 be a year in which our financial industry and economy roar vigorously under the energy of the valiant tiger. I appreciate it.

As I have been working at the Bank of Korea for more than 40 years, I would like to share a few reminiscences based on my experience over the past eight years. First, let me begin by introducing each of the promises I made to myself when I took office as governor. I started my first job by reminding myself that the only basis for the existence of a central bank is the trust of the people. The trust of the people can only be gained through consistent and predictable policy operations. It is only when there is a record of words and deeds that are said and done that trust is built. Therefore, the starting point of the policy has always been communication with the market, and we have done our best to reduce the gap in perception with the market participants without missing the right time for policy decision-making. However, from the perspective of the market and the general public, it is still a matter of regret whether our communication was sufficient and whether trust was fully formed. We need to communicate based on insight into the current situation and future trends, because this is not as easy as it sounds. Let me elaborate a little more. Just as there has never been a time in the past when we have not experienced a period of upheaval, the past eight years have been marked by a series of high-profile events, both internally and externally. The Sewol ferry accident, the Mers crisis, Brexit, the U.S. It is difficult to predict how and to what extent the impact of individual events will ripple out, and it is not easy to predict in which direction the whole economy will be driven by the synergistic effect of a series of events.Russia Didn't the eminent economist John Kenneth Galbraith compare economic forecasting to astrology? Recently, banks in major economies have been criticized for their poor economic forecasts and inconsistent policies after the coronavirus crisis, which can also be attributed to high uncertainty. Nonetheless, I think we should accept the fact that public confidence determines the outcome of monetary policy. The difficulty of monetary policy was not only in the uncertainty of economic conditions. Since the global financial crisis, there has been a steady stream of opinions about the need for a fundamental reconsideration of economics (111). In fact, for most of the past eight years of my tenure, I have spent most of my time operating monetary policy in a new macroeconomic environment that is very unfamiliar to me, with a lot of experience and knowledge that I have not been able to receive. Despite the prolonged accommodative monetary policy after the global financial crisis, the world economy has not been able to get out of low growth and low inflation. It was enough to make me say that I needed to rewrite my textbook. These mysteries, which have not been easily solved, have become more complex and difficult higher-order equations during the Corona crisis. As financial imbalances such as the accumulation of household debt deepened and inflation that was thought to have disappeared after the financial crisis reappeared, we could not help but think about what is the desired policy framework for the stable growth of the economy. While preserving growth, there is a need for a silver bullet to control prices along with financial stability. But that's not all. Right now, our society is undergoing irreversible changes due to the acceleration of digitalization, and adapting to the new normal, which we do not yet know what form it will take, is a challenge that even central banks cannot avoid. I think that the Zamot economy is not a system that moves mechanically according to a certain formula, but rather a kind of ecological environment that continuously evolves according to changes in the structure of society and technological development. I think that only flexible thinking suitable for the changes of the times will be the solution to wisely solve the various difficulties in front of us. The extent to which the central bank's role should be reached was another matter of concern. Since financial stability was added to the legal responsibilities of Korean banks in the wake of the global financial crisis, there has been a growing interest in employment in recent years, and discussions have been underway on how this should be reflected in monetary policy operations. In addition, some voices are calling for the central bank's participation in quasi-fiscal activities. Others say central banks should also be concerned about polarization and inequality. Central banks' response to climate change risks is already taking shape through the development and implementation of policy measures. The more we try to use economic prescriptions to solve various social problems, the more expectations and dependence on central banks will increase. If there is a fundamental change in the structure of the economy or the environment, the role of the central bank may inevitably change. While preserving its original identity as an administration, the center should conduct in-depth research and discussion on how to establish its role in the future. As well as the operation of monetary policy, internal management was also a very important task for me. Thinking about how important a healthy organization is and what we need to do to build it has never left my mind. Although the business environment surrounding the organization is changing day by day, the timeless and unchanging management truth is the importance of the organization and its people. I focused on two tasks related to the operation of the organization: one was to increase productivity by eliminating inefficiencies in the existing personnel system and the way work was carried out, and the other was to strengthen the policy capacity of the central bank by enhancing the expertise of each won. Clearly, the results were not small. However, I don't think it was enough to bring about a change that employees could feel. As we can all agree on, it takes a lot of time and effort to change the culture and institutions of any organization. This is because the perceptions and practices of society as a whole are incorporated into it, and the values pursued by the organization and its members can sometimes be in conflict. There is an old saying that goes a thousand miles in a small step. Organizational reform requires decisiveness, but it also requires perseverance. After about two years of hard work by our staff , the organization. I have drawn a rough sketch of the personnel reform plan, and it is now up to the new governor and you to decide how to implement it in the future. I look forward to the Bank of Korea steadily advancing step by step as an excellent and healthy organization. Looking back, the past eight years have been a time when I tried to further strengthen the big tree of the Bank of Korea in my own way. We have made efforts to deepen the root of the people's trust by developing individual abilities and policy capabilities by developing policies predictably through won communication. I believe that all of you have worked together in this process and as a result, we have been able to faithfully fulfill our role as a central bank. Of course, the achievements of the Bank of Korea during my tenure are all on your shoulders. However, I am well aware that not all of my efforts have turned out to be as successful as I expected, and that the shortcomings are solely due to my shortcomings. I believe that the person who has been nominated to be the next governor is a wonderful man of outstanding character and great knowledge. I look forward to seeing the new Governor's rich experience, combined with your enthusiasm, see the Bank of Korea develop further. When I was sorting things out before leaving the office, I suddenly saw a book called "Beautiful Finish" by Monk Dharma Jung on the bookshelf. "Realizing that there was no other path for me than the path I walked, and affirming and thanking me that path has made me grow is a beautiful ending." Every moment of my 43 years at the Bank of Korea, which is my whole life, and the past 8 years with you as the Governor , will remain as a precious memory that I will never forget. Even if I leave the Bank of Korea, I will always be proud of you and will cherish a long-standing relationship with each and every one of you. I've been so grateful.

Title: Keynote Speech at the roundtable on East Asia's Regional Financial Safety Net
text: BANK OF KOREA Enhancing East Asia's regional financial safety net1 Keynote Speech by Chang Yong Rhee Governor of the Bank of Korea Roundtable on East Asia's Financial Safety Net 22 August 2022 Introduction Thank you, Governor Shamsiah. I am honored to participate in this roundtable on East Asia's regional financial safety net. And it is a great pleasure to see my old friends and colleagues again, though I dare not name everyone due to time constraints. We are living in a time of heightened uncertainty. After a decade of persistently low growth, low inflation, and low interest rates since the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), inflation is back and has soared to levels not seen in recent decades. Central banks in major economies are raising interest rates rapidly, causing unwelcomed spillovers into emerging economies such as capital flow volatility and currency depreciation. Fortunately, many East Asian economies have strengthened the financial safety net and adopted better macroeconomic policy frameworks following the Asian Financial Crisis (AFC) and the GFC. As a result, the present moment seems different from 1997 or the taper tantrum period, but we cannot be complacent. In this time of heightened uncertainty and market stress, Governor Shamsiah and BNM colleagues have shown very timely leadership in hosting a roundtable on this important topic. Assessment of multi-layered financial safety nets As the starting point of my remarks, I would like to briefly review the progress of the multi- layered financial safety nets since the painful experience of the AFC. The first layer is self- insurance, i.e., building up reserves; the second is Regional Financial Safety Nets (RFSNs) 1 The views expressed here are mine, and not necessarily those of the Bank of Korea or the Monetary Policy Board. I would like to thank Sungyup Chung, Hyosung Kwon and Jiwon Lee of the Bank of Korea for their comments and contributions. 1 such as the CMIM; and the third is Global Financial Safety Nets (GFSNs) including IMF lending facilities and Federal Reserve swap lines. Data clearly shows that the first line of defense provided by accumulated reserves has got much stronger in Asia. The level of FX reserves in the region has increased nearly tenfold since 1997, and the ratio to GDP rose to 23.5% in 2021 from 8.0% in 1997.2 So, this deserves a very strong A grade. In evaluating the RFSN, I would like to include the Asian Bond Market Initiative (ABMI) together with the CMIM and the AMRO as they were launched to address the same root causes of the AFC, i.e., how to resolve the double mismatch problem in Asia and improve recycling of Asias savings within the region. In last two decades, the CMIM has made significant progress such as doubling its lending capacity, introducing the CMIM Precautionary Line, increasing the IMF de-linked portion, and extending program maturities. Despite all the progress, however, no country has turned to this facility and its effectiveness has not yet been market-tested. In contrast, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), which was launched a decade later than the CMIM, has been actually used and has contributed to preventing several regional contagions.3 As for the ABMI, the size of regional local currency bond markets has increased more than four times since its launch.4 And there have been other tangible results too, including improved bond market liquidity.5 But the situation is still far from satisfactory. The development of local currency bond markets is very uneven across the region.6 And when it comes to recycling of regional savings, intra-regional debt securities investment remains small at around 12% while most FX reserves are still held in US dollars and euros (Arslanalp et al. 2022).7 2 For 9 countries (CN, ID, JP, KR, MY, PH, SG, TH, and VN). (Source: IMF) 3 The ESM and its predecessor, the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) have disbursed a total of 295 billion euros to five countries: Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Greece, and Cyprus (Source: ). 4 The size of LCY bonds increased from 7.8 trillion at the end of 2003 to 32.6 trillion at the end of the second quarter of 2022 (Source: AsianBondsOnline). 5 See ADB (2017). 6 China and Korea account for 90.0% of EM East Asia's outstanding LCY bonds as of the end of Q2 2022 (Source: AsianBondsOnline). 1 As of June 2021, ASEAN3 (including Hong Kong) accounted for only 11.7% of the cross-border debt securities investment assets of 8 regional countries (CN, ID, JP, KR, MY, PH, SG, and TH) (Source: IMF, Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey). 2 Therefore, I am afraid the progress of RFSNs in Asia hasnt earned a satisfactory grade. Lastly, the global financial safety nets provided by IMF facilities and the Feds swap lines have been greatly enhanced in last two decades. Above all, the nature of IMF programs has changed significantly to reflect the many criticisms about their handling of the AFC. The IMF also introduced several lending facilities to strengthen global safety nets such as the Short- term Liquidity Line (SLL) and a number of emergency lending facilities since the outbreak of the COVID crisis. Also, the Fed's temporary swap lines, which were extended to nine additional economies during the GFC and the COVID crisis, played a crucial role in stabilizing global financial markets. Therefore, I think this area deserves high marks, too. Toward a more accessible CMIM Whether or not you agree with my not-so-generous assessment of RFSNs in Asia, we are all here today to discuss how to improve them further. So, let me now share my views on what urgently needs to be done to make the CMIM at least as effective as the ESM in the near future. Transforming into an institutionalized fund First, it is necessary to convert the CMIMs operational design from the pledge-based system to an institutionalized fund with paid-in capital so that funding uncertainty can be reduced.8 I think the institutionalized fund nature of the ESM allowed it to provide financial assistance promptly by making its balance sheet separate from those of the member states. In contrast, the CMIMs financing through a network of FX reserves swaps comes with a significant political and economic burden, especially when financial stress is mounting in most economies in the region simultaneously due to a common shock. This fundamental weakness is one of the reasons the CMIM remains untapped since its inception and hence untested in the market, raising suspicion that pledges may not be honored promptly when a crisis starts (Rhee et al., 2013). The recent change in the IMFs FX reserve classification makes this issue more critical. According to the recent IMF policy change, disbursed bilateral swaps are no longer counted as FX reserves. Therefore, if bilateral swaps are disbursed under the current CMIM system, the FX reserves of swap-providing countries will be decreased and, as such, the incentive to 8 See Hyun and Paradise (2019, 2020) for discussions of the benefits from an institutionalized fund. 3 honor previous pledge will be reduced. Therefore, to make the CMIM effective, it is critical to transform it into a fund with paid-in capital and develop a proper institutional design so that its paid-in capital can be always regarded as a part of FX reserves. Prolonging the Maturity Second, we need to extend the maturity of the CMIM programs. Although the CMIMs original purpose is to respond to a liquidity problem, in many cases, illiquidity can easily develop into solvency problems, which require more time to resolve. Also, the short period of financing assurances reduces the incentive for member countries to turn to the CMIM. Recently, the CMIM has adjusted the maturity of their financial assurances and improved compatibility with IMF programs. However, given that the structure of the facility still requires annual rollovers, the borrowers financing remains uncertain. One of the factors that made the ESM successful is that its loan maturities have very long terms of 10 years or longer, reducing the borrowing countrys burden and uncertainty about the repayment schedule. Admittedly, it would be difficult for the CMIM to use very long-term maturities like the ESM, considering most Asian currencies are not internationalized and convertible unlike the euro, but we could at least consider adjusting the repayment period to those of the IMFs Stand-By Arrangement or Extended Fund Facility. Strengthening AMROs capacity Lastly, for the institutionalized CMIM to be more effective, I hope AMRO is able to play a bigger role in providing first-class policy recommendations and independent and alternative views on Asia with a regional perspective distinct from other global international organizations. If AMRO did not have independent and sufficient surveillance and program design capacities, it might be a more efficient option to rely on global organizations such as the IMF, without having a separate regional safety net. So, I believe well-functioning, professional, highly respected and capable AMRO is a pre-requisite to the success of the CMIM. New opportunities The Asian Financial Crisis in 1997 was a wake-up call for us to understand the importance of developing regional safety nets and enhancing recycling of Asian savings. I believe the recent advance of IT technology and the growing interest in improving cross-border payment systems and developing CBDCs provide another great opportunity for us to redouble our efforts. 4 For example, studies on payment innovations such as Project mBridge, Project Dunbar, and Project Nexus led by Hong Kong, Singapore, and other Asian economies together with the BIS Innovation Hub are proceeding briskly. In addition, Asia is no longer in a position of catching up in blockchain technologies but is now at the forefront of research in this area. Such innovations in cross-border payments could serve as a catalyst in promoting regional capital markets. More specifically, local currency bonds can be settled on a Delivery versus Payment (DvP) basis using local currency CBDCs, lowering cross-border and cross-currency transaction costs and risks, not to mention the third time zone problem.9 And using distributed ledger technology (DLT) may make it possible to settle cross-border securities transactions without relying on global custodian banks and securities depositories. Such changes will allow us to overcome many legal and political issues as well as the insufficient market infrastructure which have been major obstacles to regional capital market development. For several decades, Asia has been the engine of global growth in real activity, but not in financial markets. If we make good use of technological innovation, it will help to develop our regional financial markets much faster and enable Asia to remain the growth engine of the global economy going forward. Conclusion Today, I talked about the multi-layered safety nets to guard against financial crisis in the region. But, before concluding my remarks, let me emphasize that while these safety nets are an insurance mechanism to protect us, the best way to prevent such a crisis is to secure sound macroeconomic management with strong financial supervision and regulation. And although I wish I could have given better grades to the CMIM, AMRO and the ABMI today, please take my assessment as encouragement. I hope that we can work harder together to make Asia regional safety nets more effective and stronger in the future. My best wishes for very productive roundtable today.
