Title: Keynote Address at the IMF STI Peer-Learning Webinar
text: BANK OF KOREA Central bank digital currency: what we have learned from a recent hands-on experiment1 Keynote Address by Chang Yong Rhee Governor of the Bank of Korea IMF STI Peer-Learning Webinar 28 September 2022 Introduction I would like to thank Director Schipke and the IMF-STI for hosting this webinar series and inviting me to speak here today. It is also great to see Governor Talukder and my old colleagues at the Fund Deputy Managing Director Sayeh, Ann-Marie, Raul and others. Today I would like to speak about the recent CBDC experiment at the Bank of Korea. Supported by accelerated digitalization and technological innovation, the landscape for payment and settlement systems has been changing rapidly. And this has led interest in central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) to grow considerably. Currently, 105 countries are exploring CBDC issuance.2 What is noteworthy is that nine emerging market economies including the Bahamas have already made an official launch of their CBDC, while central banks in major economies are still at the stage of laying the groundwork for their own digital currency. CBDCs could promote financial inclusion by serving as a gateway to wider access to financial services. This explains why CBDCs are issued first in emerging market economies. And we have come together today to discuss fintech and financial inclusion particularly through the strategy and efforts of Bangladesh. As for Korea, however, financial inclusion is not a key factor for considering potentially issuing a CBDC, as bank account penetration is almost 100% and various digital payment services are already well-developed. Rather, a top policy goal of our CBDC research is to prepare for changes in the payments landscape driven by digital 1 The views expressed here are mine, and not necessarily those of the Bank of Korea or the Monetary Policy Board. I would like to thank Dongsup Kim and Hyosung Kwon of the Bank of Korea for their comments and contributions. 2 Atlantic Council (2022). 1 transformation and the growing presence of big techs in financial services. In this regard, my speech might not be directly related to todays topic but please understand that our experience of developing CBDCs is highly relevant for the entire seminar series. In particular, the Bank of Korea has recently completed its first experiment which lasted for ten months on a retail CBDC based on distributed ledger technology (DLT). We are now working on a follow-up experiment linking our test system to those of commercial banks and also reviewing additional design options for a CBDC. We have learned a lot during the hands-on experiment and I would like to share four lessons from it with you today. Lessons learned from the CBDC experiment First, introducing a CBDC involves not just developing technology but also a process of balancing trade-offs between various goals. We have realized that there is no such thing as perfect technology or CBDC designs that can satisfy all the various goals and expectations at the same time. Lets take design choices between a centralized versus decentralized ledger system, for example. Our test system was designed based on DLT which is decentralized and has been referred to as a revolutionary innovation. Since we dont have any urgent need to introduce a CBDC, we thought it would be better to test such a disruptive technology. In particular, DLT has a significant potential in a token economy with a more decentralized internet (called "Web3") and in the metaverse economy. However, immediately the trade-off between innovation and stability kicks in. During the experiment we found that DLT still has not overcome the limitations of scalability to support a retail CBDC in the Korean economy. So, if the primary use case of a CBDC is for day-to-day payments to online and offline merchants, without further technical advancements of DLT, we may be better to use the standard centralized ledger database. Another example is the trade-off between privacy and compliance. At the earlier stage of our experiment, we considered allowing holders of small amount of CBDC to own unhosted or non-custodial wallets, so that they can send and receive CBDC with a high degree of anonymity and privacy.3 However, we found that it would become almost 3 An unhosted wallet is a digital account that is not hosted by a third-party financial institution, which allows the 2 impossible to carry out certain functionalities such as freezing wallets in the event of court orders. So, in our design for the experiment we chose to improve compliance at the sacrifice of privacy. Inevitably, designing a CBDC involves a continuous process of compromise. Therefore, it is important to put more effort to forge a consensus on the appropriate design of a CBDC by actively communicating with various stakeholders, such as the legislature, the government, financial institutions, and the public from the early stage of research. Second, developing a successful CBDC is much more complex than anticipated. There are two opposing risks regarding the success of CBDCs: being too successful and crowding out private payment solutions, or being not successful enough and generating insufficient demand.4 In fact, as the experiment progressed, our concerns grew larger on the latter risk. Since we, as a central bank, have little experience in providing retail payment services, it is not easy for us to provide services convenient and innovative enough to satisfy consumers in the way that fintech players do. Concerns about reputational risk could also make us more cautious about providing innovative functions. In addition, with there being no solid use case for CBDCs yet, we cannot give incentives such as bonus rewards that credit cards or other private payment service providers offer to customers. In this respect, if retail usage is the first criterion of the success of a CBDC, it would be difficult for us to meet. Therefore, for the success of a retail CBDC we need to ramp up our efforts for convenience, versatility, and incentives from the end-users perspective. And more importantly, we need to make people understand that building technological infrastructure for a retail CBDC is necessary to prepare for future changes such as the rise of the metaverse. Third, it may never be too early to establish effective private-public partnerships for CBDCs. There is a consensus that collaboration with the private sector is prerequisite to the success of a CBDC. However, the devil is in the details, and it could be very tough to figure out exactly how such cooperation or division of roles should be performed. account-holder (the user) to store, send, and receive cryptocurrency. 4 See Panetta (2022). 3 At the Bank of Korea, we are currently conducting a follow up experiment jointly with more than a dozen commercial banks to link with our test system under a virtual environment. They have been willingly and gratefully cooperating with keen interest, even though no final decisions on the launch or the design have yet been made. These private participants have to carry out a lot of tasks including provision of customer services and compliance with regulations like the Know Your Customer (KYC) rule, and transaction approvals under a DLT model, even if the CBDC business model is not clear. When we approach the final phase and see more developments, it is more likely that we could face difficulties in establishing right governance for the sharing of authority, responsibility, and costs. Therefore, I believe that it is better to start collaboration with private partners earlier on to enhance mutual understanding and reach consensus on a desirable way of dividing roles. Lastly, further exploration of wholesale CBDCs is essential. After finding several obstacles to the success of a retail CBDC such as a lack of solid use case in an economy with a well-functioning financial system and limitations of the current state of DLT to support a retail CBDC, we have found it is warranted to devote more effort to developing a wholesale CBDC and combining it with a retail CBDC. Various studies have been conducted on wholesale CBDCs based on DLT in the region that aim primarily at improving efficiency of securities settlement and cross-border payments. For example, studies on payment innovations such as the mBridge and Dunbar projects led by several Asian economies together with the BIS Innovation Hub are proceeding briskly. The Bank of Korea also plans to participate in a project led by the BIS Innovation Hub to improve cross-border payments. Some people suggest an ideal division of roles would be that central banks issue a wholesale CBDC and the private players offer their own stablecoins fully backed by the CBDC.5 Such a private-public partnership model could lower the costs of issuing a CBDC and take advantage of capabilities of the private sector in terms of technology and marketing. For such a model to work effectively, however, it is important that central banks should attain the authority and capacity to supervise and monitor private money issuers. Conclusion Let me conclude. 5 See Adrian and Mancini-Griffoli (2019) and Auer and Bohme (2021). 4 The Bank of Korea will step up its CBDC-related efforts going forward, but no final decision has been made as to whether to issue a CBDC. We will make a careful assessment while considering the results of follow-up research. I think it is still a good idea to proceed cautiously, even in deciding the design and operation, not to mention the actual introduction of a CBDC. Many central banks around the world are still reviewing various designs and operation models without making a final decision. Against this backdrop, we need to consider the risk that a front runners design could end up being out of sync with global standards, as in the case of the videotape format war between Betamax and VHS in the 1980s, rather than enjoying the first mover advantage. In this regard, further international cooperation is required to set global standards and ensure interoperability of CBDCs. It is also necessary to conduct more extensive studies on potential risks caused by a CBDC such as disintermediation and digital runs, and impacts on the transmission channels of monetary policy. In closing, another reason I have taken interest in CBDC personally is that I think CBDC could serve as a golden opportunity to strengthen regional financial cooperation. CBDCs could contribute to integrating global and Asian financial markets and act as a catalyst in developing regional capital markets, by improving efficiency in cross-border payments. More specifically, local currency bonds can be settled on a Delivery versus Payment (DvP) basis using local currency CBDCs, lowering cross-border and cross-currency transaction costs and risks, not to mention alleviating the third time zone problem.6 And using distributed ledger technology (DLT) may make it possible to settle cross-border securities transactions without relying on global custodian banks and securities depositories. Such changes will allow us to overcome the many legal and political issues as well as the insufficient market infrastructure which have been major obstacles to regional capital market development. For several decades, Asia has been the engine of global growth in real activity, but not in financial markets. If we make good use of technological innovation, it will help to develop our regional financial markets much faster and enable Asia to keep its place as the growth engine of the global economy going forward, while promoting payment system stability, financial inclusion and enhancing cross-border payments. Thank you very much. 6 For the third time zone problem, see Park and Rhee (2006). 5 References Adrian, Tobias, and Tommaso Mancini-Griffoli. 2019. The rise of digital money. Title: Speech Commemorating the Bank's 73rd Anniversary
text: BANK OF KOREA Speech Commemorating the Banks 73rd Anniversary 12 June 2023 RHEE, Chang Yong Governor Bank of Korea I would like to thank Byungkuk Kim and Moonsun Bae for their help in preparing this speech. (This is an unofficial translation of the original speech released on 12 June 2023.) Dear fellow members of the Bank of Korea, Today marks the 73rd anniversary of the establishment of the Bank of Korea. I wish to express my sincere gratitude to our predecessors. They devoted themselves to the growth of the Bank of Korea and to our economic development. I would also like to thank the members of the Monetary Policy Board for their ongoing efforts on behalf of the national economy, as well as the staff across all departments, including policy, management and field operations, for their hard work in their respective roles. Additionally, I also extend my appreciation to the families who have consistently supported our staff behind the scenes. The anniversary of our founding carries great significance every year. However, it feels even more meaningful this time as it marks the first time for us to return to our newly renovated headquarters after six years. Just two weeks ago, the Bank of Korea hosted the BOK International Conference 2023 in this very building. It was great that the Bank was able to cut down on expenses by utilizing our own Conference Hall. I was even more pleased to hear congratulatory remarks from many esteemed guests, saying that our new building might be unrivaled internationally. There is more. Like the famous saying, We shape our buildings. Thereafter, they shape us. suggests, our staff can now communicate freely and creatively not only in their offices, but also in various open spaces, including the central lobby, 2nd-floor lounge, 4th-floor break area, and library. Once again, I would like to convey my genuine appreciation to everyone involved in this renovation project, including our staff in the relevant departments, such as the Renovation Project Office and the Office of Property Management, for faithfully fulfilling their duties despite numerous challenges during the construction period. In particular, I have observed a significant increase in the workload related to security and property management in the new building. I want to acknowledge and thank the security and maintenance staff in charge. Moving on, as this is the anniversary of our founding after a year as the Governor, it is a time to reflect on the past year. We have worked tirelessly together to navigate the challenging economic situations. Amid rapidly rising inflation in major economies, Koreas consumer price inflation also rose to as high as 6.3% last July. The Bank of Korea responded 1/8 swiftly to this by raising the Base Rate to 3.5%, and, fortunately, inflation came down to 3.3% last month. However, since core inflation, an indicator of underlying inflation trends, has been moderating at a slower pace, it is premature for us to lower our vigilance. Therefore, we should conduct our policy more elaborately in overall consideration of downside risks to growth, financial stability risks, and monetary policy changes in major economies, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, while closely monitoring the pace of slowdown in consumer price inflation going forward.1 As you may well recall, amid the U.S. Federal Reserves acceleration of its stance of monetary policy tightening in the second half of last year, the Korean won to U.S. dollar exchange rate surged. And then to make matters worse, the default of a Legoland developer occurred on top of that, deepening the stress in domestic financial and foreign exchange market. In response, the Bank of Korea, in close policy coordination with the government and supervisory authorities, actively strove to stabilize markets and played a crucial role in overcoming the crisis.2 In the process, the sound banking sector played an important part as the bedrock of support. Although the sluggish housing market has shown signs of an easing recently, it is still necessary to remain attentive to risks in the financial sector, as the delinquency rates of real estate loans rose. Over the medium- to long-term horizon, we will have to explore avenues to carry out modest deleveraging of household debt through cooperation with relevant government agencies to prevent further buildup of financial imbalances. We have witnessed considerable changes in internal management as well. We swiftly implemented a plan to innovate our organization and HR management, which had been drawn up through a series of discussions. We also began to make efforts to improve our organizational culture, by, for example, spreading a culture of debate and expanding the sharing of information. Thanks to everyones participation, I believe that, we are seeing 1 For details, see Key Risk Factors in the Conditions of Medium-term Policy Operations (Bank of Korea Blog, May 2023, only in Korean). 2 For details, see  I -4. Financial and Foreign Exchange Markets in the Monetary Policy Report (Bank of Korea, December 2022); and Increasing Risks in the Financial Sector in the Monetary Policy Report (Bank of Korea, June 2023). 2/8 positive changes in becoming the vibrant Bank of Korea, from the image of us being the temple-like Bank of Korea. I am grateful that more reports on major economic issues have been published externally, and that staff at our regional branches are actively engaging as ambassadors for the Bank. However, it is also true that there have been no visible outcomes concerning the wage issue, delegation of authority, or our work diet. As these issues require more time to resolve, we need to make continuous efforts toward improvement. The past one year has been challenging, but it seems that the next one will not be any easier. In particular, the Banks genuine capability will face a crucial test. Over the past one year, most central banks, including the Bank of Korea, rapidly raised their policy rates due to high inflation, and there was a consensus among our citizens that price stability was the top priority. However, it is highly likely that inflationary trends and economic conditions will vary from country to country this year. This means that a sophisticated policy response has become more important considering the trade-off between prices and growth, and the true capabilities of central banks in each country will be clearly revealed in this process. This also applies to our organizational management. Without tangible results, there will only be disappointment surrounding our organizational innovation. Now is the time to intensify our endeavors to achieve concrete outcomes so that there will be no complaints that our management is all talk and no action. Dear fellow members of the Bank of Korea, For the Bank of Korea to make progressive changes in both policy and internal management, a shift in mindset is required. This is because the environment surrounding us is changing rapidly. The overall economy is experiencing significant changes, affected by not only internal factors, such as low birth rate and aging population, but also by the new normal after the pandemic, fragmentation of the global economy, a deepening of geopolitical conflict, and the proliferation of innovative IT, such as artificial intelligence. Rather than sticking to our past successes, we need to be prepared to make bold changes that align with this new landscape. 3/8 For instance, the primary target for our policy has been banks. In the Bank of Korea Act, the phrase financial institutions refers to banks only. However, the share of deposits at non- bank financial institutions already surpassed that at banks in the early 2000s, and their settlement via BOK-Wire has grown continuously. Transactions between banks and non- banks have also increased, leading to greater interconnectedness among them. Given the increasing importance of non-banks and the complexity of the system, relying solely on addressing banks poses challenges in achieving our financial stability goal for the overall economy. We cannot turn a blind eye to this issue just because we do not have supervisory authority over non-banks. We must come up with a way to achieve financial stability by further strengthening policy coordination with other supervisory authorities, or even by reforming the system itself, if necessary. Another example would be the effectiveness of liquidity management. As the persistent current account surplus has continued to provide a large volume of liquidity from the external sector to the Korean economy,, the Bank of Koreas liquidity management has centered on absorbing this liquidity. However, it is time for us to prepare for potential changes in our current account balance and in what are adequate amounts of liquidity, as a result of the changing economic structure at home and abroad. In this regard, we need to break away from focusing on liquidity absorption and improve our management system to ensure flexible liquidity provision in peacetimes as well. At the same time, as shown in the recent collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, the development of mobile banking and other information technologies has also enabled rapid movements of massive amounts of funds between institutions, thereby accelerating the speed of stress propagation. In order to better respond to this evolving environment, we need to consider augmenting our policy tools for immediate use when a stress is detected, such as new lending facilities. We should also work out a way to use rapidly-developing IT and apply software like ChatGPT to our jobs to improve the efficiency of our daily tasks. This year, particularly, in line with the latest trends in payment and settlement innovation, we will focus on getting ourselves fully ready for the shift of our retail payment system to a real-time gross settlement 4/8 (RTGS) method and for the launch of a central bank digital currency (CBDC).3 We must also change the way we conduct our internal management in an effort to adapt to the structural changes of the environment that I mentioned earlier. Over the past several decades, the Bank of Korea has been able to attract top-tier talent quite easily. As the private sector has developed rapidly, however, competition to secure talent has now become more intense. That is why our salaries and benefits should be stepped up to a competitive level. Furthermore, the focus of our personnel policy should also be on developing incoming employees into top-notch experts, going beyond efforts to recruit high-fliers. The days when a prestigious university degree alone certifies your excellence has now come to an end. Given the fast-evolving nature of work-related knowledge, we all need to strive to improve ourselves and develop expertise, while the Bank needs to provide you with its full support. It is time for us to focus our endeavors on replacing the outdated belief, that only exceptional talent can get into the Bank of Korea, with a new perspective, where anyone with a decade of experience at the Bank of Korea will be worth scouting by headhunters. In order to achieve this, it is necessary to delegate job authority effectively, empowering individuals to take responsibility and make key decisions even at lower levels. Also, we need to break away from the existing framework, where authority and responsibility were concentrated in a few hands and where only the Governor represented the Bank of Korea. Sharing information across the bank is crucial to prevent any monopolization of information within our organization. Furthermore, when engaging in external communication, each one of us needs to embody our role as representatives of the BOK and as experts in our respective fields. I will support these changes by reinforcing our human resources and performance evaluation systems, to ensure that employees who take the lead in driving these changes receive appropriate rewards and recognition for their contributions. 3 For details, see HI. Future Policy Directions in the Payment and Settlement Systems Report 2022 (Bank of Korea, April 2023). 5/8 Dear members of the Bank of Korea, I want to highlight once again that the upcoming year will be a crucial period that requires changes in both policy decisions and in our own organizational management more than ever. Given the diverse economic conditions prevailing across countries, it is imperative for us to conduct a more sophisticated policy operation to promote the stability of the Korean economy. At the same time, we must actively perform our role as a government policy advisor, contributing to the medium- to long-term direction of the Korean economy. Also, in terms of organizational management, our focus should be on ensuring that our staff can tangibly experience the benefits of a more rewarding and fulfilling work life. As the old saying goes, we should create the new by learning from the old. Lets build upon the achievements of our predecessors and create a new tradition to elevate the status of the Bank of Korea. I specifically would like to encourage our younger employees to be at the forefront of this transformation. Ive heard that these days younger people often ask, Why? or, Me? or, Now? when assigned a task. Here at the BOK, I hope that our younger employees will feel more confident and proactive in asking such questions to their superiors. If they were to ask me these questions, my answers would be something like this. Why? Because we need to change. Me? Yes, you, because you are the very generation that feels the need to change the most. Now? Absolutely, because if not, we will be left behind. As I have repeatedly emphasized, this is that everyone can express their own views regardless of seniority. I encourage you to move away from the mindset of merely accepting instructions from your senior officials, even when it is challenging to agree with them, and to step forward actively to bring about a change in this regard. Also, I would like to kindly remind our senior officials that they must recognize their duty to nurture future leaders and to cultivate an environment where younger employees can fearlessly question conventional practices. In order to learn from the past, to forge a new path forward, we need to combine the fresh ideas of our younger employees with the wisdom of our senior members. This year, let us work together to make the Bank of Korea a pioneer of change without compromising its core essence as the central bank of Korea. I will take the lead and spare no effort. 6/8 As we celebrate our 73rd anniversary, I would like to once again express my sincere appreciation to all of you for your hard work. I wish you and your family all the very best. Thank you. 12 June 2023 Governor RHEE, Chang Yong References Hong, K. S., & Choi, I. H. Title: Reform of the International Financial Architecture: A Way Forward
Subtitle: Governor's Opening Address at the 2011 BOK International Conference
text: Reform of the International Financial Architecture: A Way Forward Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea 2011 Annual Bank of Korea International Conference May 26-27, Seoul, Korea Good morning. Distinguished governors, scholars, and ladies and gentlemen, I welcome you all to the 7th annual international conference of the Bank of Korea. I should like to begin by expressing special thanks to Kiyohiko Nishimura, deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, for being with us today despite his difficult national situation. Taking this opportunity, I wish to convey once again our deep condolences and wholehearted support for the Japanese people, who have been facing the plight due to the earthquake with an unparalleled courage and national determination we have all admired. I am also very grateful to Professor Eichengreen and Professor Sargent, for their invaluable help in organizing this conference, and to all of our speakers and participants as well, who have made long journeys to contribute to the conference. This conference addresses the future of the international financial architecture, a topic that is of enormous complexity but also of paramount importance to all nations, and of particular relevance at this critical point in time. By now, the world economy appears to have pulled out of the Great Recession, albeit at speeds that differ between advanced and emerging 1 countries. Swift and active policy responses, at both the national and the international levels, have certainly played a central role in this regard, by limiting the scars from the global financial crisis that would have otherwise been much deeper and lasted longer. Despite some commendable successes in post-crisis policy response, however, it is also true that we witnessed a number of shortcomings in the international financial architecture, which had arguably nurtured unsustainable financial excesses and amplified the subsequent crash. And yet these shortcomings remain largely unresolved. Extensive research in academic and policy circles has fortunately helped us to better understand the nature of these shortcomings, and to identify a corresponding agenda for reform of the international financial architecture. Although these research findings are by now well known, let me touch briefly upon a few key issues, as this conference aims to explore new ideas and insights that can help shape the future of the international financial architecture. Global rebalancing The first of these issues is global rebalancing. I think broad consensus has been reached on how global imbalances, if they persist too long, can lead to or at least set the stage for a global crisis, in the form of an abrupt and disorderly correction. One strand of views suggests that the root causes of the global imbalances were a failure of monetary policy and a sustained 2 misalignment of exchange rates. Another view highlights structural factors, such as the gaps in financial development between the North and the South, which can be closed only gradually. Countries in the South, with abundant savings but insufficient safe domestic stores of value, have increasingly looked for safe assets in advanced markets. And the resulting uphill flows of capital have helped to finance large current account deficits in the North, at low cost. While it is still premature to make any accurate prediction of the future evolution of the global imbalances, it is evident that the three years since the global crisis are not long enough for major surplus and deficit countries to bring their external positions to normal. Some have even argued that the post-crisis world will remain subject to Triffins dilemma for a considerable time, until the emergence of a system of multiple reserve currencies. Under the current international financial setting, therefore, the global imbalances are likely to persist. And if this old problem finds no new and durable solution soon, the world economy may repeat its dangerous course to another global crisis. In this light, establishing a durable mechanism for global rebalancing is the urgent need of the day. At the international level, some notable progress was achieved last year at the G-20 summit hosted by Korea, where it was agreed to establish indicative guidelines for external imbalances as a trigger for peer pressure. Reform efforts at the national and regional levels are equally important, however. There are many good welfare reasons for the deficit countries to save more and put their public 3 finances in order, as well as for the surplus countries to spend more and reform their financial markets. Containing systemic risks The second issue I wish to bring up is that of containing systemic risks. Perhaps the most dramatic feature of the global crisis we have just experienced was the speed and range of the shock spillovers across markets and national borders. Financial markets collapsed one after another, with arbitrage virtually halted, triggering massive fire sales of assets and severe foreign exchange market disruptions. Many innocent bystanders, including Korea, fell victim to the shock wave and ensuing abrupt capital flow reversals. And there is no doubt that financial interconnectedness was at the center of all these events, enabling the transformation and amplification of isolated shocks into systemic risks. The policy lessons from this are clear. The framework of prudential regulation must be upgraded and, more importantly, augmented with effective macro-prudential measures to deal with spillovers and systemic risks. Along this line, a number of reform measures have been discussed internationally, ranging from new accounting and reporting standards to counter-cyclical capital requirements and liquidity coverage regulations. In parallel, the IMF has speculated on the merits of temporary controls on cross-border capital flows, in cases where prudential regulations are weak and macroeconomic tools have been exhausted. 4 The international discussions thus far have proven useful in identifying common areas of acute regulatory concern, but are yet to produce sufficient detail as to the design and implementation of specific macroprudential measures. There are many known unknowns in setting regulatory bars in such a way as to strike the right balance between efficiency and safety. More daunting tasks are to avoid unintended conflicts among individual measures, and to take adequate account of endogenous market responses in the form of regulatory arbitrage or regulation-driven portfolio shifts. In this regard, I expect our country's recent experience might usefully inform such discussions. Last year, Korea introduced two macroprudential measuresa bank levy on non-core foreign currency liabilities that will take effect from the second half of this year, and a cap on the FX derivatives position of banks that is already now in place. Both measures aim at addressing excessive risk-taking in foreign currency short-term debt, which was a key source of vulnerability during the global financial crisis. The results of these measures will be closely monitored going forward, and then shared with interested parties. There is also another important area of policy concern related to macroprudential regulation, namely governance structure. My reading of the new global trends points to the strengthened role of central banks in securing financial stability, and I see many good reasons for this. First, the strong linkages between the real and the financial sectors, as observed during the global crisis, imply that price stability can hardly be separated from 5 financial stability. Second, monetary policy matters for both price and financial stability but not always in the same direction. Third, central banks must have accurate information on banks balance sheets in order to perform their lender of last resort (LOLR) functions in times of crisis. And combining these three arguments brings us to the natural conclusion that the central bank must be part of the macro-prudential regulatory framework. Of course, the governance structure should be, and indeed is, countryspecific, in reflection of the diverse historical and institutional backgrounds of countries around the globe. But the above discussion suggests that, at minimum, the central bank must have full access to macro-prudential information whenever necessary by retaining the authority to undertake onsite inspections of financial institutions under its own initiative. Putting public finances in order Last but not least is the issue of disarray in public finances. At present, one of the most pressing issues for the global economy is the deteriorating fiscal sustainability of advanced economies. As we are all only too aware, public debt has profound implications for the financial markets, not to mention the real economy. In normal times, government bonds typically serve as default-free reference assets, against which private debt securities and derivatives are priced. In crisis times, the evolution of public debt or fiscal space is itself a crucial determinant of crisis dynamics. In this light, 6 putting public finances in order is a prerequisite for any well-functioning international financial architecture. In the aftermath of the global crisis, fiscal consolidation has been called for in many advanced countries, to put their public debt dynamics on sounder footings. In this context, several questions naturally follow: Should they try to live with high debt, or reduce it? How far and how fast should they act if they wish to reduce debt? Should they act in unison or individually? What mechanisms should they put in place to enforce orderly debt restructuring, if necessary? And in fact, these questions are more complex than standard economics suggests. Political incentives and irrational market sentiments often matter more for public debt dynamics than economic rationales, as we have seen from the still ongoing debt crisis in the Euro zone. Nevertheless, it would not be unreasonable to predict that a comfortable or safe level of public debt in advanced economies will generally be lower in the future than in the past, as financial markets will demand higher risk premium for tail risks. Population aging and fiscal fatigue, among others, would add further to this prediction. But maintaining a sufficiently low level of debt, albeit desirable for financial stability, may hamper financial development and intertemporal smoothing. In this respect, by reducing the likelihood of costly crisis, reform of the international financial architecture would help advanced countries to achieve better tradeoffs in their public finances. 7 Closing Remarks Addressing these issues is by no means a complete road to determining the future of the international financial architecture. But I hope it is a good starting point for our discussion. Reforming the international financial architecture demands new thinking, new institutions, and new policies that differ markedly from those that prevailed prior to the crisis. We are living in a world in which systemic risk in any one country invariably poses a global risk. Over the past three years or so, the international community has achieved notable progress in identifying the causes of the global crisis, and potential remedies to address remaining gaps in macroeconomic policies and prudential rules. But more challenges lie ahead of us. We will have to navigate through uncharted territory before we find better and more durable solutions. And only creative thinking and candid analysis will guide our way. I look forward to productive exchanges of views and exciting discussions throughout this conference. Thank you. 8

Title: Chile-Korea Economic Cooperation : Now and in the Future
text: Chile-Korea Economic Cooperation : Now and in the Future September 2005 Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - Content . History of Chile and Korea Interchange  1 . The Korean Economy: Its Development Process and Current Status  2 . Economic Cooperation between Chile and Korea  4 . Closing Remarks  9 . History of Chile and Korea Interchange I should like to begin by expressing my deep thanks to Governor Dr. Vittorio Corbo and all of those involved at the Central Bank of Chile, for so graciously inviting me here. Last April, when Dr. Corbo visited Korea, he and I shared a particularly warm time together. And now it is a deeply meaningful experience for me to be the first Governor of the Bank of Korea to visit the Central Bank of Chile. Most Koreans know Chile as a land famous for its flourishing cultural and artistic life, with a gem-like quality to its poetry and hauntingly beautiful music, in addition to its delicious wines. The Korean people, who also pride themselves on their historical culture, feel a deep affinity for the Chilean people, with their love of culture and the arts. Besides this, Chile was the first country in Latin America to recognize the newly established Republic of Korea after the Second World War, and was also very helpful to us during the Korean War. We always feel grateful to your country. Since the signing of our 1962 treaty, exchanges between Chile and Korea have steadily continued. And since the dawning of the 1990s, the growing importance of the Pacific Rim area has brought us closer together. Notably, after Chile and Korea concluded our free trade agreement last year, exchange and cooperation between our two nations has expanded greatly, not just in the economic sphere, but also in the technological and cultural areas. As such interchange deepens our mutual understanding and confidence, I am sure that it will provide a rich seedbed for the great opening of the Pacific era in the coming years. In this light, I would like to take some time today to think about some ways of increasing the economic cooperation between Chile and Korea. - 1 - II. The Korean Economy : Its Development Process and Current Status Before launching into a discussion of economic cooperation between Chile and Korea, to help you in your understanding I would like to briefly explain the past development process and current state of the Korean economy. One half century ago, Korea numbered among the poorest, most underdeveloped agricultural countries in the world. Today, however, Korea has achieved a successful advance to modernization during the span of just one generation, and has transformed itself into an open industrial country, exporting high technology products such as semiconductors, information technology equipment, computers, and liquid crystal displays. From 1960 to 2000, Korea's annual average rate of growth was 7.7%. No other country in the history of world economic development has achieved a record of such high growth continuing over such a long period. In 1960, our per capita national income stood at just 80 dollars a year, but in 1995 it topped 10 thousand dollars a year. For this year, it is estimated to rise to 17 thousand dollars. Nowadays, Korea has become a powerful economic country, ranking 11th in the world in terms of its economic scale, 12th in terms of its trade volume, and 4th in terms of its foreign reserves. This high rate of economic growth was for the most part achieved in an environment of low wages, excess domestic demand, high yields on investment, protectionism, and the latecomer's advantage that Korea had. This was what is called 'early stage growth' or 'growth through industrialization'. Nowadays, however, Korea has moved on to 'mature growth stage', where economic growth must be driven in a climate of high labor costs, flat demand, low returns on investment, and of course the loss of our latecomer's advantage. Especially, external structural changes are swiftly altering the Korean economy's growth environment, as we now face the rapid rises of large low-wage economic powers such as China and India. It may in fact be said that the reason Korea was hit by its currency crisis at the end of 1997 was its inability to adapt quickly enough to these kinds of environmental changes. - 2 - Today, in the face of such structural changes in its growth environment, the Korean economy is experiencing no small amount of hardships and difficulties. Our potential growth rate has dropped from its former level of 78% to 45%. At the same time, the polarization of the Korean economy has intensified. The gaps between the export sector and the domestic sector, and between large companies and small and medium-sized companies, have widened further. And while corporate profits have risen greatly, household incomes have remained flat. Meanwhile, many small and medium-sized enterprises and many labour-intensive industries have disappeared due to lost competitiveness, and our agricultural economy is deeply depressed. Additionally, a reluctance on the part of Korean businesses to invest domestically has also been growing. As our manufacturing competitiveness, especially in labour-intensive sectors, has weakened, production facilities are being moved to low-wage countries such as China. As a result, we are now experiencing the phenomenon of 'jobless growth' and a very high level of unemployment among our young people. Things are not only gloom and doom, however. Fresh and exciting opportunities are opening up for the Korean economy, as well. Over the last few years, first of all, the Korean economy has acquired a much sounder foundation. The soundness and transparency of our corporate management is now much improved. As one example, our overall corporate debt ratio fell from 400% in 1997 to just 104% in 2004. Considering that the average corporate debt ratio of American companies is around 140%, the financial structure of Korean businesses thus qualifies as very sound. In the financial aspect, stability of the Korean financial system has been greatly enhanced through a strengthening of its structure. The non-performing loan ratio of the domestic commercial banking sector has fallen from 14% at the end of 1999 to its current 2% level, while the average BIS capital ratio has risen steeply from 7% to 11%. - 3 - Secondly, the vigorous pursuit of industrial restructuring has enabled Korea's core industries to secure global competitiveness. Korea is now among the five leading producers worldwide in shipbuilding, semiconductors, digital household electronics, petrochemicals and steel. In the automobile and information technology sectors, as well, it possesses truly outstanding world-class technological competitiveness. At the same time, we are seeing rapid growth in the knowledge-based service sectors that will lead next-generation growth, which are said to include finance, communications, distribution, business services, culture and the arts. These knowledge-based service sectors are set to spearhead Korean economic growth in the 21st century. Throughout the course of its economic development, Korea has always shown a pattern of quick adaptation during periods of massive change. This can truly be referred to as the source of the Korean economy's dynamism. In view of this dynamism and the results of its adaptations to the recent changes in its growth environment, the Korean economy should be capable of sustaining a solid rate of growth at the 45% level, and achieve a successful soft landing into the mature economic development stage. This year, Korea's overall macroeconomic numbers have been sound, with GDP growth to come in at around 4%, consumer price inflation of 3%, a current account surplus of 13 billion US dollars, and total foreign exchange reserves of 206 billion US dollars. Moreover, corporate profits are expected to turn in another record performance, following that of last year. III. Economic Cooperation between Chile and Korea I would like to speak now concerning the status of economic cooperation between Chile and Korea, and look at ways of driving it forward. - 4 - (Common Historical Experience of Chile and Korea) As you may all be aware, Chile and Korea have experienced historically similar political and economic hardships. We also hold in common the experience of having overcome these hardships, through sturdy strength of will. Firstly, both Chile and Korea have undergone the painful experience of being occupied by great world powers. Both of our countries overcame this, however, through their burning desires for independence and their unswerving defiance. Following our colonial periods, both of our countries have achieved astonishing economic growth, by bringing to bear resolute determination for development on the basis of the high educational levels of our people and our traditions of integrity and intolerance of corruption in public servants. Additionally, Chile and Korea have certain similar dark and bitter historical memories, such as of military dictatorships that crushed human rights. At the time when Chile won back its democracy, Korea also entered into an age of genuine democracy, after a lengthy struggle. The people of our two countries are keenly alert now to the values of democracy, after their very severe hardships of the past. And by their strong commitments to conquering poverty and their resolute wills for advancement, they have achieved the political democracy and economic prosperity they now enjoy today. Our common experience inspires mutual confidence and friendship between us. This, I believe, will be one of the forces making for development of closer ties linking Chile and Korea as special companions within international society. (Chilean Economic Development) These days, the world calls Chile the rising star of Latin America. For almost 20 years, from 1985 to 2003, the Chilean economy achieved a high growth rate averaging around 6% per year. Last year it recorded low inflation and unemployment rates in the single digits, together with a substantial trade - 5 - account surplus. It seems to me that such achievements by Chile, a model for other Latin American economies, are the precious harvest reaped from the shrewdness of the country's leaders and the exertions of its people. Strikingly also, despite the high rate of Chilean economic growth, prices have maintained stable trends at an annual average level of 3% since the late 1990s. This would obviously have been impossible without the devoted efforts of all staff at the Central Bank of Chile. Even when facing difficult economic circumstances in the 1970s and 80s, Chile consistently pursued a market economy and policies of openness, so that the groundwork for its prosperity of today was laid. Boldly casting aside the protectionism pursued by most Latin American countries, and dynamically pursuing policies of openness, Chile was the second only to Mexico in the region to enter into free trade agreements. Moreover, in shifting toward a new digital economy nowadays, Chile has laid the foundation for its long-term national development in the 21st century. Consequently, Chile ranks first among Latin American countries in terms of Internet access and mobile phone penetration, and is second only to Brazil in terms of computers per person. All of this leaves me with no doubt that, continuing to make great strides in its development, Chile will also be at the forefront leading the dynamic Pacific era in the coming years. (Status of Economic Cooperation between Chile and Korea) Up until the 1980s, there had not been many opportunities for exchanges between Chile and Korea, because the cultural links between our two countries were weak and we were separated on either side of the vast Pacific Ocean. Since the early 1990s, however, in keeping with the globalization of the world economy and the gradually mounting mutual interests of our two countries, the cultural and economic exchanges between us have deepened. - 6 - Notably, since Korea and Chile entered into a free trade agreement in 2004, economic cooperation between us has truly increased by leaps and bounds. In the 14-month period from April of last year until June this year, the volume of trade between us grew by 62% to a total of 3.5 billion US dollars. What is more, the shares of our two countries' products in each other's markets are also rising sharply. For example, the Korean market share of Chilean wines has soared from 3% to 20% during the past one year alone. Accordingly, Korea has become Chile's fifth biggest export market, and Chile is now Korea's second largest trading partner in South America. (Directions for Improving the Cooperative Relationship in the Future) The world is now moving forward strongly into the Pacific era of the 21st-century. The Pacific region has recently shown more dynamic growth than any other area of the world. These days, the Pacific region has become one of the central axes of the world economy; massive new investment and production activities in our region have become extremely energetic, and we have come to account for more than one half of all world trade. Accordingly, for the sake of the common prosperity of the Pacific region, I believe our two countries need to work together to build still stronger amicable cooperative relations in the following ways: Firstly, on the basis of the mutual complementarity of our two nations, we need to cultivate mutually beneficial economic cooperation. If we combine our forces effectively, joining our strengths in resources, technology and capital, we can advance successfully in the world markets. Secondly, our two countries could cooperate closely as well in the areas of social overhead capital construction and natural resource development, which Chile is now ambitiously engaged in. I think that Korea's entry into the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) will serve as an effective firm - 7 - foundation enabling us to participate in this kind of development cooperation with Chile. Thirdly, we need to work together to promote free trade and increase economic openness to realize the promise of the 21st century Pacific era. Our two nations might at the same time act as strong bridgeheads supporting each other's entries into our respective regions, Asia and Latin America. Fourthly, Korea and Chile can pool their experiences of industrialization undertaken until now. Regarding this, the Korean government is actively planning to support projects aimed at reducing the digital divide between our two countries, taking advantage of Korea's experiences in rising from its past as a poor agricultural economy to become a global IT powerhouse. Meanwhile, the Bank of Korea intends to continue strengthening its financial cooperation with other central banks in Latin America, including the Central Bank of Chile. Based on what we learned while successfully overcoming the 1997 currency crisis, we are at the moment spearheading efforts to improve financial cooperation in the Asian region. Notably, in line with the Chiang Mai Initiative, the Bank of Korea has signed currency swap agreements worth 8 billion US dollars overall with six East Asian countries. In this way, we are helping to bolster regional countries' capacities to respond to possible future financial crises. The Bank of Korea will work to build up similarly close cooperative relationships within the Latin American region including Chile. In addition, leveraging off the momentum provided by the exchange of visits of our governors, I wish to step up our exchanges of staff and strengthen our cooperation with the Central Bank of Chile further. As a start to exchanges of personnel between our two banks, I propose first considering exchanges such as mutual visits by short-term study teams interested in specific individual areas. In the long-term, I feel we should aim at carrying out joint research and studies on matters of common interest to our two central banks. - 8 - IV. Closing Remarks Through their unceasing efforts, Chile and Korea have demonstrated the most dynamic growth potential in the world economy. I expect that this growth potential will be further enhanced as our two countries strengthen their cooperation in the years ahead. I hope to see Chile and Korea emerge as a new double-headed engine, leading Latin America and Asia onward into a new era of cooperation. The Pacific Ocean has long been a barrier dividing Korea and Chile. From now on, however, it will become a marine highway linking our two countries in cooperation. We know that Chile sees Asia as very important for its continued economic development. Chile's policy focus on Asia will serve as a force bringing the young 21st century Pacific era into full bloom. The Bank of Korea is also committed to leading efforts with the Central Bank of Chile aimed at increasing economic cooperation between Latin America and Asia. We will exert all-out efforts to make this cooperation beneficial for both of our two countries, Chile and Korea. - 9 -

In other words, despite low inflation, it is highly likely that monetary policy will be tightly managed to keep an eye on financial stability, but despite high inflation, finance is 'excessively' stable, making monetary policy more relaxed. It's hard to imagine a case. Not only is the concept of ' financial security' very comprehensive, but there will never be a situation in which potential risk factors have been completely eliminated in the entire complex financial market. The general public's perception that inflation is lower is better seems to be one of the main factors. For most people, inflation is perceived as a negative phenomenon that weakens their purchasing power. In fact, in any country, it is difficult for the general public to understand the " general balance" meaning of inflation, which is determined through a very long path (such as that inflation as a result of expanding total demand is a factor that also drives up wages and interest rates). It does. In addition to this, in most countries, including our own country, ordinary people perceive that the actual inflation is considerably higher compared to the inflation statistics that are officially compiled. For example, even in Japan, which has experienced deflation for more than 20 years, the general public perceives inflation to exceed 3%. This general perception shapes the public opinion that the lower the inflation, the better, and monetary authorities may not be free from a social atmosphere like this. I personally assess that monetary policy since 2012 has maintained a tighter tone compared to the monetary policy required by inflation targeting, and I understand that the outcome and actual inflation have fallen below the target level. The Bureau of Monetary Affairs has explained that this monetary policy is intended to counter potential financial risks, and general public opinion in favor of low inflation does not appear to have raised much of this objection to this explanation.
