Title: Evolving Regional Frameworks and Global Challenges: Koreas Perspective
text: Evolving Regional Frameworks and Global Challenges: Koreas Perspective Choongsoo Kim Governor, Bank of Korea Before presenting my views on the subject, I would like to thank the Bretton Woods Committee for inviting me to speak at this international council meeting. Regional frameworks: potentials and limits Let me begin by discussing the potential, as well as the practical limits, of Asias current regional framework as a collective insurance mechanism for preventing crisis. Asias regional framework, developed under the Chiang-Mai Initiative Multilateralization, is intended primarily to facilitate liquidity risk pooling at the regional level. As we know, the efficiency gains from risk pooling increase with the number of individual risks to be pooled and the less positively correlated with each other these individual risks are. Regional risk pooling should in principle therefore be less efficient than global risk pooling. As such, Asias regional framework may be considered less effective than originally hoped, because the Asian economic and financial cycles are synchronized, and because they are collectively vulnerable to common global financial shocks given their heavy dependence on the US dollar in international trade and finance. In reality, however, there are many other factors that might affect the effectiveness of a regional framework. I will focus here on two of them, which I believe to be highly relevant in the Asian context. The first is the strong trade linkages among Asian countries. Intra-regional trade accounts for more than one-half of Asias total trade. This fact will then imply a high likelihood of real contagion across countries in the region. If Asias regional framework can help to stop contagion before it spreads, it would be valuable. The second is the governance structure of global risk pooling, as currently organized by the IMF. Many Asian governments have been averse to receiving financial assistance from the IMFmainly because of the politically unpalatable stigma effects. Moreover, they appear less assured of the transparency and uniformity of IMF decisions regarding conditionality and financial support, and of the fair representation of their own voices in the IMF decision-making process as well. 1 During the global crisis, no Asian countries tapped IMF resources made available to qualified members, even though the terms were very favorable and there was no ex post conditionality attached. This could of course an indication that liquidity shortages among Asian countries were far less severe than they appeared at that time. Nonetheless, I believe they would have utilized these IMF resources for precautionary purposes, had there been no fear of stigma effects. Building a multi-layered system of financial safety nets Having said all of this, I would like to move on to the issue of how to build an efficient system of global financial safety nets that offers good protection to countries while minimizing moral hazard. My views here may be speculative, given the complexity of international coordination of national interests and the limited availability of empirical evidence on the effectiveness of safety nets. Nevertheless, I hope that I can offer some good food for thought. To summarize, I believe that we need a multi-layered system of global financial safety nets, with the IMF taking center stage in the system to capitalize on the potential efficiency gains from global risk pooling. The various regional frameworks could then be nested within the global pool. Under such a system, a global crisis would be dealt with primarily through the resources of the global pool, while the regional frameworks would focus on individual home-grown crises triggered by idiosyncratic shocks. Such a dichotomy would not have to be absolute, however, and some overlapping in roles would be necessary and even desirable. In order for the IMF to play the central role in this system, its resource base for lending would need to be increased and its governance structure improved. In this regard, there has been considerable progress in recent years, and further progress is within sight in the G20 process with regard to IMF quota reform. As part of our contribution to the global safety nets, the Bank of Korea recently committed US15 billion to the IMF under the bilateral borrowing agreement. Nesting the regional frameworks into multilateral efforts for crisis prevention is of course no easy task, and would require clever thinking on the design of conditionality and lending. I speculate that, if warranted, the IMF could lend to the regional frameworks which would in turn lend to their members in need. Alternately, both institutions may lend jointly to individual countries. A nested scheme is easier described than implemented, however. There are many technical but nonetheless 2 critical issues to be tackled. For instance, who should own the conditionality of IMF lending to a regional framework the regional framework itself or the ultimate borrower country? Who should be responsible for surveillance? And when multiple institutions lend jointly, whose money should receive seniority? I hope that the IMF will lead the research on the design and modus operandi of a multi-layered system of financial safety nets. Greater role of major central banks Finally, I would like to draw your attention to the complementary roles that major central banks can play in crisis prevention. While it is hard to predict with precision what any future global crisis will look like, we can say with some confidence that it will be preceded by pervasive global liquidity disruptions. In this light, and given that the IMF resources are limited, the major central banks should better serve as the international lenders of last resort. And we should work together to find ways of integrating their roles into the system of financial safety nets led by the IMF, while at the same time also not undermining their independence. Thank you for your attention. 3

Title: Governance and Oversight of Central Bank Reserves Management
text: 2011 BOK-World Bank   ()      Governance and Oversight of Central Bank Reserves Management 2011. 12. 5.       (Opening Remarks and Meaning of the Forum) Ladies and Gentlemen, I am truly delighted that this Forum on Governance and Oversight of Central Bank Reserves Management, hosted jointly by the Bank of Korea and the World Bank, is being held here in Seoul. First, I would like to extend my warmest welcome to all participants, from 15 countries in the Asia-Pacific region and 3 international institutions; World Bank, ADB and BIS. Thank you for attending the Forum despite your busy year-end schedules. I believe that the location and the timing of this Forum give it a special meaning. The global economy has not yet escaped from the financial crisis that broke out in 2008. And the European fiscal crisis, to which a credible solution has still not been found, has grown into a destabilizing force in the international financial markets. Related to this situation, our Asian region is attracting attention for two reasons. First, the successful resolution of the Asian financial crisis in the 1990s, through the courage and self-sacrifice of our region's people, contains some important lessons for resolving the financial crisis currently - 1 - facing European countries. Second, because Asia holds two-thirds of the world's official foreign reserves, there are some controversial opinions that Asian countries should play a more active role in resolving the European crisis. In both regards, I believe that the holding of this high-level forum on governance and oversight of central bank reserves management in Seoul has considerable significance. (Changes in reserve management environment since financial crisis) The official foreign reserves are a nation's foreign assets of last resort. In managing them, therefore, priority must be given to ensuring the liquidity and safety of the foreign reserves, before enhancing their profitability. These basic principles of reserve management cannot be altered. The actual details of reserve management, however, must be adjusted in  concerned line the with circumstances in the country size of its foreign reserves, its own domestic economic conditions, any changes taking place in the international financial market environment, and so on. Reserve management is thus a dynamic process, that needs to develop and evolve in response to changes in the - 2 - foreign and domestic reserve management conditions and environment. In this respect, we should of course also take note of the recent structural changes in reserve management environment taking place in the world economy and financial market. The first point to note here is the continuing growth in foreign reserve holdings of emerging market countries including those in Asia. Global foreign reserves total approximately 10 trillion U.S. dollars today, having increased more than five times over the past 10 years. And emerging market countries foreign reserve holdings, at 6.8 trillion U.S. dollars, have increased more than nine times during this same period. This increase has been basically the result of emerging countries rapid economic growth, and their current and capital account surpluses. Also countries with past experience of financial crisis have accumulated foreign reserves for self-insurance as well, to protect their economies from external shocks. The second point about the environmental changes now going on concerns the potential for transformation of the international monetary order. The international credibility of developed countries currencies, which played leading roles as reserve currencies, has weakened with the current financial - 3 - crisis. And the importance of emerging market countries in the world economy has at the same time grown significantly. These changes could strengthen the argument for foreign reserve diversification. The next point to consider is that, given the phenomenon of ultra-low interest rates in the international financial markets, the opportunity cost of holding foreign exchange reserves has now risen significantly. The ultra-low interest rates in major industrialized countries are likely to adversely burden central banks balance sheets by increasing their negative carry costs, the gap between their funding costs and their investment returns. There is a widely-accepted view, of course, that the central banks balance is not directly related to management performance. However, it is difficult to ignore the fact that central bank credibility can in reality be very significantly threatened by its running a deficit. The final point I would like to note here is that both volatility and risk in the international financial markets have increased dramatically. To benefit fully from diversification, for example, central banks have continuously expanded their investment asset classes and - 4 - currencies as their foreign reserves have grown. Their confidence in diversification is now weakening, however, because of the changes in risk/return profile of investment assets that followed the recent crisis. We must especially bear in mind the heightened possibility of tail risk occurring, in line with the current increased volatility and shorter economic cycle. (Future Challenges) All of these changes in our foreign reserves management environment are presenting central banks with many challenges. And I would like now to share some thoughts on these new challenges confronting us. First and foremost, we should not lose sight of the primary goal of reserve management. There is a Korean saying that the more of a hurry you are in, the longer the route you should take. During difficult times like the one we now face, it is important that we strive even more to pursue the basic reserve management objectives of securing liquidity and preserving asset value. More fundamentally, it is necessary to reexamine the - 5 - strategic allocation of our foreign reserves across various currency and asset classes. From a long-term perspective, diversification that reflects structural changes in the international financial markets should be continued. At the same time, however, we must take into account the fact that the investment returns and risk level for each asset class are changing. There is also a need for reconsidering our reserve management governance structures and decision-making processes. As the size of our foreign reserves increases, their opportunity costs, returns and management practices are coming increasingly into the spotlight. We must be careful not to let any failure in reserve management damage the publics trust in the central bank. In particular, all decisions related to management of the reserves should be made on the basis of careful and reasonable procedures. And measures should be strengthened to control all possible risks effectively at every step of the reserve management process. Finally, to improve our reserve management capabilities, it is also critical to strengthen the expertise of our reserve management organizations and staffs. In this time of increased uncertainty and price volatility, the result of - 6 - reserve management is more affected than ever before by portfolio managers abilities to assess and handle market changes. In this regard, early this year the Bank of Korea reorganized its reserve management organization into the Reserve Management Group, to strengthen its reserve management capability. (Closing) Given the current international financial market conditions, enhancing profitability while at the same time ensuring the liquidity and safety of our reserves is more difficult than ever before. I therefore hope that, during this forum, participants will engage in in-depth and open discussions on a variety of topics on reserve management. I look forward as well to this forum serving to strengthen the cooperative relationships in the reserve management area between our many participating central banks. Finally, let me express my sincere gratitude to all of you once again, for taking part in this forum. - 7 -

Title: 41st Savings Day Celebration
text: 41st Savings Day Celebration 2004. 10. 26 Bank of Korea President Park Seung Dear citizens! And here you are the Guest, the Savings Confucius and the Unknown! Today is the 41st Savings Day. This one is busy I would like to express my deepest gratitude to Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hun-jae, Minister of Finance and Economy, and to all the guests of the country, including the employees of financial institutions, for attending the meeting. In addition, I would like to express my heartfelt congratulations to the winners who have set an example of thrift saving and saving. Savings Day is a day to reflect once again on the precious beauty of saving and saving in our lives. Recently, our economy has been struggling with sluggish consumption, so it is easy to neglect the importance of savings. However, if we look at the development process of the economy from a longer perspective, this should not be the case. As you well know, savings were the driving force that brought a national economy that had been struggling in absolute poverty half a century ago to the threshold of today's advanced economy. In the 1960s, when our country was embarking on economic development, we had little accumulated capital, and most of the resources needed for economic development were financed by foreign capital. However, as a result of the whole nation tightening their belts and striving for savings, the total savings rate, which had been in the 10 % range in the 1960s, steadily increased, reaching over 40% in 1988. So big With the increased savings, we were able to expand our investment from the light industry to the heavy chemical industry. The high and low heat of the people has become the basis for accelerating the industrialization of our economy and achieving high growth. However, the gross savings rate continued to decline from its peak in 1988 and began to fall below the gross domestic investment rate in the 1990s. In the late 1980s, foreign currency earned on the basis of the current surplus was used for intemperate consumption or for excessive-and-heavy-handed fighters. The resolution and the current water supply turned into a multi-hour deficit, and as the scale accumulated, by the end of 1997 it was facing a foreign exchange crisis. The neglect of savings resulted in a disastrous state of affairs in which the foundations of the national economy were shaken and the home economy collapsed in a hurry. The difficulties that our economy is experiencing now are also due to the neglect of savings. The recent slowdown in consumption is caused by the fact that our people have not been able to live a reasonable consumption life in the meantime . During the past 2001-2002, our people have over-increased their consumption by relying on debts such as credit cards and loans to financial institutions rather than saving money. As a result, the financial condition of households has deteriorated significantly, and the resulting contraction in spending power is one of the causes of the sluggish economy. On the other hand, if the savings rate continues to fall, it has that much growth potential. It means to fall , and it implies that the economy has entered a stage of aging. In this regard, the need for savings is great for the future of our economy. In the current situation where the international competitiveness of traditional industries has fallen significantly due to the progress of liberalization and high wages, in order for our economy to continue to grow in the future, we will have to develop high-tech intensive industries based on steady R&D investment. This growth strategy requires a huge amount of investment resources , which in turn must be built through the savings of our people. Even from the standpoint of each individual, the importance of saving is high. Through savings, you must be prepared for unjust accidents and illnesses, and you must also design a comfortable old age. In particular , as life expectancy increases, the aging society is advancing rapidly, and the need for savings for old age is increasing. The quadruple and orthogonal significance of the low axis is still high. That axis is the key to creating a healthy consumption climate. Those who live a frugal life will not waste the money they have saved for luxuries or fleeting pleasures. In addition, the livelihood of saving and saving instills in people's consciousness a forward-looking value that seeks to overcome the difficulties of the present for a better future. This will naturally lead to the formation of a healthy social ethos. In this regard, the winners of today's honors are an example to all of us, not only economically but also mentally. The sound and forward-looking discipline of life that you have been practicing is a great force that will develop our economy in the right direction and brighten our society. With sincerity, I offer words of respect and congratulations. Finally, I would like to ask the winners to take the lead in ensuring that a healthy consumer climate spreads throughout our society , and I would like to replace it today in the celebration of that Celebration Day. Thanks. 2004. 10. 26. Bank of Korea President Park Seung

Opening Statement Translation Contact: Hwang In-sun, Deputy Director of the Policy Cooperation Team of the Policy Planning Bureau Tel : 759-5360 , Fax : 759-6677, E-mail : ishwang@bok.or.kr Bulletin : Tel (02) 759-4015, 4016 "The Bank of Korea press release is on the Internet ( ).  - 1 - (Attachment 1) Opening Address delivered by Dr. Seung Park Governor The Bank of Korea at the 3rd Workshop for Worldwide Central Banks on Beyond Financial Reform: New Challenges and Policy Responses Seoul, 5 July 2005 Ladies and gentlemen, Let me welcome all of you to the workshop for worldwide central banks, which is being held for the third time this year. I believe that these workshops provide good opportunities for sharing our varied experiences on overcoming financial crises and also for broadening friendship among central bankers. The theme of this year's workshop is "Beyond Financial Reform: New Challenges and Policy Responses". Many East-Asian countries including Korea have achieved good results through financial reforms since the Asian currency crisis of 1997, but many tasks still lie ahead. In this respect, I am sure that this workshop will be useful to all of us as central bankers. It is well known that Korea carried out intensive financial reforms after the currency crisis of 1997. In the course of the drive, only 19 out of 33 banks survived and about 40 percent of employees in financial institutions lost their jobs. In addition, 165 trillion won of public funds was injected into the financial system in order to clear off non-performing loans and recapitalize financial institutions. This amount is equivalent to around 160 billion US dollars, in terms of the current exchange rate. Thanks to this drastic structural adjustment, domestic commercial banks' NPL ratio fell sharply from 14 percent at the end of 1999 to 2 percent at the end of last year, and their average BIS capital adequacy ratio rose from 7 percent at the end of 1997 to 11 percent. Last year, the scale of their net income registered its highest-ever figure of around 6 billion US dollars. In addition, the financial infrastructure including related legislation and practices has been improved to approach global standards. These reforms have not only bolstered the management status of individual financial institutions, but also increased the stability of the whole financial system. We cannot rest on our laurels from these financial reforms. Korea has the ambitious vision of becoming a financially-advanced country and, what is more, acting as the financial hub of Northeast Asia. To realize this vision, we intend to consistently strengthen our efforts for the reform of the financial sector from a medium- and long-term perspective. Now, I would like to say a few words about the future course of Korean financial reforms from this viewpoint. First, future financial reforms should be market driven. Just after the currency crisis, almost all financial institutions were hit by non-performing loans and the financial markets did not function well. In this situation, it inevitably fell to the government to initiate financial reforms. However, the management soundness of individual financial institutions has been improved and financial markets are operating as they should. In these circumstances, it is desirable for financial reforms to be driven by the market mechanism. This is expected to promote financial development further by heightening the competitiveness of individual financial institutions and the efficiency of the financial markets. Meanwhile, the government and the central bank should play a pivotal role in enhancing the stability of the financial markets and consolidating the financial infrastructure. Second, the financial industry should be developed into a knowledge-based industry that creates high value-added in its own right. Before the currency crisis, the Korea's financial industry was content to play a passive role, supporting quantitative growth in the real economy, while the business autonomy of financial institutions was not fully assured. This state of underdevelopment has already improved in the course of the reforms following the currency crisis. The financial industry is now evolving as a major business sector in its own right. For its ongoing development, it should strive for international competitiveness in line with the pace of financial globalization. What is more, Korea is creating an advanced industrial structure centering on knowledge-based services as well as high-technology manufacturing. Korea's financial industry should emerge as a core provider of knowledge-based services. Third, the direct financial markets should be given further encouragement to achieve balanced development with the indirect financial markets that have traditionally centered on banks. If the financial markets can thereby achieve a multi-layered structure, the efficiency of financial intermediation will be upgraded. At the same time, the multiple channels of financial intermediation will act as a buffer, absorbing and dispersing negative impacts, even when a financial shock occurs. Fellow central bankers, Over the coming four days, we will have deep discussions about these topics. I look forward to all participants having the opportunity to pool their countries' experiences and to gain useful information and insights from this workshop. Now, Korea is entering the height of summer when the weather turns sultry. Although you may not find it easy to get accustomed to this weather, I hope all of you have a healthy and happy time during the period of your stay here. Thank you. (Attachment 2) Opening Letter Dear Central Bank Participants! We sincerely welcome you to attend this year's third World Central Bank Workshop. The workshop is proud to have provided a great opportunity for central bank employees in each country to share and socialize with them in their diverse experiences in overcoming the financial crisis. The theme of this year's workshop is "New Policy Challenges and Response Directions After Financial Reform." A number of East Asian countries, including South Korea, have embarked on financial reforms since the 1997 foreign exchange crisis, and although they have achieved considerable results , they still face many challenges. In this regard, we believe that this workshop will also be a beneficial place for all of our central bankers. As you well know, South Korea pursued intense financial reforms shortly after the foreign exchange crisis of 1997. In the course of these reforms, only 19 of the 33 banks survived, and about 40% of the employees of financial institutions lost their jobs. In addition, a total of 165 trillion won of public funds were put into the clearance of bad debts and capital raising by financial institutions. This drastic restructuring has led to a significant reduction in the ratio of wealth bonds of domestic general banks from 14% at the end of 1999 to 2% at the end of last year, and the BIS equity ratio has increased from 7% to 11% at the end of 1997. Last year, the net profit of the domestic general bank reached about 6.4 trillion won, the largest on record. In addition, since the foreign exchange crisis, the financial infrastructure such as financial laws and practices has been improved in a way that is in line with international standards. The results of these financial reforms have not only led to the improvement of the management of individual financial institutions, but also to the stability of the entire financial system. But we are not proud of the achievements of these financial reforms. South Korea has a dream of making the leap to become a financial developed country and a financial hub in Northeast Asia. We will develop a medium- to long-term vision and work tirelessly to achieve it. In this context, I would like to say a few things about the direction of financial reform that Korea should be heading in the future. First, in the future, financial reform by market mechanisms should be steadily pursued . In the immediate aftermath of the foreign exchange crisis, when almost all financial institutions were insolvent and the financial markets were dysfunctional , the government had no choice but to lead the way in financial reforms. In today's situation where the management health of individual financial institutions is increasing and the financial market is functioning normally, financial reform by market autonomy is desirable. It is hoped that only in this way will the competitiveness of individual financial institutions and the efficiency of financial markets be increased, thereby accelerating the advancement of finance. The role of policy authorities, such as the government and central banks, should focus on promoting overall financial market stability and overhauling the financial infrastructure. Second, the financial industry should develop into a knowledge-based industry that creates high added value on its own. Prior to the foreign exchange crisis, South Korea's financial industry remained in a passive role in supporting the quantitative growth of the real economy while the management autonomy of financial institutions was not guaranteed. This backwardness has already been liquidated in the post-foreign exchange reform process and the financial industry is growing as a stand-alone industry. In order for the financial industry to continue to develop in the future, it must keep pace with the globalization of finance and become competitive at an international level. Moreover, Korea has been promoting the advancement of its industrial structure centered on technology-intensive manufacturing and knowledge-based services. Korea's financial industry should develop into the core of the knowledge-based services industry. Third, the direct financial market should be actively nurtured so that it can develop in balance with the traditional bank-oriented indirect financial market. Through this, when the structure of the financial market is stratified, not only will the efficiency of financial intermediation be greatly increased, but multiple financial intermediary channels will be established, which will serve as a buffer to disperse and absorb the negative effects even in the event of a shock such as a financial crisis. Dear Participants! Four days from today , there will be a more in-depth discussion on a topic like this. In any case, we hope that this workshop will be an opportunity for all participants to share their experiences and gain valuable information and implications through serious discussions. Right now, South Korea is entering a summer when the seasonal heat begins. It will not be easy to adapt to the different weather, but we hope that everyone will have a healthy and enjoyable time during their stay in Korea. Thanks.

I believe that these workshops provide good opportunities for sharing our varied experiences on overcoming financial crises and also for broadening friendship among central bankers. The theme of this year's workshop is "Beyond Financial Reform: New Challenges and Policy Responses". Many East-Asian countries including Korea have achieved good results through financial reforms since the Asian currency crisis of 1997, but many tasks still lie ahead. In this respect, I am sure that this workshop will be useful to all of us as central bankers. It is well known that Korea carried out intensive financial reforms after the currency crisis of 1997. In the course of the drive, only 19 out of 33 banks survived and about 40 percent of employees in financial institutions lost their jobs. In addition, 165 trillion won of public funds was injected into the financial system in order to clear off non-performing loans and recapitalize financial institutions. This amount is equivalent to around 160 billion US dollars, in terms of the current exchange rate. Thanks to this drastic structural adjustment, domestic commercial banks' NPL ratio fell sharply from 14 percent at the end of 1999 to 2 percent at the end of last year, - 1 - and their average BIS capital adequacy ratio rose from 7 percent at the end of 1997 to 11 percent. Last year, the scale of their net income registered its highest-ever figure of around 6 billion US dollars. In addition, the financial infrastructure including related legislation and practices has been improved to approach global standards. These reforms have not only bolstered the management status of individual financial institutions, but also increased the stability of the whole financial system. We cannot rest on our laurels from these financial reforms. Korea has the ambitious vision of becoming a financially-advanced country and, what is more, acting as the financial hub of Northeast Asia. To realize this vision, we intend to consistently strengthen our efforts for the reform of the financial sector from a medium- and long-term perspective. Now, I would like to say a few words about the future course of Korean financial reforms from this viewpoint. First, future financial reforms should be market driven. Just after the currency crisis, almost all financial institutions were hit by non-performing loans and the financial markets did not function well. In this situation, it inevitably fell to the government to initiate financial reforms. - 2 - However, the management soundness of individual financial institutions has been improved and financial markets are operating as they should. In these circumstances, it is desirable for financial reforms to be driven by the market mechanism. This is expected to promote financial development further by heightening the competitiveness of individual financial institutions and the efficiency of the financial markets. Meanwhile, the government and the central bank should play a pivotal role in enhancing the stability of the financial markets and consolidating the financial infrastructure. Second, the financial industry should be developed into a knowledge-based industry that creates high value-added in its own right. Before the currency crisis, the Korea's financial industry was content to play a passive role, supporting quantitative growth in the real economy, while the business autonomy of financial institutions was not fully assured. This state of underdevelopment has already improved in the course of the reforms following the currency crisis. The financial industry is now evolving as a major business sector in its own right. For its ongoing development, it should strive for international competitiveness in line with the pace of financial globalization. What is more, Korea is creating an advanced industrial structure centering on knowledge-based services as well as high-technology manufacturing. Korea's financial industry should emerge as a core provider of knowledge-based services. - 3 - Third, the direct financial markets should be given further encouragement to achieve balanced development with the indirect financial markets that have traditionally centered on banks. If the financial markets can thereby achieve a multi-layered structure, the efficiency of financial intermediation will be upgraded. At the same time, the multiple channels of financial intermediation will act as a buffer, absorbing and dispersing negative impacts, even when a financial shock occurs. Fellow central bankers, Over the coming four days, we will have deep discussions about these topics. I look forward to all participants having the opportunity to pool their countries' experiences and to gain useful information and insights from this workshop. Title: Designing for the Tomorrow of the Korean Economy
text: Korea National Competence Association.Korea Martial Arts Association Ju Choi "Summer CEO Seminar" Invited Lecture Designing for the Tomorrow of the Korean Economy 2005. 7. 25 President of Bank of Korea Park Seung (Preface) Hello everyone! Our economy is in a very difficult situation. Because of this , our people are deeply concerned about what our economy will become. I will spend about 1 hour today asking why these economic difficulties are occurring, and whether or not we should recognize these present economic difficulties as necessary for our development, and whether this is What is the significance and the connection to the advancement of our country's economy, and how will our economy become in the next year and the next year, so that we can face this difficulty? In order to sublimate it into an occasion for development, I would like to focus on what and how to do it , and roughly that question. I think there may be some people who are curious about various current issues , so Dama would like to encourage them to use the question discussion time in the future. (Changes in the growth environment of our economy) As we all know, over the past 40 years, the Korean economy has grown at an average annual rate of about 8%. South Korea is the only country in the world that has grown at an average annual rate of 8% over the course of 40 years. South Korea succeeded in turning an economy that had a per capita income of 80 in 1960 into a 10,000 per capita income in 1995. Therefore, in the 1990s, our economy took off the framework of the backward countries and entered the middle stage of the country. For Korea, the 1990s were the time of moving from a middle-income country to a developed country, a time when we were turning around the middle return point to say marathon. Under these circumstances, our economy is facing tremendous changes in the growth environment. Such a change in the growth environment is something that you are well aware of, and I will summarize it into three things. First, the Korean economy entered a high-wage stage , during which a huge low-wage economy called China and India emerged. You know that the wage level in our country right now is the highest among the countries that are in competition with us. The fact that we have entered the high-wage stage and at the same time that low-wage economies such as China and India have become wealthy means that an environment has been created that will overnight bring down the myriad of small and medium-sized enterprises and the small and medium-sized business owners of Uri and LA who can only survive at low wages. The second change in the environment is the advent of the open age as we are familiar with it. The transition from protectionism to the open age has two particularly important implications. One is the fact that the market we compete with is out of the country and becomes a world market. Second, if you don't have a competitive edge in the global market, you can't survive, you're bound to go bankrupt and be expelled. In other words, in the era of protectionism, the weak could survive and live without competitiveness or without the world's first-class technology, but now we must accept that without global technology and without global competitiveness, we will inevitably be expelled and bankrupt . This is a very important message. The third change is the advent of the era of IT technology. The advent of the era of IT technology is said to be that the determining factor for international competitiveness is not capital, but technology. These three environmental changes have important implications for cataclysmic changes in the development of the global economy. Again, will it come once in a millennium? I can tell you that it is a change in the survival environment of cataclysmic change. As a result of this, not only our country but also in all the countries of the world, people with global economic power and enterprises with global competitiveness have expanded infinitely, and the sphere of activity has been broadened, more welcomed, and names have been made known in all corners of the world. . This is evident today in the fact that Samsung, LG and the modern trade name permeate every corner of the three worlds. Conversely, people who don't have international competitiveness , people who don't have those skills, and companies that don't have that kind of competitiveness are either going to have to be expelled or unable to survive. The explicit nailing of the so-called polarized world economic order is the change in the global economic environment that I have now mentioned. Our country's economy is now suffering from extreme polarization, but this is not because of anyone's fault. The world economic order is supposed to go through polarization in order to develop the economy. That's why polarization is not a bad thing in the long run. First of all, I would like to say that if you look at it from the front of your nose, it is painful, painful, and painful, but in terms of development, it is a path that teaches you a dynamic pattern of development that is very dynamic. Because of these environmental changes, we had the bitter experience of the IMF crisis in 1997. The IMF crisis was caused by this direct onslaught of global environmental change. Without such environmental changes, there would have been no IMF crisis in Korea. And even now, I can't tell you exactly in numbers, but I think we've adapted about 40 to 50 percent to those environmental changes. The remaining 50 to 60 percent is the way to go. The task of enduring more pain and adapting to it lies before us. This is the pain and difficulty that our economy is experiencing right now. I tell you that it is a difficulty that inevitably arises in the process of adapting and adapting my body so that our economy can survive and overcome environmental changes. (Three factors that caused difficulties in our economy) Then, in order to adapt to such changes in the environment, let us consider what kind of suffering our economy is suffering now, and in other words, if our economy is currently a crisis, then where is the cause of the crisis, and how and in what form the crisis is manifesting. There are three factors that make our economy difficult at present: The first is the bankruptcy of the competitive inferior industry. Due to the changes in the global environment, the phenomenon of the bankruptcy of the competitive inferior industry is showing up in the process of expelling people who are not competitive, industries that are not competitive, and organizations that are not competitive. As a competitive inferior industry, the three major sectors in the bankruptcy ranks are traditional small and medium-sized enterprises, self-employment, and rural areas. This competitive inferior sector, in whatever form, is bound to stagnate, atrophy and suffer. This is an unavoidable order. By the way, SMEs, self-employment, and rural areas are the basis of people's lives. As these three sectors that form the bottom of people's lives are shaken and atrophied, our people are increasingly appealing for suffering. The second factor is the foreign outflow of investment. The link in the cycle of households and businesses is investment, where companies make money and that money is reinvested in the bureau, so that the enterprise makes money again, and that money flows to the household , so that the household makes money to the enterprise through consumption. However, the companies in our country as a whole are experiencing the greatest boom in history. Again , there is polarization when we divide companies into small and medium-sized enterprises and large corporations, but the corporate sector as a whole is experiencing the greatest boom since the Dangun. That said, the profits from it are not circulating through domestic reinvestment and are all going out to foreign countries such as China, India, Russia, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines. The automotive, steel, and electronics industries are all no exception. It has to be. Because there is only that way for a corporation to live , it will dry up. Nor can't. It is a natural trend in the age of globalization. Compared to China, we are 10 times higher in wages, 4 times higher in land values, and 2 times higher in taxes. If you go to China or India, there are virtually no trade unions, but there is no obstacle to management. Here, it is the trade unions that should pay the most attention to investment and appeal to the difficulties. That's why when you compare China, the Philippines, India, and South Korea and talk about which companies would invest in Korea, there's no way to protest against it. In any case, the money earned by our businesses has not been invested in the country, and now there are 900,000 unemployed people in our country. On the other hand, the employment that our companies are creating there by going abroad and building factories is 1 million. If wages were cheaper, taxes were cheaper, logistics costs were cheaper, and peaceful labor relations had been established in our country, and our companies had not gone abroad and invested in the country altogether , we would not be worried about the employment problem now. The logic holds that it doesn't have to be. The third factor is employment-free growth. In our country, the phenomenon is showing that the economy is growing, but employment is not increasing. The main reason is the result of the rationalization policies that companies are forced to choose to live in a changing environment. Entering a department store or discount store and talking about the retail business is a necessity for the sake of economic development and for the sake of raising the standard of living of the people. But when a discount store or a department store comes in, thousands of hole shops and self-employment are ruined. In other words, with the creation of discount stores and department stores, the enterprises make huge profits, the stock price rises a lot, the people's lives become easier, the welfare of the people increases, but in return, a large number of unemployed people are bound to be created. What's more, self-employment is usually done by people like me, so even if you close your doors, you won't be able to find a job for re-employment. Where will the older people go to get a job and give them a history book? Under the current system, if you don't find a job within a month, you won't be caught in the statistics as unemployed. Therefore, if a large number of self-employed people lose their jobs, they are not included as unemployed. This is the painful part of our economy I can tell you that it's one of the blind spots. In the case of banks, not so long ago, everything was done by human hands. Now, more than 80 percent of the bank's work is done by machines. We do not borrow people's hands by processing automatic cash, such as an ATM or Internet banking. That is why banks continue to make a lot of profits, and the banking industry grows , but, on the contrary, the number of bankers keeps decreasing. There is no way to say this. Don't keep using people and don't fire them, for example, if you compete with a bank in the United States or Germany and the bank in Korea fails, you can't just put up with it and just use a person. I have said three things now. What happens if uncompetitive self-employment, small and medium-sized businesses, rural areas stagnate, investment flows overseas, and employment does not increase even as the economy grows. Household incomes are bound to decrease. The people's livelihood is bound to be difficult. The life of the people is bound to be painful. Therefore , I can say that the most painful part of our country's economy is that the people's livelihood is difficult and the people's lives are difficult. (The current situation is a springboard for the re-leap of the Korean economy) Does this mean that the Korean economy is hopeless, or that if the people's livelihood deteriorates in this way, will the national system falter? The Korean economy has been growing at a high rate for 40 years , but the dynamics of this high growth have come from overcoming and overcoming the crisis. In the process of coping head-on with the new environment that has now surged upon us, overcoming it, the lives of our people are difficult and various polarization phenomena are emerging . As such, at the moment, the people's lives are only showing difficulty, but at the bottom of our economy, which is invisible to the eye, new flesh is sprouting at a very rapid rate. I have told you earlier that we have digested about 40-50% of the changes in the global economic environment, and 50-60% from now on. I told you that it was the remaining task to be done. I think it will probably take another 5 or 10 years to do this. Harua needle does not solve it. In the midst of such suffering, the potential for a re-leap is being built up for our economy to become an advanced economy. That's our chance. The shock of the global economic environment has come and is giving us the pain of the difficulties of people's livelihood, but at the same time it is giving us an opportunity. This meeting provides the basis for a re-leap in the Korean economy. What it is, specifically, how the new flesh is sprouting in our economy right now, if you say that you can't see it, and then you can prove it, let me tell you in detail with three branches. First, the constitution of our economy is becoming unknowingly strong. The economic constitution of our country before and after the IMF is different from heaven and earth. First of all , the business is shedding all its debts. No debt. The debt ratio of the Korean Ministry of Enterprise (the ratio of debt to equity is the ratio of debt to equity capital) has been reduced from 400% at the time of the IMF crisis to 100%. Debt, which used to be 4 times the amount of equity capital, has now come down to the equivalent of equity capital. In Japan or the United States, this debt ratio is 140%. Therefore, the financial structure of the Korean flag industry is stronger than that of the United States and Japan. So, in fact, one of the difficulties that the ROK is having in formulating and estimating the economic and monetary policy is that even if the Bank of Korea sends out money or lowers the interest rate, The point is that companies don't borrow money because they don't have debt. In the old days, all the businesses were taking out debt from the banks , so when the Bank of Korea sent out the money, the currency swelled on the market and the economy came to life. Not only that, but transparency has increased. Nowadays, corporate transparency is being emphasized a lot, and compared to the past, corporate management has become very transparent. Banks have also become transparent and sound. Before the IMF crisis, banks in our country had bad debts of more than 15% on total loans. At the time of the IMF crisis, the percentage of money that could not be received was 16%. That's down to less than 2% right now. At present, the banks of Korea are also more robust than in Japan. Banks in Japan now have a lot of bad debt. So the banks in Korea are strong enough to be on par with the banks of Germany and the United States. In this way, the corporate constitution has become stronger. Second, the fact that new flesh is sprouting is that the number of globally competitive businesses is rapidly increasing. Professor Hwang of Seoul National University is one of them. The number of scientists in the 1st place in the world is increasing: large enterprises, 1st place is small and medium-sized enterprises, and 1st place is scientists. Before the IMF crisis, there was not a single world-class company in Korea. To give you an example, we could have talked about Pohang Season. But, ladies and gentlemen, isn't our country the No. 1 in the three worlds of shipbuilding now? 70% of the world's most expensive ships are monopolized by one country. Because of the high level of Korean technology, even if the price is expensive, it is inevitable that you will come to Korea. Therefore, now the shipbuilding industry in our country has secured 4 years of work and orders continue to be flooded. The same goes for the auto car, semiconductor, and steel industries. As a businessman, you know it when you go around the world market, but everywhere you go in the rural villages of South America, Africa, Europe, Asia, the trademarks of the representative companies of our country, such as Samsung, Hyundai Motors, Po Chul, LG, etc . You can browse . This is the gift of the era of globalization. Again, every company, every organization in our country should be like that. You have to be like Samsung, like Hyundai, like LG , and like Po Chul. In this way, globally competitive organizations and businesses must be spread to all industries and sectors. And the entire 50 million population must be internationally competitive. This is the path that Korea should take. Finally, the knowledge service industry that should tie our country forward is growing rapidly. Yet, manufacturing is feeding our country. However, in the future, the more manufacturing industry grows, the less employment there will be. Employment in manufacturing is not acceptable. As I said earlier, in the manufacturing industry You have to keep sending people out to live. Therefore, as the economy develops and passes a certain level, the share of manufacturing continues to decrease. Our country has also passed the peak. Manufacturing accounted for the largest share of GDP in 1998. After that, the manufacturing industry in our country is getting its share low. The United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, and Japan have already seen a decline in manufacturing since 20, 30, or 40 years ago. The industry that will feed Korea in the future is the knowledge service industry. These include finance, telecommunications, logistics, education services, healthcare, environmental services, leisure, relationships, culture, the arts, corporate services, and so on. Such a knowledge service industry should continue to bind the Korean economy in the future. However, the share of these service industries is growing rapidly year by year. You probably don't realize it. But in terms of overall employment and GDP growth , this share continues to grow. (The two-sided reality of the Korean economy) Our economy is now facing a number of problems of polarization, which are difficult for the people's livelihood to live, but these difficulties are at the same time a good opportunity on the one hand. Therefore, the current Korean economy has a mix of dark and light aspects. Those who only look at the bright side say that they have no worries about our economy , while those who only look at the dark side say that the Korean economy has fallen or is now over. But that's not the case. The Korean economy is in great difficulty right now. But at the same time, the hope for development is immensely filled. When it comes to a person with very slow progress, there is no problem, and there is no progress. The most problematic and comfortable state for a person is death. When you die, there is no problem, no pain, no suffering. But at the same time, there is no dynamism and no development. The same is true of the economy. Economy is a creature. The fastest developing economy has the most serious problems, and the power to overcome them at the same time is immense. Such has been the case with the Korean economy of the past 40 years. Usually, when assessing a country's economy, it refers to three things: growth, prices, and the international balance. These are the three frameworks. If we look at the case of our country this year, the economic growth is 3.8%, the price is 3% of the consumer price, the current water supply is 13 billion months surplus, and the foreign exchange reserves are 200 billion. If you look at the indicators, the stock price is at an all-time high, and if you look at the exchange rate, the value of the yuan is rising. The value of our country's yuan continues to rise. If we look at it only as a macro indicator , the rate of economic growth is a little inadequate compared to our past performance. But if you compare this to other countries, countries that are less than us, such as India or China, have a much higher growth rate than we do, but if you compare it to a country that lives like us or lives better than us, our growth rate is in the upper group. It is higher than the United States, higher than Japan, and all the countries in Europe. However, the growth of 3.8% in our country is not up to our expectations. But if you look at the other sectorsprice stability, the international surplus, foreign exchange reserves, stock pricesall of these situations together, it's not that wrong or so bad. Mervyn Davies, president of Standard Chartered (SCB) Bank, who acquired our country's First Bank last week , came to visit me. In the course of many stories of Gazi, I have told such a story. I explained the situation while talking about the Korean economy. And since I have been doing the number of universities for almost 30 years, I think that the rating that I see as a macro indicator such as prices, growth, international balance, etc. should not be given at least a B, but my people are not willing to give a C. That was it. Then Davis laughed when he said that if Iyagi was like himselfof course, this is a British bankhe would give him an A-grade. But as a university professor, I said that I am objectively confident that I will give a B grade on a macro basis, but I also think it is right that our people are not willing to give me a C grade. Then President Davis asked why. I explained. Our economy is very strong and nothing wrong with it in terms of macro indicators or in terms of development prospects, but when it comes to people's lives alone, it is now a sense of C credit. now Because the people's life is difficult, the business is difficult, and the employment is difficult, the people said that I think it is right to give them such credits because they only look at the problems of the people's livelihood, the problems of their own food and living. But I also said that as the governor of the central bank, I think it is right to look ahead and look ahead and give a rating. There has been a time when this cause has been shared in a similar way to a joke. So if our economy is in a state of good enough to give a B in terms of macro indicators, what is the problem, especially if the growth rate is higher than that of other developed countries, and if both prices and international numbers are satisfactory ? Why is the people clamoring? This is the difficulty of our economy. That's the polarization. It is the divergence between the people's livelihood and our macroeconomy. The power of our economy as a whole is separated from the lives of our people. How to stay apart, let me tell you with a specific number. Last year, Korea's economic growth rate was 4.6%. However, by dividing this 4.6% into the corporate and household sectors, and dividing the growth rate of disposable income, the growth rate of disposable income on the corporate side grew rapidly to 41%, while the disposable income in the household sector increased by only 0.9%. What if the national economy as a whole increased by 4.6%, households increased by less than 1%, and businesses increased by 41%. The changes in the global economic environment that I spoke to you at the beginning are relevant to this. Since the world order has changed, so are the three economies, but the Korean economy, too, is growing on the corporate side , while the households are shrinking when it comes to companies and households. The corporate side is not just growing as it usually gets, but is growing to the point where it makes the best profit ever . If we divide the enterprises again, the small and medium-sized enterprises and the self-employed side are splintering , while the side with global competitiveness is spreading. In a way, the phenomenon of the poor and the poor and the bad continues to be the one who is good is happening. In our sensibilities, the poor and the poor should not happen, it is a bad thing. The side that is good continues to be good and not good It is bad for the side to continue to be naughty. But the world order is not. Take a look at the restaurants in our town, for example. A house that does well continues to do well and attracts a flood of guests, but a house without taste does not have guests. The same is true of the global economy. For this reason , companies are also deeply troubled by the polarization of the so-called side with international competitiveness and the polarization of the side with which they do not have, and the polarization of the corporate sector and the household side. In the past year, the net profit of listed companies in Korea has increased by 100%, but the employment of listed companies has increased very little. Publicly traded companies hold a whopping 66 trillion won of cash, which is not invested domestically, but is tied up in the form of paying off debts, investing abroad , or making deposits in the 2nd financial sector. Meanwhile, because household incomes are not increasing, the economy has grown by 4.6% over the past year, corporate net profits have increased by 100%, while private consumption has declined by 0.5%. This is what speaks to the difficulties of the people's livelihood, the difficulties of the people's livelihood in the country. Therefore, the difficulty of living for the people has nothing to do with what percentage of economic growth is achieved or how much profit the company is making. I can tell you that this is a question that emerged in the process of distribution. So why are households struggling like this, even though the economy is growing and businesses are making a lot of profits, and here are three reasons: The first is the employment slowdown. Employment is not increasing. Because the economy is growing and companies are making a lot of profits, employment needs to increase, but employment is not increasing . Employment is not increasing because companies are struggling to live, and they have no choice but to reduce their high capacity. The second is investment outflow. Investment is leaking overseas. The third is the downfall of self-employment. These three things are the cause of this difficulty. So what does this polarization mean? Industries with global competitiveness, organizations with global competitiveness, and people with world competitiveness are increasingly stretched. While the market is expanding into the world, the sectors that are not, such as small and medium-sized enterprises, self-employment, etc., are stagnating, creating difficulties for the people's livelihood. The impact of this polarization that our economy is currently experiencing means that the Korean economy is undergoing intense restructuring in order to adapt to the new growth environment. That is why polarization is a phenomenon that, in the current cross-section, is a painful, difficult, and bad thing, but in the midst of the great current of medium- and long-term development of our economy , it is a phenomenon that should be very welcome and painful but that we should not go through. It is not as persistent as the heat in the body that occurs when surgery is required to cut the affected area, but it is temporary, and it is an unavoidable phenomenon that inevitably accompanies the restructuring process. Therefore, the pain should in a sense be seen as a pain that appears on the road to advanced evolution to further develop the national economy in the future. (5 Factors That Can Prevent the Aging of the Korean Economy) With the progress of globalization, the competition between Korean companies in our country has become meaningless. We have to fight the companies of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, China, all the companies in the world and win our companies. So are our people. Competition between our people is meaningless. We have entered such an era when we have to compete with the world's population of 50 million and win the world's 65 billion people. In this situation of globalization, in order for the Korean economy to become an advanced economy that lives better than other countries, the entire sector, the whole industry, must become a competitive sector and a competitive industry. Not only large corporations, but now SMEs and self-employed people must all be internationally competitive. So are organizations. So did the Bank of Korea where I am. If the Bank of Korea does not compete with other banks in Korea but with the central banks of 190 countries in the world and does not lead in policy formulation and policy efficiency , the Bank of Korea will have no land to stand. So are the corporations , and so are the individual citizens of our country. The mindset of the individual, The state of mind, the spirit of rationalism, these things must be ahead of the competition with the 65 billion people of other countries. Otherwise, there is no way for us to live. Moreover, in Korea, where the land is narrow and the economy is only 2% of the world, I can say with certainty that the only way to become the No. 1 country is to become the No. 1 country by making the entire population international, the international competitiveness of the entire organization, and the international competitiveness of the entire industry. . So what's the way to do it? Strip away the labor force and capital in the competitive inferior sector , the uncompetitive sector, the traditional SMEs, the self-employed, the agricultural sector, the high-tech industry, the highly productive sector, the semiconductor industry, the IT industry, the venture industry, and the Gita Large supermarkets, department stores, etc. should continue to be recounted in a way that has international competitiveness. This is what we are not doing. Developed countries do this well. In developed countries, even if the self-employed are eliminated , the state will take them to train, and send them back to the productive side. You have to keep going like this. If we continue this cycle, self-employment, small and medium-sized enterprises, agriculture, etc. will be eliminated, but the people will not only suffer because of it, but will also gain new productivity and move to higher productive forces . What will happen if the cycle of factors of production between the competitive advantage and the competitive inferior sectors continues to be promoted? Manufacturing is increasingly focusing towards high-productivity manufacturing. And all other industries will move to a knowledge service industry-centric system. This move is a key task for the development of the Korean Border. That's how you go. This is not a day in the morning. I said it might take 5 years or 10 years. Maybe it will take 10 years or more. In the meantime, we will suffer. But we must endure the pain and go that way. In this sense, our economy is struggling tremendously right now, but this is by no means abnormal. In the process of taking our economy to the next level, we are now on a normal development trajectory. We're not going wrong. It is on a normal development trajectory. Suffering and overcoming it, our economy has become an overall international competitive system. We are on the path of the Great Trek that we are doing. Therefore, we should not think of this as a cyclical economic fluctuation. The economy has become booming, then it has become a recession, and the economy is difficult because you think of it as going up & down like this, so use all the symptomatic stimulus measures to save the economy, and why the government is not going to go this way. There are factors like that , but more fundamentally, we have to go that way because there is a flowing path that our economy is on. We should go with a policy that alleviates the pain through a partial stimulus package , and we should not go that far with a simple short-term stimulus package to get out of this pain right away. So what could be the problem? You have to go that way, but if you want to go that way, do you have to stay still, or not? If you stay still, you may go down a hesitant path. So what can we do to go down such a bright path? What we need to do from now on is to stop economic aging. I don't think our economy has yet to enter the aging stage of the economy like the European countries. But our economy is now exposed to risks that could lead to economic aging. The economy is exposed to the risk of aging, so if you do it wrong, you have the potential to go that far. The fact that the economy is aging is that the economy is getting old. It is aging that the growth rate falls to 1% or 2%, the unemployment rate is high, the dependence on the welfare of the government alone and the cries to continue to raise welfare, the prices rise, the needs rise, the discontent increases, and the government is crippled. So we have to stop the aging of the economy. How do we stop it? From now on, I will tell you five factors that prevent aging , or the five factors that are causing the aging of our country's economy. The first high-wage and high-cost phenomenon can cause aging. Urina Ra wages are the highest among competitors. High wages, high housing costs, high prices, High education costs , high transportation costs, this is the so-called phenomenon of high wages and high costs. Wages are high, housing costs are 2-3 times higher than in other countries , and the cost of living in Seoul is 56th highest among cities in 60 developed countries. The cost of education is the highest among OECD countries because of the cost of private education. If this continues, our economy is bound to grow old. The second is the inefficiencies of the labor market. Avoid hard work, avoid 3D even in the midst of high unemployment, and small and medium-sized enterprises cannot save people. Because of the rigid labor market and confrontational labor relations, domestic companies also avoid domestic investment, and foreign capital also avoids investing in Korea. As a result, if employment declines and people's livelihoods continue to suffer , the current German rum economy is bound to age. The third is the welfare needs of low-burdened and high-benefit people. They should enjoy their welfare as much as possible for free. Both pensions and health insurance become deficits if you pay less money and maximize your benefits. You all know that if we have a pension or health insurance in our country, how much of it becomes a deficit? People who pay pensions in their 30s now will not receive a penny of their pension when they reach their 60s. No one knows it. The government knows it, and the NGOs know it . So what should I do? Shouldn't we increase pension withdrawal or reduce benefits? I mean, you can't do both. Political circles can't do that, either. If you do that, the people in charge will not give you the ticket, so you just drag it away. Later, if you hit a cliff, it will all be handed over to the state finances. Isn't that the case with the subway? The Seoul Subway is running a huge deficit. So you have to either raise the rate or reduce the cost by reducing the staff, but aren't you doing both? One is because of the resistance of the citizens, and one is not doing so because of the resistance of the unions. What if we go this way? It's becoming like Germany now. The next fourth factor is population suspensions and aging. When this happens, the productive forces are bound to drop. Finally, the fifth is the weakening of government control. When a problem arises, the government has to control and govern it, but the government's weakness doesn't work. Government words don't work. There is a prevalence of collective egoism and local egoism. The voices of NGOs, doctors, pharmacists, lawyers, and others put their own interests ahead of the interests of our society as a whole. In a situation where these people are actually leading the national public opinion, the media must correct it. When the media fails to play its role, it becomes what Myrdal calls a soft state, a soft state. A soft state is a so-called unordered state with no decree. That's why Murdal said that economic development should never happen in soft countries. In other words, if the government's decree is in place, and the control is not in place, economic development will not be achieved. There are two kinds of control. One is how to stand in a dictatorial power, as Korea has done in the past. Another is how to build on civic rationalism. This is how we do it in developed countries. In South Korea , the autocratic power has disappeared and civic rationalism has not survived. So it's becoming a problem now. Let's wrap it up. There should not be an aging phenomenon in the economy. You need to catch this quickly and take action. Germany and other European countries have been aware of the aging problem and have failed to correct it. This is because the state has not been under control. But in my view, South Korea has that kind of control. I think our people have their own control. For these five age-inducing phenomena, I believe that the government, the people, and the corporations are capable of solving problems through awareness. I repeat, the past 40-50 years of development in our country are a series of crises. If we only looked at that crisis, the Korean economy would have already collapsed. There is no room for further development. Was there a crisis or two? however The many crises we experienced in the '60s, '70s, '80s, and '90s were the driving force behind the development of the Korean economy. I think the same is true of our current economy. We must join in building the advanced Korea of the future with confidence and perseverance . I will conclude by concluding that if the government, the business and the people all work together to overcome the pain of the present situation and alleviate it, the prospects for tomorrow's Korean economy are very bright. Thanks.

Title: Findings on the Korean Economy
text: Hosted by the Korean Economic Association Luncheon Address of the President of the International Conference Matters Concerning the Korean Economy 2006. 8. 9. Lee Sung-tae, President of Bank of Korea Dear Honorable President Chung Un-chan of the Korean Economic Association, President Kim Seok-hee of the Korean Economic Society, and Dear Attendees , First of all, it is very nice to meet you at a conference organized by the Korea Economic Association on the theme of "Prosperity for All". As experts at home and abroad have had a difficult time together , we expect that good measures for the future of the Korean economy can be derived. Now let me briefly share some of the thoughts I have about our economy. As you are well aware, the Korean economy has faced many trials since the beginning of industrialization in the early 1960s, but it has continued to develop while overcoming them well. The devastation of the homeland caused by the war, the constraints of lack of capital and resources, the two oil shocks, repeated social unrest and geopolitical risks , etc. Nevertheless, the Korean economy has succeeded in compressive growth. In particular, the foreign exchange crisis that occurred at the end of 1997 has also been able to overcome in an unprecedented short period of time. These economic achievements are thought to have been possible after World War 2 because the open world economic conditions and policy efforts to maximize latecomer profits by utilizing quality human resources were well combined with the will of the people. However , after overcoming the foreign exchange crisis, as the growth pattern has changed from the past, the voices of concern for our economy are rising again. Growth is showing a tendency to weaken as the cycle of economic fluctuations shortens, and as exports increase, investment and employment are not increasing as much as in the past. These phenomena seem to lead to concerns that there may have been a problem with the growthteam. On top of that, there seems to be concern that the phenomenon of polarization between sectors and classes, which is rarely mitigated, will continue to hold back growth, and that the Korean economy will gradually lose strength between China and Japan. As such, the weakening of the growth momentum of the Korean economy is believed to be a phenomenon that occurs as restructuring proceeds in a way that allows it to adapt to the new international economic order. Recently, the environment surrounding our economy has changed significantly, with the center of growth shifting to technology and knowledge-based industries, and competition between companies intensifying across borders , and the rapid emergence of a huge low-wage economy such as China. Sectors that have adapted well to changes in internal and external conditions and have succeeded in restructuring are gaining momentum and vitality , while those that lag behind in the restructuring process are either stopping or retreating in growth. In the process of restructuring the industry around high-tech industries such as IT and knowledge-based services, SMEs and self-employed people centered on the traditional chimney industry are gradually declining. As a result, many sectors are suffering, and the entire economy is experiencing weaker growth and increasing uncertainty. In addition, the difficulties are being aggravated by the addition of the price of oil and the strength of the yuan. In such a situation, it would be preferable to prepare for the future by striving for a restructuring rather than being nazily tied to short-term growth figures. Improving the unreasonable system of external opening that is accelerating and the sphere We should use the coordination as an opportunity to accelerate coordination to further strengthen the international competitiveness of manufacturing while at the same time transforming the low-productivity service sector into a high-value industry. At the same time, the aging phenomenon of the economy must be prevented. We must eliminate the high-cost structure and improve the inefficiencies of the labor market and the welfare needs of low-burden, high-benefit people. We will also need to be prepared for the rapid slowdown in population growth and the fast-paced phenomenon of aging. In order to solve these challenges efficiently, we believe that it is necessary to first operate the economy in a way that makes full use of market functions. In line with the rapidly changing domestic and international economic environment, the market and We will have to continue to adjust the role of the government. It is important to leave the sectors that need creative innovation from the private sector to the market to prevent the possibility of a government failure that may result in a greater reduction in economic benefits than market failure. The government should use the function of coordination based on civic rationalism to quickly eliminate various economic aging people, including collective and regional egoism. In particular, it is urgent to encourage entrepreneurship and create an environment where companies can boldly challenge the uncertain risks of the future. On the other hand, I think it is desirable that macroeconomic policies be pursued based on an accurate perception of the economic situation. For example, if the slowdown in growth is primarily due to a pre-structural crisis , the policy focuses on strengthening the quality of the economy while enduring some degree of suffering rather than short-term stimulus measures . That would be great. If you can accurately understand the economic situation, it may not be too difficult to determine the direction of the policy. The problem , however, is that the perception of the situation can be different depending on the view of one and the same economic pattern. That's why I think it's very important to create a consensus through in-depth discussions with experts. We expect that such a  to be provided by this conference. I hope that there will also be ways to go to a prosperous Korea. Thanks.
