Title: BOK International Conference 2015 Opening Company
text: Opening Address Juyeol Lee Governor The Bank of Korea 2015 Annual Bank of Korea International Conference June 8-9, Seoul, Korea Good morning, Distinguished speakers and participants, I welcome you all to the 2015 Bank of Korea International Conference. I would like to begin by expressing special thanks to the conference co- orgnizers, Professors Thomas Sargent and Barry Eichengreen', to the keynote speakers, IMF Deputy Managing Director Mitsuhiro Furusawa and OECD Economic Development and Review Committee Chairman William White', and to all of the session speakers, moderators, discussants, and panelists for their contributions to this conference. In the wake of the global financial crisis, countries policymakers undertook prompt and proactive policy measures to relieve financial turmoil and revive the momentum of economic recovery. As a result, the global economy, recovering to some degree from the impact of the crisis, is now at the stage of seeking transitions toward a New Normal including monetary policy normalization. Monetary policy normalization, which the U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to commence on the premise of economic recovery, may prove positive for the global economy. Amid recent economic slowdown in China and other emerging-market economies, however, concerns about weak growth and low inflation still remain in many countries. 1 Against this backdrop, I believe that this conference is both meaningful and timely in exploring and coping with potential risks associated with global interest rate normalization. Unconventional monetary policy including quantitative easing in major advanced economies has largely been recognized as a positive contribution to the recovery of economic and financial stability. However, various potential risks have piled up with the expansion of global liquidity in the post-crisis era. We should hence be keenly aware that these risks could be realized in the course of advanced economies monetary policy normalization. Let me touch briefly now on some of these risks. First, during the prolonged period of accommodative monetary policy to date, economic agents resilence to shocks from rising interest rates may have weakened. With global liquidity expanding due to large-scale quantitative easing and zero interest rates, economic agents have piled up debts and investment in risky assets. Should interest rates rise with the Feds monetary policy normalization, there are concerns that households, firms and financial institutions will bear increased payment burdens and incur investment losses, resulting in financial system unrest. This can in turn lead to a contraction of the real economy. Next, when the U.S. Federal Reserve embarks on interest rate normalization, the withdrawal of the international investment funds from emerging-market economies could heighten volatilities in the foreign- 2 exchange and financial markets. As we saw during the "taper tantrum in May 2013, abrupt capital outflows can bring about surges in exchange rates and interest rates in emerging-market economies having weak fundamentals, and thereby affect growth and inflation. The continued quantitative easing by the ECB and the Bank of Japan can of course ameliorate the risk of capital outflows. Given the large dollar exposure in total global liquidity, however, U.S. interest rate normalization is likely to cause escalating capital flow volatility. Now, I would like to say a few words about policy tasks to contain these potential risks from three aspects. First, we need to enhance our economic resilience to external shocks, through continued efforts to strengthen our economic fundamentals. To this end, monetary and fiscal policies should assign priority to appropriate responses to this low-growth and low- inflation phenomenon, ensuring that economic vitality does not decline. Nonetheless, such counter-cyclical measures alone may not suffice to reverse declining growth potential owing to structural factors, so that structural reforms need to be steadily pursued as well. Importantly, resolving sectoral imbalances and other structural weaknesses will help countries enter better states of the New Normal, with higher productivity and efficiency in resource allocation. Second, by deploying macro-prudential policy, we should alleviate financial risks such as debt accumulations. Highly-indebted countries are at greater risk of financial system turbulence stemming from increased debt service burdens and capital outflows following interest rate 3 normalization. Managing the associated risks is thus critical. If financial risks are well-managed, through appropriate macro-prudential policy, then the flexibility and effectiveness of monetary policy can be enhanced as well. Third and lastly, I think that international cooperation in monetary policy conduct and in supporting financial stability is also crucial. Given the deepening interconnectedness of the global economy, the global effects of monetary policy in major advanced economies have become substantial. Hence, central banks in these countries should maintain transparency and consistency in their conduct of monetary policy, while also communicating closely with central banks in other countries, to minimize negative spillovers including market overreactions. Also, to strengthen our capacity of crisis management, we should keep striving for global coordinationfor example, through enlarging the global financial safety net including currency swaps. Ladies and Gentlemen, The world economy is now facing a turning point, which calls for unwinding of the unconventional monetary policy introduced after the global financial crisis. The world economys New Normal, and thus the welfare of both our current and future generations, will depend on how we respond to the evolving situation down the road. 4 I look forward very much to a variety of insightful ideas being proposed through enthusiastic discussions and constructive sharing of opinions in this conference, and hope that the proposed ideas lead to tangible outcomes. Thank you. 5

Title: Opening of the Bank of Korea-Yonsei University International Conference
text: Opening Address Juyeol Lee Governor The Bank of Korea The Bank of Korea-Yonsei University Conference October 23, 2015 Seoul, Korea Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. It is a pleasure for me to welcome you to the Bank of Korea-Yonsei University Conference. I wish first to express my sincere gratitude to Mr. Claudio Borio, Head of the Monetary and Economic Department at the BIS, who will deliver the keynote speech; to Professor Kap-Young Jeong, President of Yonsei University, for his welcoming remarks; and to all of the speakers, discussants and panelists participating here today. And let me congratulate Yonsei Universitys College of Commerce and Economics, on celebrating their 100th anniversary this year. As we all know, the international financial markets are experiencing frequent unrest now due to the so-called G2 risks  from the forthcoming policy rate hikes in the US, and from the economic slowdown in China. Uncertainties concerning global growth have also been growing. Against this backdrop, I believe todays conference provides a valuable platform to assess financial stability, and to discuss ways to strengthen the financial system. From the financial stability perspective, the biggest risk confronting our world economy is the international spillover from US monetary policy normalization. Once it begins, the rise in US interest rates may lead to outflows from emerging markets of the liquidity that had once overflowed into them. This could have a heavy toll on EMEs, through channels in both the financial and real sectors. The capital outflows from these economies could fuel financial market instability, such as currency depreciations and stock price declines. And increases in their market interest rates could delay the recoveries of their real economies. Another major risk is the unrest in Chinas financial sector and real economy. For emerging countries that have grown together with - i - China, this could undermine their financial stability and weaken their growth momentum. In particular, a decline in Chinese import demand, along with weakening commodity prices, could aggravate financial and economic conditions in both Asian emerging and commodity-exporting countries. And considering that emerging markets share in the world economy has now grown greatly, their economic difficulties could also negatively affect the world as a whole. In fact, the international financial market shock in August, fueled by China risk, turned out to be a global phenomenon that affected advanced and emerging economies alike. The world economy is now at a critical juncture. But this is an inevitable consequence of US monetary policy normalization, and of the Chinese normalization of their growth model. In the case of the US, as its economy gradually recovers, it is moving its monetary policy away from the ultra-accommodative stance of the past few years. Chinas economic slowdown, meanwhile, has appeared in the course of its transition to a more balanced and sustainable growth model. As we can see, the US rate hike and the slowdown in China are far from being one-off events. They are expected to persist for some time, and so it is imperative that countries be prepared for this. Fortunately, since the global financial crisis our capacities for responding to external risks have grown, in both the country-specific and the international dimensions. Korea and other emerging economies have worked to improve their external soundness, by enhancing their current account balances, foreign reserve holdings, and exchange rate flexibility. Many countries have strengthened their - 2 - financial regulations, while also deepening their international cooperation with one another. These efforts have ensured the soundness of financial institutions and increased their resilience to external shocks. However, there are some emerging markets with weak fundamentals still exposed to considerable difficulties, due to the G2 risks combined with their own inherent vulnerabilities. Their overvalued currencies and assets are likely to fall in value in the event of large capital outflows and rising interest rates. This may worsen their financial stabilities, and cause their economic downturns to deepen. In consideration of all these points, I believe that emerging economies need to redouble their efforts to enhance their financial stability going forward. First, they need to continue the efforts to ensure macroeconomic and financial soundness, in preparation against any future external shocks. They need to boost their external payment capacities, for instance, by improving their current account balances through enhancement of their export competitiveness. They also need to establish proper macroprudential policy frameworks in the FX sectors. More essentially, it is important that emerging markets work to improve their economic fundamentals. They will also need to promote balanced growth, through increasing domestic consumption and carrying out structural reforms of their labor markets. Second, emerging countries need to reduce excessive private debts, and to improve their debt structures. Any increase in market rates will heighten households burdens in repaying their accumulated debts. And as this may degrade financial stability, and stall economic - 3 - recovery, the policy authorities need to bring household debt under control. They should also devote efforts to restructure marginal companies, while closely looking into the potential vulnerabilities of domestic and foreign debts in their business sectors. Third, cooperation among our various policy authorities domestically, and among our various countries internationally, is even more important now than ever. The authorities are urged to seek country-specific policy mixes, in order to achieve the somewhat conflicting policy goals of supporting economic recovery while at the same time securing financial stability. Advanced economies must also try to minimize any negative global spillover effects of their policies, by carrying them out as transparently and predictably as possible. Todays conference is especially significant, I believe, since we will examine major risks to financial stability at this critical turning point for the global economy, while also looking into what the policy authorities roles should be in this regard. And I think this event will also be a valuable opportunity to share our individual knowledge and experiences. Let me thank you all once again, for taking the time from your busy schedules to be with us here today. - 4 -

Title: Commissioner Hamjunho 2015 AEPC Presentation (US)
text: FRBSF 2015 Asia Economic Policy Conference Safeguarding Financial Stability in a Diverging Global Economy Joon-Ho Hahm Member of Monetary Policy Board, Bank of Korea I feel truly delighted and privileged to speak in the policy panel discussion at this renowned conference. In my remarks today I will start with a contextual preamble, by characterizing the current state of the global economy in comparison with previous episodes of U.S. interest rate hikes. I will then discuss the macroprudential policies introduced in Korea since the global financial crisis, and the potential risks and policy challenges that Korea now faces. Finally, I will conclude by considering the financial stability policy framework and the role of the central bank. 1. Upcoming Federal Reserve Rate Hike and EMEs: How Is This Time Different? Compared with the three most recent episodes of U.S. interest rate hikes, in 1994, 1999, and 2004, the current state of emerging market economies (EMEs) appears quite different. First of all, in the past both advanced economies and EMEs were in the midst of business cycle upturns prior to the U.S. rate hikes, and the upward growth in EMEs actually accelerated after the hikes. However, the currently approaching U.S. rate hike is expected to occur during business cycle downturns in EMEs, and may thus lead to further divergences in growth between EMEs and advanced economies (see Figure 1A). Second, not only is the amount of global liquidity that has flowed into EMEs much higher now, due to the unprecedented volume of quantitative easing, but the composition of capital inflows to EMEs has also changed noticeably. While banks were the main channel of cross-border capital flows in the past, it is now equity and bond portfolio investment that account for 65 percent of total capital inflows (see Figure IB). And the sheer volume of portfolio investment flows has led to a stronger coupling of financial asset prices across EMEs and advanced economies, irrespective 1 of their recent decoupling in terms of their business cycles. As one example, due to large cross-border bond investment flows, the correlation between long-term interest rates in the United States and EMEs has changed from -0.3 before the global crisis to 0.8 since the crisis. Third, the expansion in global liquidity has led to a dramatic compression in credit risk and liquidity premiums on emerging market assets. Term premiums on long-term emerging market bonds have fallen to levels similar to those in the United States (see Figure 1C). This compression of risk premiums and cheap credit have brought about a significant rise in debt leverage in EMEs, in contrast to the case with advanced economies that have seen deleveraging since the crisis (see Figure ID). While the accommodative monetary policies in the Euro zone and Japan may continue, and offset the capital outflows from EMEs to some extent, these features of the current situation suggest that the upcoming U.S. interest rate normalization could have larger than expected impacts on EMEs, if it is combined with other destabilizing factors such as the slowdown in the Chinese economy and a further decline in commodity prices. They also suggest that the financial markets and shadow banking could become important channels of crisis propagation this time. If the U.S. rate hike leads to a collapse in global risk appetite, credit and term premiums on emerging market assets could soar. And the resulting fire sales of global risky assets could precipitate crises in some EMEs, irrespective of their banking sector and external balance sheet soundness. 2. Macroprudential Policies in Korea since the Global Financial Crisis As emphasized in our paper presented at this conference four years ago (Hahm et al. 2012), for addressing financial imbalances preemptively in open EMEs macroprudential policy is more desirable than monetary policy. This is because financial cycles in open EMEs are often driven by global liquidity conditions, irrespective of the local economic situation. And monetary policy leaning against the credit cycle is often unavailable for EMEs, as tighter monetary policy would only attract additional capital inflows, further amplifying the credit cycle. In the aftermath of the global financial crisis, Korea has introduced a variety of macroprudential policy tools to make its financial system more resilient and less 2 procyclical. On the external front, Korea introduced a leverage cap on foreign exchange derivatives positions in 2010 and a macroprudential bank levy on noncore foreign currency bank liabilities in 2011, while reinstating taxation of foreigners bond investment in 2011 as well, in efforts to ensure that capital inflows through banks and the bond markets do not lead to excessive procyclicality in our financial system. The macroprudential bank levy deserves special attention. As evidenced in Hahm, Shin, and Shin (2013) and in Bruno and Shin (2015), rapid accumulations of noncore bank liabilities signal vulnerabilities to systemic risk spillovers in EMEs, and fluctuations in banks noncore liabilities are directly linked to cross-border capital flows. Therefore, as non-core foreign currency bank liabilities may lead to complicated interconnectedness among domestic and foreign banks, and their unwinding may cause significant negative externalities, their correction using appropriate macroprudential tools is totally legitimate. On the internal front, in order to avoid credit and housing bubbles Korea strengthened its loan-to-value (LTV) and debt service-to-income (DTI) regulations for home mortgage loans in 2009, while reinstating the loan-to-deposit ratio regulation in 2010. Until now these diverse macroprudential policies seem to have helped to contain the buildup of financial imbalances. At this stage, it is estimated that the gap between Koreas credit cycle and its long-run trend is not large, and the banking sectors noncore liability and external debt structures are relatively sound (see Figure 2). It is also worth noting that our countercyclical macroprudential policies have provided the central bank with wider policy space to focus more on output and price stability. 3. Potential Financial Vulnerabilities and Policy Challenges Notwithstanding these preemptive efforts, in the run-up to U.S. interest rate normalization the containment of potential financial instabilities has emerged as a crucial policy challenge in Korea. First of all, a rise in the U.S. policy rate could trigger outflows of short-term capital, giving rise thereby to significant negative externalities for our real economy. Secondly, the trend of increasing household debt has accelerated since last year, due to the temporary easing of the LTV and DTI regulations together with our reduced policy interest rate. Let me touch briefly now on these two potential risks to financial stability. 3 With regard to the capital outflow risk, foreign capital flows in Korea have remained stable despite the recent global financial turmoil, in line with the Korean economys having been differentiated from other EMEs due to its relatively sound economic fundamentals and robust external balance. However, with the global shift in the composition of capital flows, the shares of stock and bond portfolio investment have increased rapidly in Korea as well, while bank borrowings have remained stable due partly to the macroprudential policies that I mentioned earlier (see Figure 3A). If we look at the time-series properties of foreign capital flows in Korea, the volatility of foreign portfolio investment has been relatively high compared with those in advanced economies and other EMEs. The foreign capital flow volume has been affected not only by factors such as our interest rate differential and growth gap against advanced economies but also by purely exogenous global factors such as global credit growth and the VIX (volatility index) in the global financial markets. Further, the impact of foreign capital flows on domestic financial market volatilities for example, of our stock prices and foreign exchange rateshas grown greatly in the post-global-crisis period. Koreas financial and foreign exchange markets have become much more resilient recently, as demonstrated by the impulse responses of the won-dollar exchange rate to a one-unit VIX shock, and this shows that effects are dissipating much faster in the post-crisis period (see Figure 3B). But given that Koreas financial market is quite open, that global institutional investors such as banks and mutual funds are responsible for a large share of portfolio investment flows there, and that these investors tend to reallocate their country portfolios from a global perspective, some possibility of capital outflows does exist despite our robust domestic economic fundamentals. Next let me move on to the household debt issue. Koreas household debt-to-GDP ratio, including the debt of small household enterprises, reached 85 percent at the end of 2014, possibly approaching a threshold level beyond which it may constrain consumption spending. Cecchetti, Mohanty, and Zampolli (2011), for example, suggest this threshold level to be around 85 percent. Given this large volume of household debt, any future rise in interest rates could hamper private consumption through increases in households debt service burdens, and debt defaults by vulnerable households could then undermine the lending banks capital soundness. At this point the possibility of such systemic risk materializing is judged to be low. According to our 4 stress-test results (Bank of Korea 2015), for instance, under a combined shock of a 200 basis point rise in interest rates and a 10 percent housing price decline, the proportion of households at risk would increase to 14.2 percent, from 10.3 percent at present, and the proportion of debt at risk to 32.3 percent, from 19.3 percent, which could be absorbed through the current buffers in bank capital. Housing prices also do not seem so greatly overvalued in Korea. The increases in our price-to-income ratio and price-to-rent ratio have been modest compared with those in other OECD countries (see Figure 4), suggesting that the risk of rapid housing price adjustment may not be high in Korea. However, if the current trend of growth in household debt persists, then the upturns of our credit and housing cycles may bring about excessive disparities with the underlying fundamentals such as household income and debt service capacity. It is therefore imperative that we come up with preemptive countercyclical macroprudential measures now. And in this context, the supervisory authority recently announced policy measures to (i) improve the mortgage debt structure by accelerating the switch to fixed-rate and amortized loans, and (ii) strengthen bank lending assessments of borrowers repayment capacities. 4. Financial Stability Policy Framework and the Central Bank As I have noted, the latent risk and potential effects associated with the upcoming U.S. interest rate hike could be large in EMEs, and Korea would not be exempt. In this context, the Bank of Korea has devoted persistent efforts to expanding its financial stability role. First, as a key participant in the macroprudential policy governance scheme, we conduct in-depth analyses and assessments of systemic risk, prepare the Financial Stability Report, and work hard to communicate with the public. We also conduct co-examinations of banks and participate in macroprudential councils with other government bodies. In addition to our macroprudential policy-related roles, as the monetary policy authority we devote steady efforts to improving our monetary policy strategy framework so as to incorporate financial stability concerns when formulating optimal policies. While I believe that macroprudential policies must be the first line of defense in open EMEs, there are reasons why these policies are not always sufficiently effective. Macroprudential supervision could, for example, be subject to more political 5 pressures than monetary policy, since it has direct bearings on the business of financial institutions, and policy inaction bias could result. Further, accommodative monetary policies that do not consider financial stability concerns may lead to excessive risk taking. Low interest rates may, among other results, lead to excessive search for yield, expanded leverage through valuation effects, and lower risk premiums. Various approaches can be used to consider financial stability risks in formulating monetary policy strategy. For instance, we need to consider the financial stability implications in setting our medium-term inflation target, which is currently revised every three years in Korea. And we can consider financial stability risks in setting the target path for output. One example here would be the finance-neutral potential GDP growth rate and output gap as suggested by Borio, Disyatat, and Juselius (2013). We could also use estimates of a real neutral interest rate that takes the financial cycle into consideration. However, when monetary policy is conducted with financial stability in mind, we will also need to be very cautious about any unintended consequencesfor instance, the risk of its reducing inflation expectations through weakening public confidence in the central banks commitment to inflation targeting. Ultimately, it is essential to conduct our macroprudential and monetary policies in a harmonized and complementary manner. To achieve this we need an effective, operating macroprudential policy governance scheme, which guarantees timely information sharing and cooperation among the related institutions. In addition, in order to maintain our monetary policy independence and secure political neutrality in macroprudential policy, relevant institutional devices are needed within the policy framework. For instance, we need devices to enhance the transparency and accountability of the macroprudential policymaking scheme, and we also need to clearly define the central banks role related to macroprudential policy. For open EMEs, in the end, the effective coordination of monetary and macroprudential policies will be the key to simultaneous achievement of the objectives of price stability, output stability, and financial stability. Title: Impact of Global Financial Regulatory Reforms on Asia and Challenges Posed
Subtitle: Keynote Speech for 2013 IIF Asia CEO Summit
text: Impact of Global Financial Regulatory Reforms on Asia and Challenges Posed Choongsoo Kim Governor Bank of Korea Keynote Speech for 2013 IIF Asia CEO Summit May 10, 2013, Seoul, Korea It is a great pleasure for me to speak to you here this morning, at this 2013 IIF Asia CEO Summit, and I would like to thank Dr. Yoon-Dae Euh, Chairman and CEO of KB Financial Group, and Mr. Timothy Adams, President and CEO of Institute of International Finance, for inviting me. As had been the case with other crises in the past, the costs for cleaning up the recent global financial crisis were colossal as well. Plummeting growth rates following a crisis tend to cause permanent costs, as countries cannot return to their pre-crisis GDP-growth paths even with the passage of time1), and these costs in present value terms are extremely high. It is therefore critical to detect potential financial crises before they occur, and pre-empt them. The regulatory reform proposals that are now being prepared on a global level to enhance financial system resilience, with the cooperation of policy authorities of each jurisdiction centering around the FSB, the BCBS and the CPSS, are endeavors along these lines. Once these global financial regulatory reforms are carried out successfully, I believe that they will contribute substantially to the upgrading of Asias financial system. In Asias emerging market countries, whose real economies are leading world economic growth but where finance is relatively lagging in development, there are wide gaps between the real and the financial sectors. Until now financial institutions intermediary functions have been incapable of adequately supporting the dynamic activities of the real economy, and considerable portions of the needed capital have been funded externally. We should in this regard wholeheartedly embrace the global regulatory reforms and capitalize on the opportunities that they provide us to advance our financial systems, while moving away 1) IMF (October 2009), What's the damage? Medium-term output dynamics after financial crises, World Economic Outlook Chapter 4 1/15 from any perception of these reforms as shackles constraining our financial activities. I believe this will not only be conducive to preventing future crises, but also lay the foundation for Asias continued growth. Because the financial regulatory reforms are being pushed forward at the global level, however, there could be instances in which unintended consequences result, or where the circumstances of regions and countries with different financial market characteristics and degrees of development are not taken adequately into account, and there is thus a need to devise adequate measures in response2). In my speech today, I will first explain briefly the developments to date concerning the global financial regulatory reforms, and then go over their impacts on Asia, and finally offer my views on how Asia should respond. Global Financial Regulatory Reforms to Date Let me now take you through the global financial regulatory reforms to date. The global regulatory reforms are being led by the FSB, under the mandate given it by the G20 Summit, and the related discussions evolve around the regulatory standard-setters such as the BCBS and the CPSS, covering the following areas: The first set of reforms is meant to improve responsiveness in times of crisis by enhancing the resilience of financial institutions. 2) This perception led to the G20 Seoul Summit Leaders Declaration agreeing to reflect emerging market economies perspectives more in the global financial regulatory reforms, and asking the FSB to conduct reviews of issues in which emerging market economies show particular interest with regard to financial regulation. 2/15 Some examples of the work pursued along these lines include the stronger capital regulations and new liquidity and leverage regulations under Basel III. The second set of discussions is aimed at resolving the moral hazard issue arising from the Too-Big-to-Fail problem. This involves stricter regulations on global systemically important financial institutions, G-SIFIs, as well as on domestic systemically important banks, D-SIBs. The third group of reforms attempt to eliminate regulatory loopholes. The discussions here cover stronger shadow banking regulations, and reforms of the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives markets and the clearing and settlement infrastructures. And the fourth area of reform being covered relates to the efforts underway such as the work on setting the new Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, the PFMIs, which promote seamless clearing and settlement through FMIs even under extreme market stress conditions. Additional discussions taking place include those aimed at reduction of the reliance on credit rating agencies and at the convergence of global accounting standards. The basic regulatory frameworks are for the most part complete by now, while in some other areas active discussions are currently underway internationally to draft the related rules texts. The basic regulatory designs have now been completed for the Basel III capital regulations, the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), the strengthened regulations of G-SIFIs and D-SIBs, the OTC derivatives market 3/15 reform, and the enhancement of risk management by financial institutions and FMI operators. The areas in which the work is currently still either proceeding, or in which its progress has been delayed, are as follows: First, with regard to the proposed Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), a component of the Basel III liquidity regulations scheduled to take effect from 2018, as well as the regulations on leverage and shadow banking and the fundamental review of the trading book, the specifics are currently being discussed. Second, while there has been significant progress in the work on convergence of accounting standards between the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), it still lags behind the original schedule. And finally, related to trade repository reporting, which is being pushed in order to enhance OTC derivatives market transparency, considerable strides have been made in the drafting of international recommendations and revising the relevant laws of each jurisdiction. Full-scale enforcement is expected to be delayed, however, since in many countries TRs have not yet been established. Meanwhile, for the successful completion of the global regulatory reform work, implementing the reforms consistently across jurisdictions is as important as drafting the reform proposals. The FSB, BCBS, IMF and CPSS-IOSCO are all encouraging implementation in each jurisdiction, through their progress reports, peer reviews, Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP) and monitoring of the implementation of principles. 4/15 Impact on Asia of Global Regulatory Reforms Let me now move on to the impact of the global regulatory reforms on Asia. Attempts at comprehensive, accurate analysis of the impacts on the global economy of the global regulatory reforms have limitations, because in addition to the fact that a variety of regulations are being newly introduced simultaneously, for some regulations the discussions are still ongoing. Bearing these limitations in mind, however, when judging the overall costs and benefits of the reforms I expect that, while they will have short-term costs, their positive impacts in the medium- to longer-term will be much larger. According to a study on the macro-economic impacts of the capital and G-SIFIs regulations conducted by the BCBS, global GDP is estimated to fall by as much as an annual 0.34% when the regulations are introduced, owing to higher lending costs and credit contractions, but the benefits from improved financial institution soundness and prevention of financial crisis recurrence will eventually reach 2.5% of global GDP per year3). Although this study was not Asia-specific, I would expect similar outcomes for Asia as well. Moreover, Asia has had previous experience in strengthening the fabric of its financial system, in the aftermath of the 1997 foreign exchange crisis. In overcoming that crisis, the soundness of our financial institutions was improved and their resilience enhanced through financial industry restructuring and the resolutions of non-viable financial institutions. As a consequence Asia was able to withstand the very large shocks spreading out from the major financial centers during the recent crisis. This can be taken as ex-ante material 3) Macroeconomic Assessment Group (MAG) (October 2011), Assessment of the macroeconomic impact of higher loss absorbency for global systemically important banks. Jointly set up by the FSB and the BCBS, the MAG assessed the impacts of capital regulations and the G-SIB capital surcharge regulations on the macroeconomy. 5/15 evidence that the current global regulatory reforms should also work in favor of the revamping of Asias financial sector going forward. In addition, given that these reforms are comprehensive in their coverage, which also includes non-bank financial institutions, once these reform measures are codified in the financial systems of all Asian countries I expect their shock absorption capacities to be dramatically raised and their financial system advancements expedited. When such efforts to systemize the global regulatory framework are combined with the persistent pursuit of Asian financial integration, I believe the resultant synergies will elevate Asian financial systems to higher grounds. There is a possibility meanwhile of some of the regulations exerting relatively strong influences on the Asian financial sector, or bringing about the following unintended consequences: First, while G-SIFIs headquartered in Asian jurisdictions are small in number, many G-SIFIs from advanced economies are operating actively in Asia through subsidiaries or branches4). But when the capital surcharges are imposed on these G-SIFIs they could pass on the regulatory burdens to their counterparties by raising their lending rates or respond by deleveraging, and so a rise in funding costs for Asian financial institutions and a contraction in credit could result. The fact that capital flow volatility in Asia is high is another cause for concern. Capital may now be flowing into Asia, on the back of its relatively favorable economic environment, high interest rates and expectations of local currency strengthening5). There is a potential, however, for a sudden reversal should deleveraging reoccur, 4) Of the 28 banks chosen as G-SIBs, only four are from Asian countries, but all 28 G-SIBs operate in Asia through subsidiaries or branches.. 5) Financial Stability Report (October 2011), Deutsche Bank, Emerging markets capital flows what has changed? (February 2013) 6/15 due to the global financial regulatory reforms or to advanced economies' disorderly exits from quantitative easing. Second, in a situation in which the supply of long-dated funds has been substantially rolled back, as large global banks have reduced their syndicated loans and other long-term lending since the financial crisis6), the introduction of the global regulatory reforms may have negative impacts. Third, unlike in the US and Europe, shadow banking in Asia performs functions that include the supply of financial services to small- and medium-sized enterprises and low income households, financial inclusion, and means for diversifying investment. Therefore, if regulations are applied that do not take such characteristics into account, it is feared that these positive functions will be undermined. Fourth, according to the proposal for OTC derivatives market reform, high capital and margins will be imposed on transactions that are not cleared through CCPs. My view is that this could place Asia at a disadvantage of having its regulations strengthened to the advanced country level, without meaningful benefits in consequence, given that its derivatives market size has not yet grown sufficiently7). And finally, in order for FMI operators to comply with the global regulatory standards on credit and liquidity risk, they must accumulate considerable amounts of additional financial resources. The likelihood is high, however, of this burden being ultimately passed on to their participant banks. 6) G20 (February 2013), "Long-term investment financing for growth and development" 7) In 2010 Asia's shares in the global OTC derivatives transaction volume was 2.8% for interest rate derivatives and 13.7% for FX derivatives (BIS, Triennial Central Bank Survey of Foreign Exchange and Derivatives Market Activity, 2010) 7/15 Asian Financial Sector Challenges I would now like to speak on the key challenges that the Asian financial sector must first address. To begin, despite the high household savings rates in most Asian countries, firms have been relying on external funding for substantial portions of their financing. This reliance on external funding must be dramatically lowered, by revitalizing the financial intermediary function that channels the regions savings back into domestic demand such as investment. It is a fact of life also that the major suppliers of safe assets to the global financial markets have mostly been the financial sectors of advanced countries. The Asian financial sector, too, must build up its capacity to create safe, globally marketable assets. Going forward, as financial integration progresses in Asia its interconnectedness will increase, and this will work to heighten systemic risks. This indicates to us that an ex-ante mechanism is needed for the control of risks that might arise from the cross-sectional dimension. The endeavors of individual policy authorities alone are not enough to achieve the tasks that I have just mentioned. In addition, coordination among the policy authorities in our region is needed, as well as close cooperation with our financial markets and financial institutions. I believe that we policy authorities in Asia must, to begin with, focus our policy capacities in the following areas: First, aligning and maintaining our own financial systems so that the global regulatory reforms may be smoothly implemented is essential. To maintain the momentum of the global regulatory reforms and eliminate any room for cross-border regulatory arbitrage, the 8/15 policy authorities must devote efforts to designing legal and institutional systems that will allow all countries to simultaneously implement the proposed regulations. Given that G-SIFIs activities in Asia through their subsidiaries and branches are brisk, authorities must establish a system for their efficient supervision and, in crisis situations, their orderly resolution. The Asian host countries concerned should participate actively in the supervisory colleges8) and crisis management groups9), and strengthen their close sharing of information and coordination of policies with the home supervisors. Adequate regulatory, surveillance and supervisory regimes must also be set up, to ensure that new clearing and settlement infrastructures such as OTC derivatives CCPs are built and operated. It is imperative as well that policy authorities participate actively in the process of making the global regulatory reform proposals, and unify Asias regional voice. Second, while closely monitoring for any side effects, including unintended consequences, that implementation of the global regulatory reforms might have on Asia, authorities must respond appropriately with policies as needed. Asian central banks in particular must reserve arsenals of policy responses for active reaction to any undermining of financial stability due to unintended consequences. There is a need, for example, for appropriate macroprudential policy instruments to deal with sudden capital inand outflows. Given also that Asia is greatly exposed to capital flow volatility in particular, the justification for the introduction of macroprudential instruments, and the difference between these 8) In general, supervisory colleges refer to multilateral working groups of relevant supervisors that are formed for effective consolidated supervision of international banking groups (BCBS, Good practice principles on supervisory colleges, October 2010). 9) The home and host authorities of all G-SIFIs should maintain Crisis Management Groups with the objective of enhancing the preparedness for, and facilitating the management and resolution of, any cross-border financial crisis affecting that particular G-SIFI (FSB, Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions, October 2011). 9/15 instruments and capital controls should be explained to the international community with a united voice. The fact that the IMF has recently recognized the appropriateness of macroprudential tools as a means of capital flow management represents a very significant change of perception in this regard. Third, should interest rates in advanced countries rise due to their executions of exit strategies going forward, then losses on holdings of advanced country bonds could be seen. And as the foreign funds that had been flowing in suddenly reverse, loans could turn sour from the drop in collateral value, and liquidity crunches could hit our markets. The shifts to tightening stances by the FRB, the ECB, the BOE and other major central banks could either be a synchronized unwinding or a sequenced unwinding. If its a synchronized unwinding, then the magnitude of its impacts on emerging market economies in the form of capital outflows will be very large, and in a sequenced unwinding as well, there will be a risk of the exchange rate volatilities of key currencies rising with each shift in the policy stance of a major central bank. It is therefore necessary, on the asset side, to continue our efforts to keep the market risks from interest rate surges at manageable levels, by way for example of stress tests, while on the liabilities side as well devising various measures, including macroprudential policies, to alleviate the pressures on fund outflows.10) Lastly, I believe policy authorities should work to fundamentally strengthen the fabric of Asias financial markets through financial market development, strengthening of financial safety nets, greater intra-regional financial transactions, and so forth. In order to boost our immunity to future crises and any unintended 10) Global interest rate risk: how should emerging markets prepare for the adjustment? (The Bank of Korea, April 2013) 10/15 consequences of the global regulatory reforms, it is essential that our regional economies capital markets, foreign exchange markets and derivatives markets be developed both qualitatively and quantitatively. In light of Asias past experiences, in which outbreaks of financial crises were caused primarily by international capital flow volatility, it is important that the regional financial safety net and regional financial integration be strengthened. I consider the augmentation of the Korea-China currency swap arrangement11) to be a good example of what I am talking about, and think that the CMIM, Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralization, must also be persistently improved. In Korea when the develeraging by European banks due to the European sovereign debt crisis in 2011 resulted in an exodus of their funds, an influx of Asian bond investment funds arrived in even greater amounts, relieving our burden of foreign currency liquidity management. This, in my view, illustrates the importance of financial integration through greater intra-regional financial transactions. If the global regulatory reforms are to succeed, I deem it of paramount importance to have the participation and cooperation of those of you here today in this room from the private sector. I ask that you be aware of the costs which could be incurred in the course of implementing the global regulatory reforms, and prepare thoroughly for these costs. The strengthening of regulations could result in burdens of having to raise the capital ratios and the shares of liquid asset holdings, higher overseas borrowing costs payable to G-SIFIs, and greater OTC derivatives transaction costs. It should be noted in consequence that profitability could in the short run contract. Next, it is important that you equip yourselves with the professional manpower and infrastructures required for complying with 11) In October 2011 Koreas bilateral currency swap with China (RMB 180 billion RMB 360 billion) was expanded. 11/15 the new global regulatory standards. When the proposed global regulatory reforms come into effect, the regulations will grow in variety, their rules become granular and the disclosure requirements become strengthened. In order to implement them as planned it will be vital to expand IT systems, recruit specialists, and strengthen staff education and training. The securing of the budgets necessary to make all this possible must also be considered. In keeping step with the global standards, I also ask that you strengthen your internal governance and risk management, and expand the disclosure of risk exposures. FMI operators must get on with improving their risk management arrangements in line with the PFMIs, so that while postulating various plausible market conditions and identifying the sources of risk that participants could cause, they can regulate them appropriately through regular monitoring. By introducing the LEIs, Legal Entity Identifiers12), and trade repository reporting as soon as possible to this end, the FMI operators must further strengthen market transparency, and to guarantee equal access to market participants, seek to rationalize membership criteria. There is a need as well to find a suitable growth model befitting the new global regulatory environment. Until now many financial institutions in Asia have adopted US and European business models as their growth prototypes, and gone after increasing their sizes, becoming globalized, strengthening their investment banking activities and expanding their operations in high-yield, complex instruments. With the current financial crisis and the global regulatory reforms as momentum, however, the modification of such strategies has become inevitable. You might now want to think prudently about 12) LEIs refer to unique identification numbers, and the FSB has taken the lead in preparing recommendations for systematically assigning LEIs to each entity in order to identify the parties to financial transactions (FSB, A Global Legal Entity Identifier for Financial Markets, June 2012). 12/15 new business models that leverage on Asias economic characteristics while satisfying the tighter global financial regulations. For instance, since many Asian countries external trade-oriented economic strategies have been showing limitations, due to the economic sluggishness of advanced countries, the need to promote domestic demand, for example in the service industry, has been raised. In Northeast Asia, moreover, demographic aging and support for the elderly are being highlighted as major issues13). Reflecting these kinds of changing circumstances in your business models will be something to think about. Lastly, I hope for your interest and support so that the views of the Asian private sector can be reflected in the course of drafting the proposals for global regulatory reforms. It is important to pro-actively deliver your views to your own policy authorities who are involved in making the regulatory reform proposals. Likewise, when the BCBS and other global regulatory rule-setters introduce new regulations, a process is followed in which consultative documents are prepared and public comments on them are invited. It is at these times that I hope you will work to actively advance your own views. 13) Andrew Sheng (December 2010), The new global financial landscape: Asia beware?, keynote address at the IGE/IMF International Conference on Reshaping the global financial landscape: An Asian perspective, Seoul 13/15 Concluding Remarks I have spoken at length until now on the impacts of the global regulatory reforms and on a number of the challenges that they pose, but would like to conclude by emphasizing just a couple of points. We must regard the global regulatory reforms not as a tightening of restrictions, but rather as an opportunity to rebuild Asias financial sector and actively embrace them. In particular, the main agents who will need to enforce the new global standards, and go out in search of new business models under the transformed landscape that results, are none other than those of you here today from the private sector. We policy authorities will of course lend you our undivided support. The FSBs Regional Consultative Group for Asia, which I co-chair, has for example been playing the role of consolidating the voice of Asia regarding the global regulatory reform proposals and passing them on to the international community. We will continue to serve actively as a conduit for communicating any suggestions that you may have. My hunch is that the makings of a future crisis are probably brewing right now, in some sector that we dont even suspect. It is in this regard important to prepare for new, unanticipated crises rather than crises that have already passed if we hope to prevent their recurrence going forward. If you look into past episodes, systemic risks had been building up when the economy was thriving and various indicators were stable, in a phenomenon termed the Minsky paradox14). And because Asia in particular has emerged relatively unscathed from the latest crisis, the likelihood is high for 14) Hyman P. Minsky (May 1992), The Financial Instability Hypothesis, The Jerome Levy Economics Institute of Bard College, Working Paper No. 74 14/15 risk appetite here to come roaring back when the economy recovers in the future. Should the degree of Asias financial development advance further, we can expect the global interconnectedness of our regions financial market infrastructures to deepen commensurately. And since the possibility increases of crisis contagion spreading rapidly with such a rise in interconnectedness, precautionary measures must be drawn up. In the discussions that follow, I trust that there will be dynamic exchanges of insightful views on wise and innovative ways of resolving the challenges that I have mentioned here today. Under such circumstances, the Bank of Korea will prioritize and operate the capacity of its members so that it can fulfill its assigned responsibilities and uphold its authority. text: 10-28-2010 Please handle this material from Friday, October 29, 2010 at 07:30 Title : Kim Chong-su, Governor of the Bank of Korea, Breakfast Lecture by the Chief Executive Officer of the Korea Trade Association , Bank of Korea Governor Kim Chong-su gave a lecture on the theme of "Recent Changes in Domestic and Foreign Economic Situation and Foreign Trade Conditions" at the Korea Trade Association's Chief Executive Officer Breakfast Meeting held at the Grand Intercontinental Hotel in Seoul on Friday, October 29. Attached: Part 1 of the main contents of the lecture. End. Contact: Ahn Sung-geun, Director of the Policy Investigation Team of the Policy Planning Bureau, Tel: (02) 759-4464 Public Affairs : Tel (02) 759-4015, 4016 "The Bank of Korea press release is also included on the Internet ( )." attached Korea Trade Association Chief Executive Officer Breakfast Lecture Recent economic situation at home and abroad Recent economic situation at home and abroad Changes in Foreign Trade Conditions Changes in Foreign Trade Conditions 2010. 10. 29 Hankuk Eun Row Total number of resurgences   Recent economic situation at home and abroad Recent economic situation at home and abroad  World Economy  The global economy , which contracted sharply immediately after the global financial crisis, is supported by the National Assistance Agency for the Stabilization of the Finance Sector and the active fiscal support of governments and central banks of each country. Monetary policy and others have seen a rapid recovery.  The U.S. economy has seen quarterly growth since the second half of 2009 turn into a plus (), but the pace of recovery has been modest.  This year, GDP growth has reversed its downward trend because the sluggish housing economy and delays in improving employment conditions are constraining the full-fledged recovery.  However, consumption and investment continue to improve modestly due to the progress of deleveraging households, high profits of enterprises, and the expectation of additional stimulus measures such as quantitative easing and the extension of tax cuts.  The euro economy is recovering faster than it was in the past against the backdrop of strong exports and the recovery of private consumption in key countries such as the German Empire despite the fiscal crisis in the southern European countries.  However, Greece and Spain, which have not completely escaped the financial crisis, continue to suffer from a sluggish economy.  China's economy has seen a slight slowdown in growth in recent years, but has basically continued to grow at a high rate .  Although the value of the yuan has been rising in recent years , there is still a high growth in exports .  Meanwhile, a series of policies to strengthen liquidity management have taken effect, with the rate of growth falling and the rise in real estate prices slowing.  The Japanese economy has recovered rapidly since the second half of 2009 due to strong exports and continued growth in equipment investment, but growth has fallen significantly in the second quarter of this year.  This is despite the Bank of Japan's repeated quantitative easing measures as deflation continues. The strengthening of the yen was due to a slowdown in export growth and a combination of declining inventories, sluggish private consumption and housing investment.  Going forward , the outlook prevails that the global economy will continue its modest recovery rather than fall into a double-dip despite a number of risk factors.  International Financial Markets  As the international financial market unrest triggered by the financial crisis in the southern European countries has been greatly alleviated, the overall risk-averse tendency has been reduced, and risk-averse investment is expanding .  The credit creation function of financial institutions such as banks has also been gradually restored due to the completion of deleveraging and the increase in capital in the meantime.  Along with this, the inflow of global investment funds to emerging market countries, including Korea, has increased significantly.  In the case of our country, stocks The influx of foreign portfolio-to-self-funded funds into the bond market has all been active.  Meanwhile, a surge in global capital movements has greatly expanded exchange rate volatility in major countries.  In particular, the value of currencies in emerging market countries has been strongly strengthened due to the impact of expanding capital inflows.  Domestic Economy A. Recent Trends  The domestic economy continues to rise mainly on exports.  Exports continue to boom, with average daily exports hitting an all-time high during September, and as a result, equipment investment has generally maintained a significant increase.  Driven by rising wages and employment conditions, private consumption has steadily increased, but the construction sector continues to be sluggish.  However, despite the continuation of the upward trend, GDP and real gross national income (GNI) Due to the gap in the economy, the rate of improvement is somewhat slow.  The employment situation is showing an improvement trend mainly in the private sector, with the number of employed people increasing and the unemployment rate falling to the mid-3% range.  Consumer prices are in Q2/4 2. 6% (YoY) in Q3/4 2. The increase has expanded to 9%  Especially during September, the price of agricultural products, mainly vegetables, soared, recording a high rise of 3.6%.  Home prices are still bearish after the 8.29 action  However, in recent years, trading has continued to be sluggish, but the price drop in the metropolitan area has been moving to shrink slightly.  Charter prices continued to rise high due to the impact of uncertain home price prospects. B. Future Prospects  In the future, the domestic economy is expected to continue its upward trend as the number of foreign risk factors continues to show signs of improvement and domestic demand steadily increases.  Consumer prices are expected to continue to be on the demand side as the economy continues to rise .  Despite the widening of the service balance deficit, the Gyeongsang Water Index is expected to continue its surplus mainly on the commodity balance due to the export boom.   Changes in Foreign Trade Conditions Changes in Foreign Trade Conditions  After the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy in September 2008, the economic situation deteriorated significantly as exports plummeted, and in 2009, the economy recovered as exports increased significantly .  This is because our country is a small, open economy and trade, especially exports, account for a high proportion of the total economic size.  According to the IMF data (Principal Global Indicators), during 2009, Urinara's exports to GDP were 49.9% and imports were 46.0%, making it one of the highest G20 countries in the group with the highest import and export status.  Therefore, in order for our economy to develop into a first-class developed country through stable growth, it is desirable that exports continue to show signs of improvement in the medium to long term with the expansion of domestic demand.  In this regard, the economic actors of our country are bound to be deeply concerned with the changes in foreign trade conditions, such as the growth of the world economy, the exchange rate and the issue of trade liberalization.  At the G2 0 Finance Ministers' Meeting held in Gyeongju on 22-23 October , a number of issues affecting foreign trade conditions were discussed. (Growth of the global economy)  G20 countries have pledged to work towards strong, sustainable and balanced growth in response to the weak recovery of the global economy and the constant risk of downwards.  The growth of the world economy is the main factor that determines the overseas demand for our country's export goods.  There are various uncertainties, but the basic outlook of the major forecasting agencies (baseline) According to the report, the global economy is expected to continue its recovery. The IMF and other global economic projections suggest that overall foreign demand growth will slow somewhat during the next year, but will continue to increase.  In particular, these forecasters predict that the growth rate of emerging market countries , including China, will continue to exceed those of developed countries. Given that the share of emerging market countries such as China in Korea's exports has been increasing in recent years, and moreover, the volume of trade in the Asian region is showing a rapid increase, it can be said that the positive side is great in terms of overseas demand. (Exchange rate issues)  G20 countries have generally discussed the uncertainty surrounding exchange rate adjustments between major countries and the direction of reducing exchange rate volatility.  Specifically, in response to recent disagreements related to exchange rate adjustment between major countries, the following 3 principles have been agreed upon: (1) Transition to a more market-determined exchange rate system that reflects economic fundamentals (2) Refrain from competitive depreciation of money (3) Developed countries are wary of excessive volatility and disorderly movements in their exchange rates.  In addition , at the upcoming G20 Seoul Summit on 11-12 November , we will further discuss the macroprudential policy framework for mitigating the impact of excessive capital flows.  Given that excessive capital flows have amplified exchange rate volatility in recent years , we believe that this discussion will help stabilize the exchange rate .  In the future, we will have to watch the results of the discussions at the G20 Seoul Summit and the specific implementation situation of each country, but basically the uncertainty and volatility related to the exchange rate is expected to ease to a certain extent.  This will be a positive aspect to the import and export trade. (Global imbalance)  In response to global imbalances, the G20 countries have agreed to maintain the size of the current balance sheet at a sustainable level and to pursue all possible policies and coordination of policies necessary for this purpose.  Since the foreign exchange crisis, Korea has continued to have a surplus in the current balance of economic balance except in 2008, but the surplus on GDP is small compared to that of Germany, China, Japan, etc.  As a result, even if indicative guidelines are presented for sustainable current balance sizes in the future, no separate response that could affect imports and exports will be necessary.  Moreover, in the future, if the adjustment between countries with excessive economic balance imbalance is advanced, it is expected that the uncertainty of trade conditions due to global imbalance will also be reduced. (Protectionist tendencies)  G20 countries have agreed to reject all forms of protectionism and further reduce the walls of the trade arena.  Even without this explicit agreement, the G20 countries' approach to the aforementioned exchange rates and global imbalances could have alleviated concerns about the significance of protectionist stocks.  As a result, it is estimated that the possibility of negative impact on exports has been reduced by the strengthening of protectionism, such as trade barriers in the ROK's exporting partners.  On the other hand, I think this agreement is all too natural given the following historical lessons:  In the 1930s, during the Great Depression, when the United States enacted the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, the main focus of tariff increases, European countries introduced protectionist policies in retaliation.  As a result of this so-called tariff war, the U.S. imports of European goods were reduced by about 2/3 and the imports of U.S. goods by Yurub by about 1/3.  Protectionism is expanding in the event of a global recession because it believes it can prevent a global recession from spreading to its home country by protecting its jobs and preserving income.  Historically, however, protectionism has exacerbated the global recession and ultimately failed to advance its own economy .

At the Seoul Summit, a more concrete action plan will be presented on the direction of all policies and regulations related to the reform of the international financial order.
