Title: Direction of restructuring the monetary policy system after the global financial crisis
text: 06-10-2011 Please handle this material from 12:20 on June 11. Title : Kim Jung-su Han Eun-un, Chairman of the Korean Finance Society, Luncheon Lecture Bank of Korea Governor Kim Chong-su will discuss "Direction of Restructuring the Monetary Policy System After the Global Financial Crisis" at the "2011 Korea Finance Society's Regular Conference and Special Policy Symposium" held at the Hyatt Hotel in Seogwipo City, Jeju Island, on Saturday, June 11. Luncheon Lecture Attached: Luncheon Lecture Part 1. End. Reference: Kim Yong-min, Director of the Economic and Social Research Lab of the Institute of Economic Research Tel : 759-5417 Fax : 759-5410 E-mail : kimym@bok.or.kr  : Tel (02) 759-4015, 4016 "The Bank of Korea press release is also included on the Internet ( )." Regular Conference of the Korea Finance Society Regular Conference of the Korea Finance Society After the Global Financial Crisis Direction of restructuring the monetary policy system Table of Contents  greeting  Lessons from the Global Financial Crisis  Physical-financial links and monetary policy  Key Challenges to Reshaping the Monetary Policy System  Complementing monetary policy through macroprudential policy  Monetary policy based on a new economic model  Macroprudential Policy Enforcement System  Closing Table of Contents  greeting  Lessons from the Global Financial Crisis  Physical-financial links and monetary policy  Key Challenges to Reshaping the Monetary Policy System  Complementing monetary policy through macroprudential policy  Monetary policy based on a new economic model  Macroprudential Policy Enforcement System  Closing 2011. 6. 11 Bank of Korea Governor Kim Chong-su* * I would like to express my gratitude to Kang Jong-gu, Director of the Institute of Economics of the Bank of Korea, for organizing the basic materials for the preparation of this manuscript, and to Kim Joon-won, who gave me an informative commentary. Part of this notice was presented at an international conference on the topic of "Real and Financial Linkage and Monetary Policy" hosted by the Bank of Japan on June 1 and 2 , 2011.  greeting Dear President of the Korea Finance Society, Cho Jang-ok, and Members of the Korea Finance Society who attended this meeting, First of all, I would like to congratulate you on the opening of the Korea Finance Society's regular conference and special policy symposium on the beautiful island of Jeju, and I am truly pleased to have given a speech in such a meaningful event. Today I would like to speak about the major challenges related to the restructuring of the monetary policy system, which are being posed as a new policy challenge since the global financial crisis, and macroprudence policy.  Lessons from the Global Financial Crisis It has been 3 years since the global financial crisis that began in the United States occurred. Our country, whose foundations were relatively strong, was also a victim of the global financial crisis that had hit the globe half way around. We have explained our situation with the expression of a mere innocent bystander, not the one responsible for causing the crisis, but as long as we belong to the global economy, we have not been able to avoid the crisis, and that is exactly what our country did as the G20 Chairman of the Korea Initiative last year. It is a well-known fact that it is the reason that led to the creation of the Global Financial Safety-net under the name of "Global Financial Safety-net". Although we have overcome the crisis at a faster pace than other countries, the uncertainty of the global economy , which has been expanding since the crisis, remains a risk factor for our economy. Now, 3 years after the crisis, what we need to do is to learn from the global financial crisis, so that we can overhaul the gold financing infrastructure and establish an effective policy response system to prevent new crises from occurring in the future. Let's say no. There has been a lot of research in the past, but if we look at the occurrence and progression of the global financial crisis, and the policy response after the crisis, we can learn many lessons and implications about the role of central banks and the monetary policy system. First, in terms of the causes of the crisis and the process of development, the failure of macroeconomic policies in major developed countries, such as the United States, represented by sub-prime mortgages, combined with the savings glut of major emerging market countries, has led to an imbalance in the real sector called "global imbalances." In the process of the transition of sector imbalances to the financial sector in tandem with the failure of financial supervision, shocks caused by some financial institutions or markets due to financial interconnectedness, which has risen significantly compared to the past, are rapidly becoming systemic risks. Spread. Of course, the failure of the financial markets also played an important role in this process. While advanced financial engineering has distributed risk, resulting in a lower awareness of risk, and also an acceleration of securitization, which has contributed to amplifying the transition of risk, there are aspects inherent in financial assets, especially real estate-related lending assets. By mispricing the risk , the conclusion was drafted into the systemic risk. At the same time, due to the cross-border linkage, which has been greatly strengthened by the integration of the global financial markets and the liberalization of trade, the financial upheaval that has occurred in the developed world has spread rapidly to the emerging economies, and countries with good economic conditions are also facing a crisis. As a result, the spread of the financial crisis, which began with imbalances in the real sector, was accompanied by a massive downturn in the real economy, and a vicious circle created in which the downturn in the real economy intensified again . On the other hand, in terms of policy response after the crisis, the experience of the Great Depression of the 1920s in the past has been taught by drastic macro-policy responses, including drastic rate cuts, making it impossible to avoid a serious real economic recession. The catastrophe of the 2nd Great Depression II was prevented. Along with this macroeconomic policy response, we have also implemented micro-policies to expedite the insolvency of financial institutions and minimize the occurrence of further insolvencies by utilizing the central bank's final lender function and government finances. Behind the successful crisis management, however, has been a serious after-effect, particularly in developed countries, including soaring national debt at levels where sustainability could be questioned, and concerns about ultra-low interest rates and the expansion of phosphorus plea pressure due to large-scale liquidity supply. When we look at the above crisis processes, the most important lesson that the global financial crisis teaches us, especially in exploring policy measures to prevent future crises, is that there is a strong real and financial linkage between the real and financial sectors . To reflect this, a new international financial order and monetary policy system must be established. The strong link between real and financial means that price stability and financial stability are one thing, not a big deal. In other words, the global financial crisis empirically eloquently states that it is difficult to achieve price stability without financial stability, and that it is also difficult to achieve financial stability without real economic stability, including prices. Behind the financial crisis, imbalances in the real sector are bound to exist, and if we do not understand these interrelationships correctly, we are likely to commit the right to kill the messenger without dealing with the underlying problem.  Physical-financial links and monetary policy It is still too early to be reassured, but based on these lessons as the global financial crisis has been somewhat relieved, the international community is actively discussing policy measures to prevent future crises. The focus of these discussions is above all on the design of a new monetary policy paradigm that encompasses macroprudential policy, with almost all international financial organizations, including the IMF, BIS, FSB, BCBS, etc., taking part in the discussion around the G20. As a result, our country, which has already fully opened up its domestic capital markets and made significant progress in its integration with the global financial markets, is also facing the need to revamp its monetary policy system so that it can maintain the new international norms and coherence that will be established in the future. Based on the results of the international discussions so far, I would like to talk about the direction of restructuring the monetary policy system in our country. First of all, in order to have a concrete discussion on the direction of restructuring the monetary policy system, I think the following issues need to be raised: First, is price stability and financial stability concepts in conflict with each other , or can they perform complementary functions? In other words, if you want to achieve price stability and financial stability at the same time through traditional monetary policy, what are the policies and systems that should be considered first? Second, how will the content and effectiveness of optimal monetary policy differ when comparing monetary policy objectives to price stability to those involving financial stability? Third, in preparation for asset bubbles or financial instability, is it desirable for monetary policy to respond to asset price fluctuations in a private manner using traditional policy instruments (policy rates, holding rates, etc.)? Needless to say, the issues raised above are not independent , but are intimately linked. Keeping in mind these interconnectedness, in relation to the restructuring of the monetary policy framework that we should be aiming for, I would like to address the three main challenges that are being discussed in the global forum to prevent the recurrence of the financial crisis in response to the recent changes in the international financial environment. .  Key Challenges to Reshaping the Monetary Policy System IV-1. Complementing monetary policy through macroprudential policy The first key task is to complement monetary policy through macro-prudential policy and overcome the limitations of monetary policy. Macroprudential policy is currently the most central topic in the international community's discussion of restructuring the monetary policy system, while at the same time offering some fairly specific alternatives. The strong link between real and financial suggests that the content and effectiveness of monetary policy may also be different from what we have ever understood and expected. In addition, for the sake of financial stability, monetary policy is in the process of creating an asset bubble. It raises the need for a new debate on whether to respond proactively. In this regard, the recent discussion on " Lean versus Clean" in the international community provides us with a very useful perspective. * First, if we look at the theoretical background of the Clean claim, since it is not easy to recognize in advance whether an asset bubble has occurred, a policy response based on an uncertain balanced asset price may increase macroeconomic instability, and there is a risk of increasing the instability of some asset markets. It is inappropriate to respond with monetary policy that affects the macroeconomy or the financial markets as a whole, so it is preferable to wait for the bubble to collapse on its own and then clean up the post-mortem insolvency. On the other hand, if we look at the logical basis of Lean's argument, as seen in the global financial crisis, the economic costs of bursting bubbles are enormous, and these costs will increase even greater, especially as the interconnectedness between financial markets strengthens, and the risk of triggering asset bubbles is high. The spike in asset prices can be perceived to a certain extent in advance, and at the same time some control is possible through the adjustment of quantity variables such as domestic credit, and the economic cost (dead-weight loss) incurred by preemptive policy responses based on uncertain information. is that in some cases, it may be on a second-order scale rather than a first-order. In comparing the above two opposing views , it is important to note that both views assume traditional monetary policy, and that under traditional monetary policy, both crisis prevention and crisis resolution can be ignored. It is assumed that it incurs an economic cost of a level that is not there. However, it is possible to conclude that if the scope of monetary policy is extended to include macro-soundness policies, the economic costs involved in crisis prevention will be greatly reduced, while the cost of post-crisis management will not change significantly. These conclusions mean that the "lean approach" is much more persuasive than the "clean approach". In fact, while traditional monetary policy affects both price stability and financial stability, there are limits to achieving both price stability and financial stability in that its effectiveness does not necessarily work in the same direction. Macroprudential policies can contribute to reducing the economic costs associated with crisis prevention precisely because they can mitigate these policy tradeoffs faced by traditional monetary policy. For example, if domestic credit is soaring and the economy is overheating, and the policy rate is raised for reasons of price stability, oh *   White, William R. (2009), "Should Monetary Policy 'Lean or Clean'?" Working Paper No.34, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Globalization and Monetary Policy Institute, August 2009.  It can be difficult to curb credit growth by increasing capital inflows. In this case, macroprudential policies can be a useful means of curbing excessive capital inflows and have the advantage of having less market distortion compared to direct capital control. Conversely, if the policy rate is kept at a very low level in order to relieve the financial instability caused by external shocks, there is a risk of creating an asset bubble. Even in this case, macroprudential policies can function as a complement to monetary policy by curbing bubbles. In conclusion, macroprudential policies can be found in that they can compensate for the limitations of monetary policy by providing additional policy tools to achieve various policy objectives. We believe that if the right combination of monetary policy in the traditional sense of the word, which focuses on price stability, and macroprudential policy focused on preventing bubbles, it will be possible to achieve both water stability and financial stability at the same time at minimal economic cost. Against the backdrop of this perception , our country has recently introduced a new macro-sound policy tool to stabilize the foreign exchange market. In Korea, which does not have an internationally accepted currency like other developing countries, there is a high need to control the volatility of capital outflows that arise from changes in global liquidity at an appropriate level. In fact, our financial markets experienced a lot of turmoil, such as the rapid outflow of short-term funds that had been flowing in large quantities in the short period of time before the global financial crisis , resulting in a large depreciation of the yuan in the course of the crisis. Looking back, we believe that if a well-designed foreign-related macroprudence policy had been in place, a large influx of short-term funds prior to the financial crisis could have been prevented. In recent years, as the two-speed recovery of the world economy has progressed, the inflow of funds into emerging economies, including our own country, has increased significantly again. Accordingly, as part of our preemptive response, our country has introduced macro-prudential policy measures such as regulating futures exchange position limits and foreign exchange health levy . These policies are expected to help achieve financial stability without placing an undue burden on monetary policy. Although it is still premature to empirically analyze the policy effect, the Bank of Korea plans to closely analyze the policy effect through continuous monitoring. For reference, the norms of international organizations such as the OECD do not currently establish a clear distinction between macroprudential policies and capital control. Therefore, I would like to point out that the Bank of Korea, together with the Government, is in consultation with international organizations such as the IMF and OECD to ensure that our macroprudential policy is an example of international norms. On the other hand, even before the global financial crisis, Korea implemented LTV and DTI as macroprudential policy measures to stabilize the real estate market. These regulations will stabilize house prices and curb the excessive growth of mortgages, so that in the course of the global financial crisis, It is also evaluated as having contributed to the stable management of the insolvency rate of real estate-related loans. IV-2. Monetary policy based on a new economic model The second key task with regard to restructuring the monetary policy framework is to develop a new economic model necessary for the implementation of monetary policy. * In order to facilitate monetary and macroprudential policies with strong real-financial linkage, the development of new economic models that take this linkage into account is necessary. First of all , the new economic model should be able to reflect financial friction or " financial friction " caused by information asymmetry, etc. Research so far shows that financial friction can amplify financial pro-cyclicality. A typical example is when a decline in the value of a collateral caused by an external shock leads to the recovery of loan bonds or the demand for additional collateral, which leads to a vicious cycle in which the real economy shrinks, resulting in a further decline in the value of the collateral. Along with this, a multi-sector disaggregate model must be established that can reflect the interconnectedness between financial markets. The course of a global crisis shows how shocks from one market are rapidly spillover to another and amplified into systemic risk. In designing a multi-sector model suitable for our economy, the smallest real estate market and the overseas sector should be included as the epicenter of the shock or the route of transmission of the shock. Finally, given the nonlinearity of financial and macrovariables, we need a model that can simulate the effects of monetary policy , including macroprudential policy. To do this, it is urgent to first expand and revamp the stress test model that is currently in use. In particular, the feedback effect between finance and the real world, the tail risk that market prices are difficult to adequately reflect, and macroprudential policy variables that have already been or are about to be introduced need to be designed as part of the model. With regard to macroprudential policy variables, along with regulations related to non-personal loans such as LTV and DTI, macro-prudential stability levy, and regulation of foreign exchange positions, the counter-cyclical capital regulations to be introduced in the future. buffer) and so on. * BIS (2011), "Models and Tools for Macro-prudential Supervision," Note from RTF Transmission Channels Subgroup, March 2011.  IV-3. Macroprudential Policy Enforcement System The final key task associated with restructuring the monetary policy system is to determine the governance or enforcement framework of macroprudential policies. * Broadly speaking, there are ways for the central bank in charge of monetary policy to actively participate in or preside over macroprudential policy, and for other non-central banks to dedicate themselves to macroprudential policy . Macroprudential policies affect the main goals of monetary policy, such as prices and growth, and monetary policy also affects the stability of the financial system , which is a major concern of macroprudential policy. More importantly, as I mentioned earlier, macroprudential policy and monetary policy are not in an alternative relationship , but in a complementary relationship . Therefore, if an agency that is not in charge of the policy of conciliation is dedicated to implementing macroprudential policies, there is a conflict between macrosoundness and monetary policy, which increases the likelihood of a coordination failure. For example, if a company's productivity improves, prices are likely to stabilize or fall below the target level as the credit supply increases significantly depending on investment demand, etc. In this case, simply curbing credit growth on the level of macroprudence without consideration for prices would result in a deterrent to the price stability pursued by monetary policy. On the other hand, if the central bank directly oversees or actively participates in macroprudential policies, it can escape the risk of policy coordination failures, while there are side effects. Specifically, as the policy objectives or mandates of the Bank of China are diversified, policy enforcement conflicts may arise and the possibility of regulatory forbearance by the central bank cannot be ruled out. For example, if further rate cuts are needed in response to deflationary pressures, but interest rate levels are already under zero bound constraints, there is a risk that the risk at the financial system level will increase if the central bank over-eases macroprudential policies. Both of the previous measures have a rationale, but I think the key is whether the inefficiencies and risks of failing to adjust policies will be greater or smaller than the risks of policy conflicts within the central bank or regulatory moratoriums. We will be able to examine our realities and at the same time draw implications by analyzing the experiences of other countries, including the G20 countries. First of all, since financial stability and price stability are complementary to each other, even if the central bank pursues both goals at the same time, the possibility of a serious policy conflict is practically unlikely. * Tucker, Paul (2011), "Macroprudential Policy: building financial stability institutions," Remark by Deputy Governor for Financial Stability at the Bank of England, at the 20th Annual Hyman P Minsky Conference, New York, 14 April 2011  It would be safe to look at it. The risk of a deferral of regulation is an ever-present risk regardless of who is the enforcer of macroprudential policies, which can be mitigated by increasing transparency in macroprudential policymaking. In addition, we believe that if the information necessary for the implementation of macroprudential policies is shared by the supervisory entity of the rehabilitation number, external monitoring and containment of the risk of regulatory suspension will be possible. Putting the above discussion together, we believe that the central bank's dramatic participation in macroprudential policy is a more desirable and realistic approach in terms of efficiency and risk management. Recently , major developed countries are pushing for a reorganization of their macroprudential policy systems, which is in line with the results of the above discussions. In fact, most of the G20 countries that are pushing for a supervisory overhaul are stepping up the central bank's responsibility and role in macroprudential policies. Typically, the United States has established the FSOC to strengthen the functions of information sharing and coordination between the Federal Supervisory Bodies, and in the case of the United Kingdom, it has implemented significant reforms, including the dissolution of the Financial Supervisory Authority and the transfer of macro and micro financial supervision functions to the Anglo-American Row. . In the face of this international trend, we should also closely grasp the contents and expected effects of the reforms in each country and hasten to come up with concrete measures to improve the system. In the future , a particular thing to pay attention to in the process of institutional improvement is to maintain consistency with international norms. Macroprudential policy is, after all, what governs participants in the financial markets. However, financial markets have already become globalized. If each country's macroprudential policies deviate significantly from international norms, it will be possible for participants in the financial markets to evade regulation through regulatory arbitrage, etc., and in the end, macroprudential policies will not be able to achieve the desired effect. . In order to maintain consistency with international norms, it is necessary to strengthen cooperation and share information with central banks around the world, while at the same time actively participating in the process of establishing international norms ourselves. Financial markets are already globalized , but there is no global jurisdiction governing the market. This structural imbalance is ultimately a key factor in weakening the resilience to shocks in global financial markets . It would be no exaggeration to say that the fact that the various countries together establish international norms and implement their domestic policies in accordance with the established norms is the first thing to do to prevent the recurrence of the financial crisis.  Closing Finally, I would like to conclude my speech with the words of the Speaker. In a situation where there is a strong link between physical and gold financing, price stability and financial stability are inseparable. Financial stability is essential to maintaining price stability and achieving financial stability without price stability It's also difficult. It goes without saying that in order to achieve both price stability and financial stability, the role and capabilities of central banks need to be established commensurate with changes in the global environment. In particular , in order to regulate the financial markets where globalization has advanced the most, it is necessary to actively participate in the networking between central banks in countries around the world and strengthen the provision of international assistance for macroprudential measures through this. At the same time, efforts should be made to develop new economic models and monetary policy instruments and to cultivate economic forecasting capabilities based on lessons learned from the global financial crisis. I would like to point out that the Bank of Korea, in its orientation towards the Global BOK, is working to design and establish a new paradigm of policy that has been required since the global financial crisis. However, it is not possible with the efforts of the Bank of Korea alone. Seeking answers to many of the problems that have not yet been solved will require the premise of new thinking and in-depth research. On this occasion, I would like to invite all the members of the Korea Finance Society to do a lot of research and discussion on the new policy paradigm, as well as to ask for their continued support of the Bank of Korea. We congratulate you on the presentation of various papers and lively discussions at this conference, and we look forward to the Korea Financial Society playing a leading role in the financial development of our country. I wish to conclude this by wishing the Korea Finance Society an endless development. Thank you for listening.

Title: Monetary policy after the global financial crisis
text: Feb 21, 2013 This material can be processed from Thursday, February 21, 2013 at 14:30 am onwards Title : Kim Jung-su Han Eun Announces Theme of the Joint Conference on Economics , Bank of Korea Governor Kim Chong-su presented a paper on the topic of "Monetary Policy After the Global Financial Crisis" at the 2013 Joint Conference on Economics * The 1st Plenary Session on Thursday, February 21. * Jointly organized by 56 economics-related societies, including the Korea Economic Society , and held at Korea University on 2.21-22 February for two days Attached: Thesis Summary Part 1. End. Contact : Secretary-General's Normal Money Tel : 759-4021 Fax : 759-4037 E-mail : secretariat@bok.or.kr  : Tel (02) 759-4015, 4016 "The Bank of Korea press release is also included on the Internet ( )." : Thesis Monetary policy after the global financial crisis . Preface  In the course of the response to the global financial crisis, the functions of the central banks of major countries have been extended not only to the existing price stability, but also to areas such as financial stability, real economic stimulus, and employment growth.  In retrospect, the politics of the past century Society In the event of a major economic transformation, there will also be a major change in the role of the central bank.  This global financial crisis has also prompted us to rethink the new role of central banks and monetary policy, as well as the monetary policy operating system, including nominal reference indicators.  This paper seeks to examine the changes in the role of the central bank that have been raised in connection with the global financial crisis and the discussion on the operating system of monetary policy from a global perspective, analyze the new challenges to monetary policy, and explore the policy implications for our country. . Historical Reflections on the Role of the Central Bank  Historically, the function of the central bank is to respond to the situation of the times and the economic problems at hand, and to change dynamically.  Under the gold standard (1870s-1930s), the role of financial stability in performing the function of the final lender in the event of a financial crisis was emphasized, but during the Great Depression and World War II (1940s-1960s), the role of financial support for economic reconstruction was emphasized.  In the wake of Great Inflation in the early 1970s, price stability emerged as the central bank's most important responsibility , and the view was formed that financial stability was desirable for supervisory bodies to promote through microprudential regulation.  However, in the wake of the 2007 global financial crisis, the central bank's function of financial stability has resurfaced due to the widespread perception that price stability is not sufficient to ensure the stability of the macroeconomic and financial systems , and that macroprudential policies are important. , the central bank is an evolutionary being that has developed in response to the demands and challenges of each era, and in addition to its basic responsibility of price stability after the financial crisis, it emphasizes its multifaceted role in alleviating the accumulation of financial imbalances and preventing severe recessions. . Changes in the Monetary Policy Operating System in the wake of the Global Financial Crisis  The need to change the role of central banks since the global financial crisis has led to discussions about whether the current monetary policy operating system is appropriate in a changed environment. (Types and characteristics of the monetary policy operating system)  Monetary policy operating systems that have historically been introduced ((1) to (3) or are theoretically discussed ((4) to (5)) are divided into five types according to nominal anchors: (1) Exchange Rate Target: Suitable for small open economies with high dependence on specific countries, but vulnerable to physical shocks due to the inability to carry out independent monetary policy. (2) Monetary volume target: A stable relationship between the volume of money and prices, and the ability of the central bank to regulate the currency, etc., should be premised, but the effectiveness of the policy has declined due to the recent destabilization of monetary demand. (3) Price Stabilization Target: Present the inflation rate target in advance As a way of achieving it, it is evaluated as having contributed to the stabilization of price stability through the stabilization of inflation expectations, etc., but there are disadvantages such as difficulties in responding to policy responses to supply shocks. (4) Price Level Target System: Since we want to achieve the price level target path, there are aspects that are desirable for the people's welfare, but there is a disadvantage that depending on the underlying effect, the volatility of monetary policy will increase, or the central bank will have to carry out micro-price management. (5) Nominal GDP target system : There is an advantage that the nominal GDP level can be used as a target variable to flexibly respond to supply shocks such as rising oil prices, but there is a limitation that the clarity of the target and the rapidity of the statistical system are poor, and it is difficult to set an appropriate target level. (Discussions and implications after the global financial crisis)  Monetary policy operating systems have their pros and cons, but before the global crisis, price stabilization targets have been rated as the most effective operating systems .  But after the global financial crisis, (1) is a flexible price stabilization target optimal for the solution of slowing growth or recession problems? (2) How will the financial stability obligations be accommodated in the monetary policy operating system? etc. issues have been raised (1) In order to restore growth, a nominal GDP target system may be more suitable, but it is expected that the transition to the operating system will involve significant risks* and is therefore difficult to call a realistic alternative. * The widespread misconception that central banks value growth over prices can significantly destabilize inflation expectations, and it is not easy to secure the credibility of monetary policy as inflation and economic volatility increase in order to maintain the path of the nominal GDP target level. (2) For the sake of financial stability, it is recognized that it is desirable to make appropriate use of macroprudential policy instruments under the flexible price stability target system. . New challenges and challenges for central banks  Since the global financial crisis, the central bank has been able to harmonize monetary and fiscal policies, strengthen policy coordination with central banks in major countries, and distribute income  Facing new challenges such as implementing micro-policy functions such as financial inclusion (Harmony between monetary and fiscal policy)  Central banks in major countries have implemented non-traditional monetary policy measures, taking into account that failure to drive demand through drastic easing monetary policies after the financial crisis could undermine the potential growth base as the low-growth momentum is prolonged.  The measures also include policies of a quasi-fiscal policy* nature, raising concerns that the central bank's ability to stabilize prices in the long run will be compromised.  For example, the Fed's purchases of Treasury bonds and MBS, and the ECB's unlimited purchases of Treasury bonds (OMT) are in effect the central bank's fiscal policy on behalf of the government.  However, this was an inevitable aspect of the stimulus in a situation where fiscal leeway was depleted and the policy rate reached the zero lower limit, and historically, the relationship between monetary and fiscal policy has changed dynamically with the economic situation.  From the time of the Great Depression until the early 1970s, the prevailing perception was that policy coordination was important in promoting employment- and growth-oriented economic policies.  After inflation in the early 1970s, the need for an independent monetary policy to stabilize prices was emphasized and skepticism about policy coordination became commonplace.  However, in the course of the response to the global financial crisis, the traditional division of labor is weakened, the mutual impact between monetary policy and fiscal policy is increasing, and bilateral policy cooperation and harmony are strengthened .  However, in order to ensure that the price stability foundation is not undermined in the medium to long term, the principles, scope, etc. of cooperation between policies must be clearly defined, as well as the policy-making process must be transparent so that private confidence in the central bank's price stability function is not undermined . (Considering cross-border linkages in monetary policy)  In the course of the response to the financial crisis, there is a growing interest in the international spillover effects of monetary policy and the need for international assistance.  The easing monetary policy of the major developed countries has a positive effect, such as boosting the domestic demand and import demand of the developed countries, thus facilitating exports to emerging countries and accelerating the economic recovery.  However, as the easing monetary policies of major countries increase global liquidity and increase the volatility of capital flows and flows, it is imperative that a response is in place.  In addition, the fact that long-term interest rates in emerging countries are in line with those of developed countries has negative effects such as deteriorating profitability of financial institutions, weakening the interest rate ripple path of monetary policy, and increasing inflationary pressures through rising prices of international commodities such as crude oil.  In response, central banks in major countries need to fully consider the international ramifications in their monetary policy decisions, and emerging countries need to explore ways to ease volatility in the flow and exit of capital, and to harmonize monetary and foreign exchange policies.  In the absence of a global policy body that is a fundamental solution , it is important to strengthen policy cooperation between countries. (Performing the micro-policy functions of the central bank)  The central bank's monetary policy focused on its impact on the macroeconomy as a whole, but in the wake of the global financial crisis, when the economic actors are heterogeneous agents, monetary policy is hierarchical The growing awareness that it can affect sectors unevenly has highlighted the importance of micro-policy functions such as income distribution and financial inclusion.  In the wake of the Occupy Wall Street protests and the like, amid the central bank's theory of responsibility for the deterioration of income distribution, empirical studies have also emerged that the Fed's monetary policy has led to a deterioration in income distribution (Coibion et al. 2012) * Easing monetary policy with profits over wages  A larger increase in interest income could result in a relatively greater increase in the wealth of business financiers than of labor workers.  In view of the fact that monetary policy can affect the structure of income distribution, the central bank is responsible for the fact that when it comes to conducting monetary policy, it is necessary to ensure that the central bank is divided into hierarchical  We also need to be concerned about the impact on sectoral income.  Meanwhile, in the wake of the global financial crisis, the social role of finance has been emphasized, and international discussions such as the G20 on financial inclusion and the introduction of country-specific policies* have also become active. * Malaysia enacted a new central bank law in 2009 that includes financial inclusion as a key function of the central bank, and the Bank of Korea has also been using cap loans since September 2012 to support banknote conversion loans to low-credit small and medium-sized lenders.  Financial inclusion encompasses the enhancement of financial access to the poor, the strengthening of financial consumer protection, the expansion of financial education, etc. , and the phenomenon of financial alienation hinders financial integrity and society. Given that it can pose political risks, it ultimately contributes to financial stability. However, the concrete policy instruments and economic impact of financial inclusion remain challenges ahead. . Policy implications and conclusions  Given the change in the role of the central bank in the wake of this global financial crisis, the following are some things that the Bank of Korea should keep in mind in the future:  First, keeping in mind that the global financial crisis has not been able to break free from the low-growth-high unemployment loop, it is necessary to flexibly operate the price stability target system on the basis of price stability, which is the basic mandate, and respond appropriately to the recovery of the growth trend of the economy*  The role of the central bank, which for decades has been perceived as to take away the punch bowl from the party, is now a policy effort with the government when there is no party or the atmosphere cools down , like when low growth persists and inflationary pressures are low. Expanding to the argument that it is necessary to contribute to the healthy development of the national economy by racing - Since monetary policy is a short-term response to the management of general demand and is not a panacea, we are seeking policy combinations in the direction that monetary policy harmonizes with this, with macroeconomic policies and structural reform policies playing a more active role.  Second, efforts should be made to ensure the successful implementation of the newly assigned financial stability responsibilities imposed by the revision of the Bank of Korea Act.  Properly develop macroprudential analysis functions so that the financial stability function can be successfully implemented in harmony with the price stability function It is necessary to take advantage of it and actively participate in global financial regulatory reform efforts  Third, in a changed environment, the monetary policy operating system must be continuously checked to ensure that it is suitable for achieving the central bank's diversified policy goals. At the moment, there is no reason to change the new price stability target system, which has contributed significantly to price stability, but it is necessary to keep an eye on the various possibilities and keep an eye on the global discussions, and constantly check the adequacy of the current system.  Fourth, the formulation of monetary policy  We should pay more attention to the ripple effects between countries in enforcement and actively participate in the provision of monetary policy  Since the central banks of each country have become difficult to achieve the desired effect through the implementation of their own policies , it is necessary to carry out policies with global equilibrium in mind and actively strive for the provision of international assistance.  Fifth, under rapidly changing circumstances, the Bank of Korea should always strive to prepare countermeasures in response to changes in internal and external economic conditions*.  For example, at the moment, the main focus is on ways to restore growth, but due to global inflation concerns due to the visualization of the recovery of advanced economies, if central banks in major countries implement exit strategies, measures such as absorbing liquidity and selling their holdings will cause disruption to international financial markets . Be prepared for the possibilities - Rule-based decision-making rather than discretionary has been the practice up to now, but in situations of high external uncertainty, there is also a risk of resulting in rigid decision-making, so a policy based on pragmatic analysis results while maintaining a flexible stance ( evidence-based policy)  Finally, it seeks to strengthen this role in the development of the national economy while maintaining the independence of the central bank.  To do this, politics  Administration It is important to be free from the influence of markets and the like, to have the ability and self-discipline to present and lead harmonious policies, as well as independent decision-making, and for this purpose, capacity building of the organization is important.

Insamal Dear President Hou Zixin, Mayor Dai Xianglong Tianjin, and Dear Staff and Students of Nankai University, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to give a lecture at the prestigious Nankai University, which produced Teacher Zhu Eun-lae, the spiritual landlord of the Chinese people and the foundation for the construction of a new China. First of all, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to President Heu Tzu Xin for inviting me to stand here, Mayor Daixiang Long Tianjin for arranging this, and to the various people involved. The first time I met Mayor Daixiang Long was on 2 0 02 when the Tonghua Swap Agreement between the two central banks of the Republic of Korea and China was signed. Mayor Daixiang Long, then the Governor of the Republic of China, took the lead in opening a new chapter in financial cooperation between the ROK and China, and has contributed greatly to the consolidation of mutual cooperation in the years since. On this occasion, I would like to thank the Mayor once again for his unwavering friendship and interest in Korea. As you well know, China and Korea are not only very close geographically, but also historically close together. The two countries shared a Hanseatic, Confucian, and Buddhist culture, and boasted a splendid civilization until the Middle Ages. But in the modern era, both countries have also suffered the historical pain of being invaded by imperialist powers. What the two countries have in common doesn't stop there. China and South Korea are similar in that they have achieved remarkable economic results in a short period of time. Nowadays, where business leaders from all over the world gather , the topic is definitely related to the Chinese economy. The interest in the remarkable development of China's economy, the world's largest and most populous country , has grown that much. The world is once again amazed by the rapid rise of China's economy following South Korea's remarkable abstinence in just over 40 years from the devastation of war, and it appears that the world is renewing its awareness of the Northeast Asian economy. Therefore, today I would like to speak to you about whether South Korea and China can continue the economic development that they have achieved so far, and how the Northeast Asian economy, including the two countries, can develop together. . The long-term sperm source of the Korean and Chinese cultivators The Yellow River region of China is one of the birthplaces of the 4 largest human civilizations. The crustal characters and various ruins excavated from the metaphor ruins of Hanan Province are already highly cultured in the Silver Dynasty period, about 3,500 years ago. It shows that you have reached a level. China also invented paper, compass, and gunpowder, which are said to be the 3 greatest inventions in the history of human beings , and passed the technology on to the West. Such a technique became the basis for the development of Western literature. Korea also has a long history and enjoyed its own culture. In ancient times, a brilliant Buddhist culture blossomed and spread to Japan. It is also said that in the Middle Ages, the art of printing press, an important scientific achievement in human history, was the best in the world. Korea created the world's first metal typeface more than 200 years ahead of the Gutenberg typeface that brought about the Western publishing revolution. Currently housed by the French National Library, Korea's Jijisimkyung is the world's best metal active capital in existence. China and Korea, which had such a brilliant civilization until the Middle Ages, had fallen into the swamp of poverty just half a century ago, and their economic development stagnated greatly. On the other hand , the West, which is neither the idea of human civilization nor the development of history for a long time, succeeded in industrialization early on and is today a developed country. How did this irony of history arise? Why did China and South Korea fall behind in industrialization? I think it's because the two countries, unlike the West, have not been able to respond adequately to the changes and challenges of a new civilization for a long time. These include the following factors: It seems to have worked. First, the two countries were overcrowded compared to their homeland. As a result, small agriculture was inevitable, which made it very difficult to accumulate agricultural surplus and expand the market. In such a situation, industrialization is difficult to succeed . Second, Buddhism and Confucianism, which flourished in both countries, also played a role in making industrialization difficult. As you are well aware, Confucianism or Buddhism was a reality resting or a reality escapist orthodoxy that placed more emphasis on the spirit than the quality of the water, and the intermediate idea of the coexistence of the strong and the weak rather than rational choice. Accordingly, the poor were respected and the quality of the water was recognized only to the extent necessary for their livelihood. Furthermore, the act of building wealth itself was considered immoral. Third, both countries have very deep roots in history and traditions. So that deep history and tradition has often served as a resistance to change. Confucian systems of identity discrimination, such as the Confucian Statue of Agribusiness, are a prime example. This entrenched culture and tradition has become an obstacle to a new adaptation to changes in the environment by showing the attribute of consolidating itself. It's as if the construction of a new city is much faster and easier than the redevelopment of an old city. Finally, the invasion of imperialism since the 19th century has made the accumulation of capital and technology more difficult. Western countries began as a British state in the mid-18th century , and in turn succeeded in industrialization, gradually transforming into imperialism as their economic power grew. The two countries of the Peninsula failed to adapt actively to industrialization and were reduced to the target countries of imperialist encroachment. . Cultivation of both Koreas and China After such a long period of stagnation, South Korea and China have been experiencing dynamic economic growth under an open international order since the Second World War. The problem of the shortage of capital and technology, which has been constraining economic development for a long time, can be solved by imports. As the rich labor force of the two countries combined with the capital and technology of the developed countries, the overpopulation, which had been a hindrance to development in the meantime, was transformed into the engine of industrialization. To summarize the characteristics of the economic development models of the two countries, which have much in common, they are as follows: First, in both countries, the main wealth resource was the low-wage labor force, which unlike other regions is well educated and has a high degree of moral discipline. Second, the necessary capital and technology are difficult to supply domestically, mainly foreign countries. Introduced from And the reduction of the development turnaround time was achieved by maximizing the profits of the latecomers who imitated the technologies and institutions of the advanced countries. This is the benefit of an open system. Third, the market for the goods produced by combining the introduced capital and technology with the domestic labor force was found in exports rather than in the domestic market. Finally , rather than letting go of all of this industrialization process to the free market, the government led the way by planning and rolling out support policies. These two models of economic development are representative success stories that best align with the theories of industrialization through the productive of the overpopulation that Professor Arthur Lewis and Professor Alexander Gerschenkron have put it in. I can tell you. In a paper published in 1954, Professor Lewis stated that in the case of an overpopulated economy, once capital is supplied and combined with the low-wage labor force in the country, such as the introduction of foreign capital, a low-wage and high-profit economic climate is created in the industrial sector, resulting in high growth. In particular, the human resources of China and Korea are not only abundant , but also well-educated, and the influence of religion and education has led to a strong transfer of moral discipline. Because of this, once industrialization began, the excesses of the two countries The population has been transformed into a strong growth drive that exceeds the expectations of the Lewis model . Industrialization in both countries was planned more than a century later than in the West, but through imitation profits, the time required for economic development could be greatly shortened. Professor Gerschenkron wrote in his book, published in 1966, that the greater the degree of backwardness compared to developed countries, and the more countries that enter industrialization late, the much greater the rate once industrialization begins. It was said to be fast-paced. In fact, South Korea and China are reducing the time to industrialization from 100 to 150 to 50 years in Western countries. . Industry-making process of both Koreas and China In this way, I will briefly describe the process of industrialization of a country and China, which has been carried out in the benefit of an open economic system.  South Korea First, Korea has been industrializing in earnest since the early 1960s. Korea, which had no special wealth resources other than the vast labor force in rural areas, pursued economic development through government-led development strategies, the introduction of capital and technology, and export drives. Everything. From the late 1970s onwards, against the backdrop of the success of the light industry, the heavy chemical industrialization was spurred. As a result, Korea has gained international competitiveness in steel, petrochemical, and shipbuilding since the 1990s, and in recent years , the automobile industry has become competitive in various fields ranging from the IT industry such as mulon semiconductor to mobile phones. Thus, Korea, which had a GDP per capita of only 80 in 1960, has grown at an average annual rate of 7% over the past 40 years, ranking 11th in the world in terms of economy as of 2005 and GDP of 10,700 per capita. It has been transformed into a nation. The success of the Korean economy was a condensed growth experience worthy of being called a "miracle" in that it was a backward agricultural country that had been colonized and experienced the devastation of the Korean War and the resulting devastation of the country , and that the country was very scarce in capital or natural resources.  People's Republic of China The 'sleeping giant' China entered a stage of full-scale industrialization in the late 1970s with the introduction of the socialist market economy principle. It can be said that it is basically the same as Korea's growth model in that it is the basic driving force for growth, that it relies on capital and technology for imports, and that it is a government-led, export-dependent growth campaign. As a result, China has continued to grow at an average annual rate of 9% since the late 1970s. The volume of trade also went from 25th in the world at the end of the 1970s to 3rd in the world in 2004 after the United States and Germany. Consumer electronics, textiles, clothing, footwear, steel, etc. already occupy the No . 1 position in the world in terms of production and export volume. China has now risen to the status of the 'Factory of the World' and has become the 7th largest country in the world economy. In addition, as the world's 2nd largest foreign exchange holder after Japan, China's influence on the international financial market is growing day by day. The rise of China's economy is having a profound impact on the global economy in many ways. First, the era of low prices has arrived with the supply of low-cost goods to the world from China, the 'factory of the world' based on a vast low-cost labor force. This means that the level of welfare will improve globally. In addition, the formation of a low-interest rate system around the world, with lower labor costs, higher returns on capital, and low prices at low prices, is driving investment and spurring the growth of the global economy. On the other hand, negative effects are also emerging. China's industrial upheaval is shrinking the growth of labor-intensive industries and SMEs in developed and emerging and emerging countries, and this is a factor in the rise in employment-free growth in each country, especially for simple workers. However, this phenomenon is due to the promotion of restructuring in each country. In the long run, you won't have to look at it so negatively in that it serves as an impetus to take the economy to the next level. Taken together , China's economic development is playing the role of a locomotive in the development of the world economy by promoting the growth of the world economy and contributing to the improvement of the living standards of the people of the world. . Complementarity of the economic development of the two countries Let me then tell you what complementary relationship the economic growth of the two countries of Korea and China has in the process of industrialization. First of all, from South Korea's point of view, China's growth is both a crisis and an opportunity. One aspect of the crisis is that with the industrialization of China, labor-intensive industries such as agriculture, small and medium-sized enterprises, and self-employment are shrinking and employment is declining in one country. The phenomenon of economic polarization facing the Korean economy, namely large and medium-sized enterprises, competitive and competitive industries, technology-intensive and traditional industries, and the widening gap between households and businesses , is also not unrelated to the rise of the Chinese economy. Meanwhile, the rise of the Chinese economy is also a great opportunity for the Korean economy. This is because with the opening of the vast market of China , a continuous growth in exports is expected. Automotive, shipbuilding, electronics, steel, etc. in Korea The reason why the flagship industries are able to sustain their growth is due to the high growth of China's economy. In this regard, China's development will contribute to taking the Korean economy to the next level. On the other hand, the impact of Korea's growth on China is not small. Above all, I would like to point out that Korea is the closest learning case to China. Since Korea is not only one step ahead of China in the process of industrialization, but also shares a cultural heritage, it will be the easiest and easiest for China to imitate. Just as Korea has learned from the Japanese experience, China can learn a lot from Korea's industrialization experience. In addition, South Korea is also providing small goods, goods, production technology, and materials that are needed in China's industrialization process. This is evident in the economic exchanges between the two countries, which have been greatly active since the establishment of bilateral relations in 1992. First, the ROK-China trade code was only 29 billion in 1 99 0 years, but in 2000 it grew 11 times to 312 billion, and in 2004 it reached 79 billion, more than doubling from that of Dashi . Yes. Since 2003, China has surpassed the United States as South Korea's No. 1 exporter, and South Korea is necessary for China's industrialization, with 70 percent of China's exports to China being accounted for by small goods and goods. It is the main source of intermediate goods. In addition, Korean companies are very active in investing in China . As of the end of July 2005, South Korea's investment in China has exceeded 10 billion dalders in total at around 10,200 million. In particular, Tianjin City, where Nankai University is located, serves as the gateway to the recently activated intermediary exchange between the ROK and the Middle East. In other words, Tianjin City accounts for 9% of South Korea's trade with China and 10% of direct investment in China , making it the 4th most active place for Korean companies to invest in China, after Shandong Province, Jiangsu Province and Beijing. In addition , Korean electronics and auto parts companies located within the Tianjin Economic Technology Development Zone serve as a bridge between the two countries' technical exchanges. Cooperation in the financial sphere between the two countries is also being strengthened. Since the 1997-98 foreign exchange crisis in Asian countries, the financial cooperation system in Asia has been strengthened, and China and South Korea are actively participating in it. Under the Chiang Mai Initiative (CMI), which was chosen at the 2000 ASEAN3 Finance Ministers' Meeting, in 2002 the Chinese people signed a 2 billion currency swap agreement between Hang and the Bank of Korea, which increased its size to 4 billion in May of this year. . As such, the economic development of China and South Korea has been and will continue to be complementary to each other , and it is likely that this trend will continue to significantly sustain global economic growth. . Northeast Asian Economy in the World Economy How much will the Northeast Asian economy, which has been attracting global attention due to the rise of China , have a significant share of the global economy in the future ? The Bank of Korea has been studying how the economic development of the Asian region will proceed for the next half century. Based on the statistical projections obtained during the course of the study, I will tell you about the future of the Northeast Asian economy. As of 2003, China accounted for 20% of the world's population but only 4% of the world's GDP. In the United States and Europe*, on the other hand, the share of the population is only 5% and 6%, respectively, but the share of global GDP is 30% and 29%. In other words, the United States and Yurub, which make up 11% of the world's population, account for 60% of the world's GDP. However, with the rapid rise of China's economy , the map of the world economy is expected to change significantly. According to a study by the Bank of Korea, China will begin to outpace Japan by 2020 and Europe by 2035, and by 2040 it will be on par with the United States, accounting for about 1/5th of the world's GDP. South Korea's share will be 2% by 2040, slightly higher than the 1.7% in 2003, but Japan is relatively slow to grow, and its share is estimated to fall by half from 12% in 2003. * 15 pre-expansion EU countries (Germany, UK, France, Italy, Spain, Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, Austria, Finland, Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Portugal) It was. On the one hand, the share of the world economy in the three countries of Northeast Asia, which is the sum of Korea, China, and Japan, has risen from 11% in 1970 to 18% in 2003, and this trend is likely to continue in the future. According to the Bank of Korea's estimates, the share of the world economy of the three Northeast Asian countries will be 22% by 2025, similar to that of Europe , and by 2035 it will be 25%, similar to that of North America. Driven by this economic growth, GDP per capita will also grow steadily. By 2040 , China's GDP per capita would reach 10,500 in 2003 in U.S. dollars, more than 10 times higher than it is now, increasing to more than 10 times that of the U.S. and Japan . At the level of 1/4 and the level of 1/3 of that of South Korea, the gap is expected to be greatly reduced. . Closing It's time to wrap up my speech. The Chinese and Korean economies will continue to develop dynamically while driving the growth of the global economy in the 21st century. Thus, in the near future, the size of Northeast Asia's economy is likely to be similar to that of Europe and North America. But such an achievement will never happen on its own. It will be possible when the strength and wisdom of our mothers are gathered to make the 21st century the central era of Northeast Asia. First of all, we must further strengthen economic cooperation in the region and move toward the Northeast Asian Economic Community such as the European Community (EU) and the North American Oil and Trade Zone (NAFTA). For this purpose, we should further expand trade and mutual investment in the region through the signing of the F-TA between the 3 countries of Northeast Asia, the ROK, China, and Japan. At the same time, cooperation in the financial sphere that will support cooperation in the physical sector will also need to be strengthened. In addition, the cooperation between central banks to stabilize the financial system, which is becoming more important due to globalization and liberalization, must continue and be strengthened. In addition, we must not only use the complementary economic structure of the 3 countries of Northeast Asia in the future in a developmental way, but also expand its scope further. For example, cooperation in the field of new technologies such as IT, BT, NT, etc., which will become increasingly important in determining national competitiveness in the future. These new technologies are extremely resource-intensive and pose high risks, so if the 3 countries work closely together, they will result in a win-win for all. Based on this multifaceted mutual cooperation, there is no doubt that Northeast Asia will do a good job of advancing the global economy in the 21st century. At the same time, however, this means that Northeast Asia must move away from the supporting role it has played on the world economic stage and take on the role of co-starring with North America and Europe. Therefore, we believe that the development of the Northeast Asian economy is not limited to the developed countries and the rest of the world. I would like to emphasize that we must also fulfill our responsibilities as a major coalition, such as economic openness and mutual cooperation, so that it can lead to the development of the economy. (attached) Regular Conference of the Korea Finance Society Regular Conference of the Korea Finance Society Finance evolution   2007. 6. 8 Bank of Korea President Lee Sung-tae ( Greetings ) President Lee Ji-sun of the Korea Finance Society, and all the experts in academia and finance who are here ! I am very pleased to be a part of the regular academic conference of the Korea Finance Society, which has contributed greatly to the academic development of the financial field in Korea. We understand that at this conference, various opinions were expressed and serious discussions were held on the topic of "The Transition of the Finance Sector and Future Challenges in the 10 Years Since the Foreign Exchange Crisis". As an extension of this discussion, I will briefly talk about the performance of the financial sector after the foreign exchange crisis and the challenges for the advancement of our finance. ( Performance and problems after the foreign exchange crisis ) As you well know, the foreign exchange crisis has caused great suffering to all of our people, but it is also true that it has been an important moment to improve the constitution of our economy. In particular, the financial sector, which along with the corporate sector has been singled out as the source of the above period , has undergone intense restructuring. With the mass expulsion of insolvent financial institutions, the principle of responsible management has been established, and market discipline has been further strengthened by the enhancement of transparency in accounting and public security systems, the introduction of the deposit subsidiary system and the bond market price evaluation system. In addition, as the principle of competition is in full swing, the acquisition and merger between financial institutions has become more active, and the consolidation of finance such as the launch of a financial holding company and the use of Bangkashrangs Heo Yong has also progressed. This restructuring has also greatly improved the profitability and soundness of financial institutions. Over the past three years, the average return on assets (ROA) of domestic banks has been 1.1%, which is close to 1.3% in the United States, and the BIS equity ratio is 12.6%, which is higher than the 12.4% in the United States. However, in the process of overcoming the foreign exchange crisis, new problems are also emerging as the behavior of economic actors changes. Companies are showing cautious investment behavior with a focus on stability-oriented management, and in the case of large corporations, investment resources are also mainly financed internally such as profit surplus rather than external funds. As a result, investment in facilities, which has been a driver of economic growth in the past, is rarely rejuvenated. Financial institutions are also showing a risk-averse tendency to focus on traditional areas of work rather than opening up new areas of work. In the case of banks in particular, the demand for borrowing funds from large companies is declining, and they are fiercely competing to increase their share in the limited domestic lending market. In the meantime, the huge increase in mortgage and small business loans at the same time or in the run-up to the street is also attributed in large part to the management behavior of such banks. It is worth noting that the intensive management of funds by the majority of banks in the door of the special government is a kind of stinging phenomenon that can act as a source of instability in the financial markets. In addition , the development of capital markets and capital market governing financial institutions has been delayed due to the fact that financial restructuring has been bank-oriented and the demand for external financing by large companies has decreased. Although it is a common phenomenon that the securitization of finance advances as the financial sector develops , the share of stocks and bonds in the total financial assets held by economic actors in our country is 31.5% as of the end of 2005, reaching a level of 31.7% at the end of 1999. I'm staying. ( Challenges for financial advancement ) As I have said so far, the constitution of our economy has improved greatly since the foreign exchange crisis, but on the other hand, the risk-averse tendencies of economic actors , such as the conservative management behavior of companies and financial institutions, are showing a thump. Such a change in the attitude of economic actors, along with low birth rate and aging, is likely to act as a factor in weakening the growth potential of our economy. Various measures must be taken to deal with such a situation, but it may also be a good idea to find a new growth engine in the financial industry that can make full use of the superior human resources and high-quality IT technology that our country has a comparative advantage in. I think. In order for the financial industry to be able to drive the growth of our economy, it is necessary to actively enter overseas markets and create offshore demand. Just as the large European banks such as UBS, ABN AMRO and others have entered an epoch of growth by expanding the scope of competition to the global market, our financial institutions will also have to overcome the limitations of the domestic market by expanding their overseas expansion around the emerging economies of Asia. In addition, in response to the expansion of the domestic presence of advanced financial institutions and the diversification of the demand for financial services of urban households and enterprises in Korea, we should also take an active role in pioneering new tasks such as the development of financial products. To do this, it is of paramount importance to have a good financial literacy. The fact that the cost of professional labor in our financial industry is 1/5 of that of Hong Kong and Singapore is a reminder that efforts should be made to distribute the professional workforce to Yangcheng. In order for our financial industry to join the advanced financial sphere as soon as possible, the formation of financial institutions must also be further advanced. Since the foreign exchange upheaval, the largesse of domestic silver lines has been achieved through acquisitions, joint ventures, etc., but as of the end of 2005, it is included in the top 100 banks in the world 4 The average asset of a bank in a country is only 1/10th the size of the world's top 10 banks . In the case of securities firms, it is even worse, and the average asset and equity size of the top 5 securities companies in Korea is only 1/80 and 1/15th of that of the top 5 investment banks in the United States. Dear Honorable Members of the Korea Finance Society ! The development of the financial industry in our country is not only a matter of financial institutions, but it is a task that we all need to achieve with the help of wisdom. The government should be more committed to the advancement of the rock system, even if the autonomy and creativity of financial institutions can be fully exercised. We must improve the legal system that restricts economic disputes between financial institutions, and eliminate or relax various regulations that make it difficult for financial institutions to go abroad. In addition, we will have to expand the scope of the concomitant business between the financial industries so that synergies can be achieved. It is hoped that the implementation of the "Law on Capital Markets and Financial Investment Industry", which is currently under legislation, will activate the mutual co-operation of the financial industry related to the capital market. In academia, we should support the development of the financial industry through the training of professional personnel and cooperation between industry and academia. No domestic financial institution will be able to compete with the world's leading financial institutions without having excellent human resources. In this regard, the fact that Bill Gates, chairman of Microsoft, said that Goldman Sachs, a global financial firm, is their strongest competitor, is highly suggestive. The Bank of Korea will also fulfill the role and responsibility given to the central bank, such as solidifying the security foundations of the macroeconomic and financial markets so that financial institutions can pursue a coherent economic strategy in the long run. ( Conclusion ) If the past 10 years since the foreign exchange crisis have been a period of strengthening the constitution of our financial institutions , then in the future the financial industry should be the time to drive the growth of our economy. To this end, it is imperative that the academic community take the lead in revealing the path that the financial industry should take through various theoretical and empirical studies. In this regard, I have no doubt that this conference will be of great help to the advancement of our finance. Finally, I would like to thank the President of the Korea Finance Society Lee Ji-sun and the people involved in this position. Thanks.
