Title: Economy Undergoes Structural Transformation
text: ADB    Economy Undergoes Structural Transformation Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - The Korean economy is showing signs of a slow recovery, pulling out of the recession caused by sharply contracted domestic demand. Although annual GDP growth fell to 3.1 percent last year, the Korean economy has shifted to a recovery trend since last September. This is attributable to policy efforts such as the Bank of Korea's (BOK's) two-step reduction of the call-rate target and the government's expansion of fiscal expenditure through the drawing-up of supplementary budgets, as well as to the sharp increase in the nation's exports helped by the rapid recovery of the global economy. To date, domestic demand has not shaken off its lackluster appearance. However, with the favorable trend in exports and the signs of improvement in employment conditions, it is anticipated that the economic recovery will be clearly felt before long. In addition, facilities investment and private consumption will recover gradually. Consequently, GDP growth for this year is expected to rise to somewhere higher than 5 percent. On the prices front, there are some signs causing concern on the cost side, such as the continuing high oil prices and the rise in international raw material prices. However, - 2 - inflation from aggregate demand pressure has not yet been felt because of the mild pace of economic recovery. Annual average core inflation is currently forecast to remain at around the 3 percent level, although an increase in inflationary pressure in the course of a future recovery of domestic demand cannot be ruled out. In the meantime, the nation's current account has remained in surplus due to the briskness of exports. The scale of this year's surplus is forecast to exceed last year's 12.3 billion. Monetary Policy Under these economic circumstances, future monetary policy will be conducted in such a way as to maintain the balance between growth and stability. That is to say, monetary policy will continue to support domestic economic recovery and the improvement of employment conditions, but preemptive steps will be taken in response to any intensified upward pressure on prices due to a possible acceleration in the pace of recovery. From the beginning of 2004, with the entry into effect of - 3 - the revised Bank of Korea Act, the Bank's inflation targeting system has shifted from the former annual targeting to medium-term targeting, and this should provide the Bank with greater flexibility in conducting monetary policy. The BOK has set its inflation target in terms of the average rate of core inflation during the 200 42006 period at 2.53.5 percent. If medium-term price expectations deviate from this target range, we will take into account the causes of this deviation, the time lag in monetary policy transmission, and overall financial and economic conditions in deciding whether there should be a policy response and, if so what the proper strength of such a response should be. In the event of a monetary policy response being judged necessary, it will be designed so as to minimize its side effects on the real economy and financial markets while seeking medium-term convergence on the midpoint of the inflation target range. A strengthening of efforts to secure financial stability is also planned. There will be intensified monitoring of factors that might potentially bring about market instability, - 4 - including the problems of credit card companies and of the considerable number of people on the banks' credit blacklist. If necessary, market stabilization measures, such as expanding the supply of liquidity, will be implemented. Structural Perspective If, on the other hand, we look at things from a wider perspective in terms of the economy's structure or of economic development history, we can say that the Korean economy currently stands at an important crossroads. Korea is now facing a rapid hollowing-out of its manufacturing sector, due to the rise of the vast neighboring Chinese economy, the unavoidable worldwide trend of market opening, the high-cost and low-efficiency structure of the domestic economy, and so forth. At this critical juncture, to turn these challenges into opportunities, it is absolutely essential to break free of the prevailing high-cost and low-efficiency paradigm through overall social reforms, to promote liberalization and opening, and to upgrade the industrial structure. With these perceptions in mind, the government has already designed a roadmap for a wide range of structural reforms - 5 - and will carry them out faithfully, while orienting itself toward the era of per capita national income of 20,000. In addition, it is vital that we step up North-South economic cooperation on the Korean Peninsula as a short-term breakthrough. Notably, it is anticipated that North-South economic cooperation will further accelerate, as some South Korean corporations are now about to move to North Korea's model estate in the Kaesong Industrial Complex, and as North Korea has recently given indications of its desire to escape its isolated position in international society. Still more importantly, the Korean people have a dynamic ability to unite as one to overcome hardships, when they share a recognition of crisis or aims to be pursued, as happened during the financial crisis in 1997 and also in the staging of the World Cup 2002. Taking account of all these factors, I am confident that the Korean people will again find the strength and wisdom to overcome the present challenges facing them, and that the Korean economy will advance toward a bright future.

Title: ADB Annual Meeting Welcome Speech
text: ADB  The Address of Welcome Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - On behalf of the Bank of Korea, I would like to extend the warmest welcome to all our guests who have come from far and wide to take part in the 37th annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank. For better or worse we are moving toward unbounded competition on a tide of globalization. Therefore, it is becoming more and more difficult for any single firm or country to survive by its own efforts alone staying within the comfortable surroundings of the known and familiar. Asian countries have been strengthening and deepening their cooperation since the outbreak of the Southeast Asian currency crises in 1997. During this year's annual meeting, we will engage in in-depth discussions of various issues with a view to the common good of the Asian region. Already close connection have been built up between countries across Asia through increasing trade and investment and this trend is set to continue in the future. Accordingly, we need to step up further our cooperation in terms of finance and policy to back up the drive to work together within the real economy. - 2 - This regional cooperation should not be a closed model seeking only the interests of Asian countries, but should be a model that matches the common interests of the entire global community. In this context it is fortunate that not only Asian-Pacific countries but also quite a few North American and European countries participate in the ADB. Therefore, in discussing plans for regional cooperation using this stage provided by the ADB we should not spare our efforts to gain the understanding and cooperation of these non-regional member countries while taking full advantage of their recommendations and advice. Jeju island's beauty with the mountain flowing down to the sea has made it Korea's premier resort area to which domestic and foreign tourists love to return. Though I know you will be busy over this brief period of the annual meeting, I hope that all of you have the good fortune to enjoy this wonderful spring on Jeju island.

Title: Opening of the World Central Bank Workshop
text: Opening Remarks delivered by Dr. Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea at The 2nd Workshop for Worldwide Central Banks on Uncertainties in the Global Economy and Financial Crisis Management Seoul, 21 July 2004 - 1 - Ladies and gentlemen, It is my great pleasure to welcome all of you, distinguished colleagues from central banks worldwide, to this workshop on Uncertainties in the Global Economy and Financial Crisis Management. I would like to extend my special thanks to Dr. Tilak Rawal, Governor of Nepal Rastra Bank, who has made the long and difficult journey to deliver a special address. Ladies and gentlemen, Nowadays society is developing ever more rapidly. This makes it difficult to forecast what lies ahead. Notably, three sea changes that took place towards the end of the 20th century have greatly increased the uncertainties that shroud the future. The first of these is the tide of globalization that has accelerated since the early 1990s. With the launch of the World Trade Organization, most trade barriers between countries have been removed. No company can now sit comfortably at ease behind its national borders, protected from the chill winds of the global marketplace. - 2 - Needless to say, the financial industry is no exception to this trend. With the integration of world financial markets, capital is now crossing borders freely on a vast scale and the volatility of financial asset prices has been greatly heightened. The second of these sea changes is the IT(Information Technology) Revolution. Development of the IT industry has completely shattered the existing order. Differentiation based on concepts of physical time and space has been swept away to yield to the synchronicity of cyberspace, and the very structure of our consciousness is changing with it. Traditional factors of production - land, labor, and capital - are losing their importance, while that of technology, knowledge, and information is increasing day by day. The third great modern change is the collapse of communism. With its disappearance, the world economy now forms one great market-based economy. But the breakdown of the old bi-polar order has sparked greater geopolitical instability and brought more frequent racial conflicts and acts of terrorism. As I have just briefly outlined, tremendous structural changes took place worldwide from the early 1990s. Unfortunately, Korea and a number of other East Asian countries failed to adapt quickly to the new world order, and were hit by financial crises in 1997. - 3 - The East Asian countries have now escaped from the shock of those crises. Nevertheless, uncertainty is by no means on the wane. Let me enumerate some elements of this. All eyes are on the future direction of the Chinese economy. Even up until last year, there was still concern being voiced that Chinas rapid pace of economic growth might trigger global deflation. Todays concerns are quite different: China may spark worldwide inflation or its failure to achieve a soft landing will throw the world economy into turmoil. Uncertainty also surrounds the speed of the current trend of interest rate increases. At the end of last month, the US Federal Reserve raised the Federal funds rate by twenty-five basis points. This may be taken as a good signal, confirming that the global economic recovery is now well underway. The market, however, is concerned about the impacts of interest rate hikes on the position of hedge funds and carry trades as well as on property prices and household credit. Meanwhile, the political situation in Iraq still remains a guessing game, and the world is suffering repeated acts of terrorism. International oil prices, already at high levels, fluctuate wildly in reaction to geopolitical developments, and the pundits are unable to agree on the future course of oil prices. - 4 - Worse to say, our world is now confronted with a series of rapid mutations of viruses including SARS, mad-cow disease, and bird flu, all of which compound the economic uncertainty. Ladies and gentlemen, Facing this cloud of uncertainty shrouding the world economy, we cannot afford to neglect our risk management. Of course, the likelihood of a serious financial crisis has decreased markedly, thanks to the efforts many countries have made to bolster the stability of their macro-economies and financial systems since the last East Asian financial crisis. But in spite of our best efforts to avoid a renewed crisis, the historical experience is that crises will always break out. After the crisis here in 1997, Korea pressed ahead with resolute structural adjustment, greatly reducing the fragility of the financial sector and conglomerates over-borrowing problems. Meanwhile, another threat has been posed to financial stability by the heavy indebtedness of the household sector and the deterioration of the financial management of credit card companies. These weaknesses have held back the recovery of the Korean economy. - 5 - Ladies and gentlemen, fellow central bankers, One certain thing in an uncertain world is that we have lived through great uncertainty, and can expect to face an even more uncertain future. Therefore, we have to keep trying to turn uncertainty into controllable risk. This will help us to prevent the occurrence of crises and, if one nevertheless does break out, to tackle it at an early stage. Unless we do so, we are fated to exemplify the words of George Santayana, the great Spanish-American poet and philosopher, who warned that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it. Ladies and gentlemen, It is my earnest hope that by means of both in-depth and wide-ranging discussions in this workshop, every participant will take back to his or her country useful information on the various global uncertainties and implications for coping with them. - 6 - In closing, I would like to thank all of the staff involved from the KDI School of Public Policy and Management, and from the Bank of Korea, for their dedicated efforts in staging this workshop. I would also like to once more bid all participants the heartiest of welcomes. Thank you.

Title: The Changing Structure of Economic Growth and Future of the Korean Economy
text: The Changing Structure of Economic Growth and Future of the Korean Economy October 1, 2004 Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - . Opening Remarks President Joseph Winder and respected members of the Korea Economic Institute of America, Ladies and gentlemen, Since its foundation in 1982, the KEI has made an immense contribution to the development of the Korean economy through its promotion of bilateral economic cooperation between Korea and the United States. Its distinguished accomplishment has been widely applauded and deeply respected by many Korean people. I had the honor of addressing your esteemed Institute in 2002, several months after being appointed Governor of the Bank of Korea. As I recall, I spoke to you at that time about how Korea had been able to recover from the 1997 currency crisis and what reforms we still needed to make. Having enjoyed that wonderful experience two years ago, I doubly welcomed your kind invitation to come here again today. My theme this time is the future of the Korean economy, in view of the changes in its growth structure. . Changes in the Structure of Economic Growth Nowadays, the Korean economy is undergoing the transition from an early growth stage to a mature growth stage. In the past, we were able to enjoy high economic growth. For about 40 years, from 1960 through 2000, our annual average rate of growth was 7.7%. It was possible because we were in an environment characterized by protectionism and - 2 - latecomer's advantage, together with low wages, surplus domestic demand, and high yields on investment. Korea's economic growth during that period may be termed 'growth through industrialization' or 'early stage growth'. Nowadays, however, we must pursue economic growth under different conditions. Protectionism is no longer possible and latecomer's advantage no longer exists. Our environment is now one of high wages, weak domestic demand, and low yields on investment. In other words, the Korean economy has entered the post-industrialization era or a mature growth stage. Any country, as its economic growth structure undergoes transition from an early to a mature stage, can expect its GDP growth rate to fall. The question, then, is how that country, after experiencing growth of 6 or 7% in its early stage of growth, copes in its mature stage. Some countries achieve soft landings, with growth holding up at robust levels of 4 to 5%. Others suffer hard landings, with their growth declining to 1 or 2%. A comparison between the cases of Japan and Germany is instructive. Both Japan and Germany experienced changes in their structures of economic growth in around the early 1970s. It was also in 1973 or so that these two countries attained levels of per capita income in constant 1995 prices, similar to that of Korea last year, which was 12,600 dollars. Although both countries had achieved high economic growth during their early stages, their patterns of growth diverged after their growth structures changed in the early 1970s. Japanese economy had grown rapidly, at an annual average rate of 9.7% during its early growth stage from 1950 through 1973. After that, Japan achieved a soft landing, with its growth holding up at a comparatively strong annual average of 3.7% for some 20 years from 1974 onwards. In contrast, in the German case, despite annual growth having averaged 6.1% from 1950 through 1973, there was a sharp drop to an average of just 2.0% for the following 30 years. - 3 - In this light, we can see the importance of how a country handles the transformation of its economic growth structure. Today, I would like to outline the state of the Korean economy as it confronts this transformation of growth structure, and how it is handling it. . Signs of Changes in the Structure of Economic Growth Nowadays, the Korean economy is showing various indications of a transformation of economic growth structure. Let me just review these indications in outline. Firstly, the increase in the Korean population has virtually halted, and we are rapidly moving toward an aging society. Average live births per woman have dropped to among the lowest in the world now, at just 1.2 children. Although the share in total Korean population of those aged 65 years or over, currently 8.7%, still remains below those in advanced countries, it is growing very rapidly. Secondly, we are seeing development of a high-cost and low-efficiency society. There are increasing calls these days for reduced working hours, while at the same time there is heightened reluctance to take on the types of jobs we term the 3D's: those that are dirty, dangerous and difficult. Meanwhile, demands for higher welfare and benefit levels are also growing. As a consequence of all of these trends, absolute wage levels in some Korean industries are virtually on a par now with those in the United States or Japan, despite their productivity levels remaining lower. Housing prices and other living expenses are also very high. - 4 - Thirdly, in this environment, returns on investment have declined and the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which are predominantly engaged in labor-intensive industries, is weakening fast. Fourthly, the interplay between the supply of and the demand for funds has undergone a dramatic change, from a situation in which an excess demand for funds prevailed to one in which there is now a lack of demand. Furthermore, changes in interest rates and money supply have lost some of their effectiveness in influencing consumption and investment. Thus, even though Korean interest rates are now at their lowest ever levels, and there is abundant market liquidity, this by itself is not sufficient to bring about the increases in consumption and investment expenditures. Meanwhile, on the external front, we are seeing the rapid emergence of vast new economic powerhouses, such as China and India, which are able to benefit greatly from their low-wage levels. Not only this, but the world economic order is evolving swiftly from one characterized by protectionism to one of openness. This means that unless Korean firms are able to compete at the international level, they will not survive these harsh and cruel economic realities. In the face of these rapid changes in our environment at home and abroad, the growth potential of the Korean economy is waning. . Pains in the Process of Transformation of Economic Growth Structure In the course of transformation of the growth structure in any country, the competitiveness of its labor-intensive manufacturing sectors - 5 - tends to weaken. Thus, the relocation of the production bases of those sectors to low-wage countries becomes common. This is what happened in the United States and Japan in the past. In the cases of these two advanced countries, however, the processes were very gradual and the impacts were not so large. For example, beginning from the mid-1980s, some elements of the Japanese manufacturing base were transferred to what were called the Four Asian Dragons, including Korea. This did not greatly affect Japan itself, however, because the scale of the Japanese economy was so much larger than those of the other Asian countries. For example, Japan's GDP at that time was some fifteen times that of Korea. Moreover, the domestic impact was also well buffered by protectionism. However, the case is greatly different in today's Korea. The size of the neighboring low-wage Chinese economy is more than double that of Korea. And, given the higher pace of growth in Chinese economy, this difference in scale seems to grow much greater in the future. Nor is that all. Under today's prevailing system of market openness, we can no longer look to protectionism as a buffer against outside competition. As a net consequence, the transformation of the growth structure of the Korean economy is proceeding at a faster pace, and its impact is even stronger and brings us even greater hardships. Let me now briefly spell out the difficulties we are currently facing. Firstly, the Korean economy's potential growth rate has dropped, from its previous 8% level to the 5% level now. What is more, our GDP growth volatility is becoming somewhat larger; in other words, the amplitude of the business cycles is expanding. Secondly, the competitiveness of most Korean SMEs and labor-intensive industries is weakening. This is one of the reasons why - 6 - we now have the phenomenon of what is termed 'jobless growth', and a very high level of unemployment among our young people. Thirdly, the polarization of the Korean economy has intensified. Although our exports have been booming, domestic demand has been sluggish for over a year. While our large enterprises have continued to grow, the business statuses of many SMEs are problematic. And at the same time while Korean corporate profits have risen greatly, centering on large companies, our household incomes have stagnated. It is because of this polarization of our economy that most members of the Korean public feel growing dissatisfaction with their lives these days, even though the overall economy continues to expand. Fourthly, the growing reluctance of Korean businesses to commit themselves to domestic investment has become an acute problem. The fruits of Korea's economic growth have become concentrated among a few large firms, with the result that these firms have piled up their largest profits ever. Instead of reinvesting these profits into domestic facilities, however, most of the firms are either investing them overseas or using them to pay down their debts. In my remarks so far, I have dwelt upon the problems and hardships that the Korean economy is now going through. These things have to be understood, I think, as transitional phenomena that were always bound to appear in the process of changes in the growth structure. . The Korean Economy's Swift Adaptation I have tried to point out that the impact of changes in its growth structure on the Korean economy, and the pains that they are inflicting, - 7 - have been particularly large. And I believe that the reason for this is because Korea is moving through the process so much faster than other countries in the past. It is also possible to look at these problems and hardships from another angle, however, and to see them positive signs of just how swiftly the Korean economy is adapting to the changes it now confronts. And historically, throughout the process of Korean economic development, the greater the impact of change on the Korean economy, the faster the Korean economy has adapted. To my mind, this dynamism is one of the most striking characteristics of the Korean economy. I should like to speak now about how this adaptation is currently making itself felt. First of all, adjustment of the Korean industrial structure is proceeding very rapidly. We are seeing a rapid shift in industrial structure now underway, from manufacturing to services and, in particular, to knowledge-based services. When we break Korean GDP down by sector, we see that the share of manufacturing in total GDP declined from 29.4% in 2000 to 26.6% in 2003, while that of services rose over the same period, from 54.4% to 57.2%. Most strikingly, the weight of knowledge-based service areas including communications, finance, education, culture and medical care moved up very sharply, from 22.3% to 26.8%. The structure of Korean manufacturing itself has also been realigned, to center now on the high value-added sectors. The weight of the heavy and chemical industrial sector, which embraces the IT industry, rose from 77.6% of total manufacturing in 2000 to 79.1% in 2003. A glance at the growth rates by sector within manufacturing shows that, during 2003, the heavy and chemical industrial sector grew by 8.0%, whereas the labor-intensive light industrial sector posted negative growth of 4.1%. In the first half of this year, the former sector expanded at a rate of 16.0%, while the latter showed negative growth of 1.5%. - 8 - Secondly, there have been great improvements in the soundness and transparency of Korean corporate management. Looking at the aspect of soundness first, Korean firms had lowered their debt ratios from an average of 400% in 1997 to 123% by the end of 2003. They had brought down their ratios of fixed assets to shareholders' equity from 261% to 132% over the same period. Given that in the United States the average debt ratio is 154%, and the average fixed ratio 176%, the financial structure of Korean firms can be seen to be extremely sound. With regard to transparency, we have greatly improved the arrangements for financial statement disclosure. And we have made great progress as well in reforming corporate governance structures, by requiring corporations to appoint outside directors to their boards, and strengthening protections of the rights of minority shareholders. Thirdly, economic openness has been constantly pushed forward. Almost all barriers to foreign capital for both direct and portfolio investment and even for participation in management have now been swept away. Back in 1997, foreign investors accounted for just 15% of the total market capitalization of listed Korean firms. Since 1998, however, when all ceilings on foreign investment in domestic equities were abolished, this figure has continued to rise, and it now stands at more than 40%. What is more, as of the end of last year, foreign investors held 43% of the total capital of domestic commercial banks. These figures show that Korea is now the highest among Asian countries in terms of foreign ownership in its economy. Not unnaturally, there is still some resistance in Korea to market openness in areas such as agriculture, labor, culture and the arts. The points at issue, however, are expected to be resolved sooner or later. Fourthly, the financial reform efforts have achieved considerable success, with the Korean financial system having become much more - 9 - stable now than in the past. After the 1997 financial crisis, Korea went through many hardships, but the overall success of the financial reform is uncontested. Only 19 out of 33 Korean banks survived the painful process of structural adjustment, and more than 40% of the total staff of financial institutions were laid off. The substandard loan ratio of domestic commercial banks has been brought down from 14% in 1999 to below 3% currently. More recently, of course, household liabilities including credit card debt have arisen as new factors increasing financial risk in Korea. In particular, credit card debt soared five times between year-end 1998 and year-end 2002. Thanks to harsh restructuring measures subsequently taken from the second half of last year, however, this figure has now been cut almost in half. Domestic demand has slumped in consequence of this household debt problem, with consumer spending declining considerably. Since March of this year, however, the rate of arrears on credit card payments has begun to decline, and from the second half of the year most credit card companies are expected to be in the black again. The problem of household debt, including that on credit cards, is seen as likely to be resolved to a considerable extent by the end of this year. If this does in fact happen, the stability of the Korean financial system will begin to show constant improvement. The final Korean adaptation to change that I would like to point to is the steady expansion of economic cooperation between South and North Korea. This will make possible a new breakthrough for the economy of the Republic of Korea. One prominent example of the expanding North-South cooperation is the Gaesong Industrial Complex in North Korea. Our plan is to develop this complex over an eight-year period, so that it eventually covers an area of 16,000 acres. Already this year, several South Korean businesses have begun to move in there. A leading - 10 - attraction of this project is the abundance of high quality human resources available in North Korea. At the same time, the wages to be paid to workers in Gaesong have been set at 57.5 dollars a month, which is just one-twentieth of the average level in South Korea and is also lower than the norm in China. What is more, Gaesong is only 40 miles from Seoul, which makes it a very advantageous location for industry. If South Korean firms can begin to shift their production bases to this and to other similar districts in North Korea, they will be able to regain a new competitive edge. This expansion of cooperation between the two Koreas will also speed up the opening of North Korea to the outside world. It is also expected to have a very positive effect in reducing the costs associated with eventual reunification of the Korean peninsula. . Concluding Remarks Ladies and gentlemen, As I mentioned earlier, dynamism has historically been a very prominent feature of Korea's economic development. And in fact, the dynamics of Korea's development may be understood as a process involving the compression and condensation of changes. Put another way, changes that take other countries ten years to accomplish were typically carried out in Korea in just one or two years. I think that the reason for this was because the Korean people, based on their innate diligence and quickness, were able to vault over the intermediary processes involved in change, and maximize their latecomer's advantage of imitating the front runner. - 11 - There are several examples of this Korean trait in action. Typical among them were our adoption of a value-added tax in 1977, our enforcement of the real name financial transaction system in 1993, and our legislation separating doctors' roles in prescribing drugs and pharmacists' roles in dispensing them in 2000. In each of these cases, Korean society accommodated themselves very quickly to the changed circumstances, and the new systems settled into effect smoothly. To my way of thinking, the Korean people will be able to adapt, in a similar way, to the changes in our economic growth structure that we are now facing. Of course, there are many tasks that we need to carry out yet, and many issues that we must resolve. Examples of things which we still need to work hard on to overcome are the confrontational relationship between labor and management and the residual reluctance within Korean society to full market opening. These issues, I am confident, should be resolved fairly soon. In drawing to a close, let me try to quickly tie together the various threads of my argument. The Korean economy is right now in the process of transition from an early growth stage to a mature growth stage. We expect that it will be able to adapt well to these changes and achieve a soft landing. Accordingly, after having been able to grow at the high average annual rate of 7.7% over the last 40 years, the Korean economy, I believe, is well on course toward attaining robust growth at the level of 4 or 5% in the medium and long-term future. Thank you all for listening so attentively.

Title: Opening of the 12th Central Banking Seminar
text: The 12th Central Banking Seminar Opening Address October 12, 2004 Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - (Opening remarks) Ladies and gentlemen, Let me extend a hearty welcome to you, central bankers gathered from all over the world to attend the Bank of Korea's "Central Banking Seminar". I would like to extend my particular thanks to Mr. Stefan Schonberg, Head of International Relations Department in the Deutsche Bundesbank. The Central Banking Seminar, now in its 12th year, is taking its place as a valued occasion for promoting interchange and cooperation among central bankers, and as a forum for the debate of common policy issues and the search for appropriate responses. (Imbalances in the Global Economy) The topic chosen for this seminar is "Current Global Imbalances and the Challenges for Central Banks". Many experts point to the huge U.S. current account deficit as the most significant problem giving rise to imbalances in the global economy. The U.S. current account deficit rose fourfold from 136 billion dollars in 1997 to 530 billion dollars last year. And the ratio of the U.S. current account deficit to current GDP similarly increased from less than 2% in 1997 to more than 5% during the first half of this year. The greater part of the U.S. - 2 - current account deficit arises from its trade with Asian countries. These countries, in turn, mainly invest foreign reserves built up from their current account surpluses in the U.S. Treasury market. Some take the optimistic view that this level of imbalance is sustainable, given the high productivity growth of the United States and its low risk premium along with the predominant position of the U.S. dollar in international financial markets. Others, however, say that the imbalance cannot be maintained because, in line with the increasing indebtedness of the United States, the burden of external interest payments will also be augmented. Anyway, as the scale of the imbalance is constantly growing, the pessimistic view can only become more persuasive than the optimistic one. (Measures to Adjust the Global Imbalance) Should confidence in the U.S. dollar weaken as a result of the continual widening of the U.S. current account deficit, there is the possibility that the demand for U.S. dollar-denominated assets may decrease. This would bring about instability in international financial markets by leading to a weak U.S. dollar and pushing up interest rates in the United States. In this respect, it is desirable that the global economic - 3 - imbalance represented by the large-scale U.S. current account deficit should be adjusted as soon as possible. Also, considering that this problem has become deep-rooted to some degree, the unilateral efforts of either the deficit country or the surplus countries will be inadequate. What will be essential is international understanding and cooperation. First of all, the United States, whose current account is in huge deficit, should strive for fiscal tightening as well as the lifting of its private-sector savings ratio. In contrast, those countries with current account surpluses, generally Asian countries, should boost domestic consumption through structural reform as well as heightening the flexibility of their currencies' exchange rates. If, however, these policy responses were to be put in place abruptly within a short period, it could give rise to various side-effects such as a slowdown of the U.S. economy and the shrinkage of Asian countries' exports. Therefore, these steps should be undertaken gradually, in line with the development of the global economy and the situation of international financial markets. At the present time, the institutional stability of the global economic system and the flexibility of international financial markets are much greater than before. Accordingly, provided the adjustment of the imbalance can be attainted step by step with the close cooperation between countries, then, in my opinion, we are sure to overcome these adversities. - 4 - (Closing Remarks) We, central bankers, therefore, should show wisdom of by preparing our winter coats before autumn fades. In this respect, I hope that this seminar will prove valuable opportunity to examine carefully problems that may arise and come up with specific countermeasures. Besides this, I hope that it will be the chance for us to share experiences as to how the global economic imbalance has influenced individual countries and how they have responded to it. For example, though Korea has recently seen its exports increase sharply, domestic demand has been held back, because production is being moved to low-wage countries and employment opportunities are not growing enough to encourage private consumption. As a consequence, various imbalances have also been growing in the Korean economy including that between exports and domestic demand and that between export-oriented large companies and domestic demand-dependant SMEs. Accordingly, Korea is conducting macroeconomic policy to support the revival of domestic demand including the Bank of Korea's reduction of its policy rate this August and the government's expansion of fiscal spending. It also involves structural reforms such as the pursuit of industrial structure upgrading. - 5 - Ladies and gentlemen, Although the schedule for this seminar is rather demanding, I hope that all participants will have the time to cultivate mutual friendships and to enjoy some aspects of Korean culture as well as the beauty of the autumnal mood. In closing, I give my sincere thanks to all those involved in the preparations for this seminar and ask them to do their utmost throughout to make it a great success.

Title: Expected Roles of the Asian Financial Sector in a Changing Environment
text: Expected Roles of the Asian Financial Sector in a Changing Environment A Keynote Speech delivered by Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea at the Sixth Meeting of the Asian Program co-hosted by the Institute of International Finance and the Korea Center for International Finance Seoul, 27 October 2004 - 1 - (Greetings) Ladies and Gentlemen, It is my great pleasure to see here this evening so many Asian financiers and experts in related fields as you round off the successful "Sixth Meeting of the Asian Program". I should like to express my special thanks to Charles Dallara, Managing Director of the Institute of International Finance and to all those involved for inviting me to join you tonight. This program has covered many of the major issues for the Asian region such as mergers and acquisitions between financial institutions, developing local and regional bond markets, and banking reform in China. It also has provided a valuable opportunity for earnest debate and the exchange of opinions between many of the top executives of renowned financial institutions and leading financial experts in the Asian area. - 2 - (A New Standing for the Asian Economy) When we look back, we realize that over the last halfcentury the Asian economy has shown dynamic growth that is without historical parallel, bringing it to today's pivotal position in the global economy. Japan joined the ranks of the advanced countries some time ago, and Korea too was able to shake off the destruction and utter poverty of the Korean War to become a member of the OECD. Once again China is maintaining very rapid growth that is making it a global superpower, with India not far behind. A very brisk picture also strikes us when we look at the ASEAN countries, notably Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam. Now sixteen Asian countries occupy a high place in the world economy, accounting for 22 percent of global GDP and 25 percent of global trade. These are the three North East Asian countries, Korea, China and Japan, and the 10 ASEAN countries, along with Taiwan, Hong Kong and India. - 3 - In making this great leap in economic development, these Asian countries have accumulated foreign exchange reserves on a vast scale. In fact, at the end of last year, they together held foreign exchange reserves of more than 1.9 trillion dollars. (Changes in the Asian Financial Environment) But despite this successful growth of the real economy in Asia, structural fragility brought upon us the experience of the Asian currency crisis in the latter half of the 1990's. This acted as a spur to all our countries, forcing them into structural reform, particularly of the financial sector. In Korea, the soundness of the financial sector has been greatly heightened through structural adjustment. It includes the exit of failed financial institutions, the recapitalization of those still viable along with the clearing of their non-performing loans, and the inducement of foreign capital and advanced management techniques. In fact almost all our Asian countries have been devoting great efforts to comply more closely, by way of structural reform and openness, with global standards for every sector of finance and the economy. - 4 - What is more, financial cooperation continues to be strengthened among the countries of the Asian region. What are known as the ASEAN 3 countries, working together closely with APEC and the ADB, are stepping up their cooperation. It aims at developing and utilizing a joint monitoring and early warning system on in- and out-flows of short-term capital, promoting local and regional bond markets, and expanding free-trade agreements. Turning to central banks, a total of 15 bilateral swap agreements have been entered into under the Chiang Mai Initiative for a value of 33.5 billion dollars. Also an investment fund was established in June 2003 for regional bonds denominated in US dollar, and the finishing touches are now being put to the setting-up of a fund for investment in bonds denominated in regional currencies. Systematic financial cooperation is brisk through central banking organizations such as EMEAP, the Executives' Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks, and SEACEN, South East Asian Central Banks. There is, notably, substantial policy cooperation between the central banks of Korea, China and Japan by way, for example, of regular meetings of their governors. - 5 - We can fairly say that the financial environment of the Asian region has seen great improvement compared with the past, thanks to this structural adjustment in every country and the strengthening of cooperation among them. It does not stop there. The financial environment will continue to be improved in future, owing to the development of competition to build a financial hub in their own country that now involves not only Hong Kong and Singapore but also Korea, China and Japan. (Expected Roles of the Financial Sector) Along with all these beneficial changes in the financial environment, there are great expectations for the financial sector within Asia. Firstly, with the rapid development of the real economy, there is fast growing demand for financial services in relation to trade, direct and portfolio investment, the management of foreign exchange holdings and so forth. The financial sector is anticipated to move swiftly to fully satisfy these financial needs, taking an extremely pro-active business approach. - 6 - We also very much hope that financial institutions will play a major role in transforming the surplus funds of the region into long-term investments within the region by taking an active part in the drive to build up the Asian bond markets. This could contribute greatly to accelerating the economic development and broadening the common prosperity of the Asian region, by efficiently distributing funds from capital surplus areas of Asia to those that have a demand for funds. This said, the development of the Asian financial sector will itself be further accelerated if the regional financial institutions and renowned global players set up a direct presence throughout the region to deliver these financial services. (Closing Remarks) Ladies and gentlemen, I firmly believe that all of you gathered here today have a deeper understanding and more acute discernment than most, concerning the immense diversity and dynamic energy of Asias history, culture and phases of economic development. - 7 - I should like to ask you now to play a positive part in transforming diversity into mutual complementarity and bringing out all the possible dynamic energies. Please be unsparing with your advice and cooperation to the policy authorities of individual countries and the international organizations. In closing, I trust every one of you will enjoy a delightful time this evening and have a safe and peaceful homeward journey. Thank you.

Title: Governor New Year's Address
text: Speech at the meeting 2005. 5. 27. Bank of Korea (Greetings) We sincerely welcome you to attend the 2005 Bank of Korea International Conference. And I would like to express my deepest gratitude to Toshihiko Fukui, President of the Bank of Japan, Zhou Xiaochuan, President of the People's Bank of China, and Professor Bennett McCallum of Carnegie-Mellon University for delivering the keynote address. I would also like to thank Christian Noyer, President of the Bank of France, as well as all those who have served as moderators, presenters and panelists. The conference is celebrating the 55th anniversary of the Bank of Korea with the theme of "Effectiveness of Economic Stabilization Policy". Recently, concerns about the rapid changes in the financial environment and deteriorating financial health of the three countries have led to growing uncertainty regarding the implementation of macroeconomic policies. In such a situation, I believe that the precious words of today's top central bank officials and world-class scholars will be of great help to the policymakers of central banks and governments in each country. (International Cooperation to Correct Disparities in the World Economy) Today's conference is attended by prominent figures from 33 central banks and international organizations, as well as from academia. I would like to take this opportunity to say a few things about the importance of economic cooperation between countries. If you look at past history, if a neighboring country becomes richer, your country will rather There were many cases of damage. But now it has become a world where neighboring countries must be strong to develop together. These interdependent relationships have spread not only between geographically adjacent countries, but also between all countries in the world as globalization has advanced rapidly. The world has now become a common destiny that no nation can develop alone. The need for international economic cooperation has also increased. But on the one hand, the widening of trade and capital movement has exacerbated imbalances in the global economy. The United States continues to have twin deficits, while Asian countries, on the contrary, are showing a large current account surplus. This imbalance could be corrected by the adjustment of the exchange rate, which is the price variable, and the economic structure, which is the real variable . Today, however, the importance of quality and technology to international trade has become more important than price. In addition , the influence of economic and structural factors such as the micro-flight situation in each country is greatly increasing. That's why currency adjustments alone are limited to resolving international imbalances. Therefore, I believe that international cooperation, which focuses on economic restructuring between countries, needs to be strengthened. The United States will have to make efforts to curb consumption and increase its low axis. Asian countries will need to expand their domestic infrastructure and increase their economic resources to improve the quality of life of their own people. (Economic Cooperation in Asia) Next, I will talk about economic cooperation in Asia. The Asian economy has the highest dynamic in the world and has developed rapidly both quantitatively and qualitatively. Asia's share of the world's sum of GDP has risen from 6% in 1960 to 12% in 1970 and more recently to around 26%. Now Asian countries must further promote openness so that they can fulfill their roles and responsibilities in accordance with their stature while striving for the common prosperity of the international community . At the same time, it is necessary to further consolidate economic cooperation in the region. In order to do this, we must overcome the unfortunate conflicts of past history with a forward-looking attitude and promote the Zen Linguan system. Through the signing of FTAs, we should further expand free trade and strengthen exchanges in various fields such as finance, science and technology, information, and culture. Central banks in the Asian region, in particular, will have to contribute to this economic cooperation, and in order to do so, they will have to continue to strengthen cooperation between central banks. (Conclusion) In this regard , we look forward to the conference being a foundation for promoting international cooperation. The Bank of Korea's revision of the Bank of Korea Act, which came into force last year, has strengthened its independence in the implementation of monetary policy and greatly increased its responsibility for price stability and financial stability. As a result of this, the Bank of Korea will be more committed to promoting cooperation between central banks and will more faithfully fulfill its responsibilities and obligations of stabilizing the economy. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude once again to all those who have taken the precious time to attend. Thanks.

Now Asian countries must further promote openness so that they can fulfill their roles and responsibilities in accordance with their stature while striving for the common prosperity of the international community . At the same time, it is necessary to further consolidate economic cooperation in the region. In order to do this, we must overcome the unfortunate conflicts of past history with a forward-looking attitude and promote the Zen Linguan system. Through the signing of FTAs, we should further expand free trade and strengthen exchanges in various fields such as finance, science and technology, information, and culture. Central banks in the Asian region, in particular, will have to contribute to this economic cooperation, and in order to do so, they will have to continue to strengthen cooperation between central banks. (Conclusion) In this regard , we look forward to the conference being a foundation for promoting international cooperation. The Bank of Korea's revision of the Bank of Korea Act, which came into force last year, has strengthened its independence in the implementation of monetary policy and greatly increased its responsibility for price stability and financial stability. As a result of this, the Bank of Korea will be more committed to promoting cooperation between central banks and will more faithfully fulfill its responsibilities and obligations of stabilizing the economy. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude once again to all those who have taken the precious time to attend. Thanks.

Title: Can the Korean Economy Sustain Growth at the 45% Level?
text: Korea Times  Can the Korean Economy Sustain Growth at the 45% Level? September 2005 Park, Seung Governor The Bank of Korea - 1 - ( Structural Changes in the Growth Environment ) The Korean economy is now at a watershed as it progresses from the early stages of growth to an advanced growth stage. For many years, the Korean economy has experienced rapid growth in an environment characterized by low wages, excess demand, high returns on investment, protectionism and late starter advantage. However, Korea must now strive for economic growth in a situation where it no longer benefits from late starter advantage or protectionism, but is burdened by high wage costs, flat demand, and low returns on investment. Various symptoms have become apparent that point to the structural changes that have taken place in the Korean economy's growth environment. Firstly, population growth has almost faltered and the ageing of society is proceeding rapidly. The birth rate had fallen to 1.16 children for each woman of child bearing age in 2004, the lowest rate of any country worldwide. Although the proportion of the population aged 65 or over, standing at a level of 9.1% in 2005, is still lower than that in major advanced countries, it is rising at a rapid pace. - 2 - Secondly, the economy is weighed down by high social costs and low efficiency. There is growing demand for a shortening of working hours while there is a widespread reluctance to engage in industries and businesses with bad working conditions. In this way, there is an ever-increasing demand for convenient employment with a high level of benefits while doing as little as possible. Consequently, the wage level relative to productivity in Korea is high, compared with those of advanced countries. Besides this, housing prices and living costs are also very high. Thirdly, with the lowering of yields on investment because of the economy's high cost-low efficiency syndrome, the competitiveness of manufacturing businesses which are small and medium sized labour-intensive and dependent on domestic demand, is fast weakening. Fourthly, from a situation of constant excess demand, we have been moved to one characterized by flatness of demand owing to the structural change in the supply of and demand for funds. Nowadays it is hard to find examples of old-style investment involving external enlargement funded by borrowings. - 3 - Fifthly, on the external front, we are now seeing the swift emergence of vast low-wage economic powerhouses such as China and India. The world economic order is shifting at high-speed from a protectionist framework to untrammelled openness. Unless they can gain international competitiveness, Korean businesses will face a bleak and pitiless economic reality where their survival is in question. ( Hardships Brought about by Structural Changes in the Growth Environment ) The Korean economy has experienced wrenching hardships in adapting to the transformation of the growth environment. A situation of jobless growth has emerged owing to the weakening competitiveness of most small and medium enterprises and labour intensive industries while the rate of youth unemployment has risen steeply. At the same time the polarization of the economy has deepened with a widening diversion between the export sector and domestic demand oriented sectors, and between large companies and small and medium enterprises. What is more, despite the great improvement in business earnings, households' economic situations have worsened owing to the standstill in household incomes. Firms' aversion to domestic - 4 - investment has deepened. Making matters worse, production facilities are shifting to China and other low wage countries in line with the declining competitiveness of manufacturing especially in labour intensive sectors. Reflecting this state of affairs, the potential GDP growth rate has tumbled back from its previous 78% level to a band of 45% while the volatility of GDP growth, in contrast, has increased in response to the heightened fragility of the domestic demand sector. ( Quick Adaptation to a Changing Environment ) Looked at from another perspective, though, the Korean economy has the chance to make a fresh leap forward through swift adaptation to the changed growth environment. For a start, industrial structural adjustment is proceeding rapidly in order to adapt to the transformation of the growth environment. The shift from manufacturing to services, and especially knowledge-based services, is being undertaken at a fast pace. Within manufacturing itself, Korea ranks among the world's five top producers in shipbuilding, semiconductors, home electronics, petrochemicals and steel. In terms of technological competitiveness, it counts among the world leaders in the automobile and information technology fields. - 5 - Secondly, there has been a huge improvement in firms' management soundness and transparency. Corporate debt ratios tumbled from around 400% back in 1997 to just 104% in 2004. When we consider that the average US debt-to-equity ratio stands at 141%, it can be seen that Korean companies' financial structure has become very sound. Thirdly, economic openness has been tirelessly pursued. For example the share of the total market capitalization of listed firms held by foreigners went up from 15% at the end of 1997 to 42% at the end of this July. Among Asian countries, the Korean market shows the highest level of foreign shareholdings. Fourthly, the financial reforms proved successful and financial system stability has been greatly heightened. The non-performing loan ratio of domestic banks plummeted from 14% at the end of 1999 to just 2% today. Over the same period, their average BIS capital adequacy ratio rose strongly from 7% to 11%. Last year domestic nationwide commercial banks achieved total profits of 6.4 trillion won, their highest ever. - 6 - ( Outlook for the Korean Economy ) In the course of its economic development, Korea has several times suffered the impact of massive change, but each time it has shown itself capable of adapting swiftly. So I think we can say straightaway that this capacity is one element in the distinctive dynamics of the Korean economy. In the light of this dynamism and the evidence so far from its adjustment to the recent changes in the growth environment, the Korean economy is on course for a successful landing on a mature growth path. This means that with 40 years of high growth averaging 7.7%, Korea can look forward to sustained robust growth in the 45% range over the medium and long term. Of course much remains to be done. Problems to be solved include the inefficiency in the course of social decision-making of labour management confrontation, the pursuit of vested interests by particular groups and the counterproductive political climate. All these issues, though, are amenable to solution within a relatively short space of time. Having overcome the currency crisis within a short space of time, the Korean economy has demonstrated its capacity to drive - 7 - structural adjustment successfully forward. Providing there is support from public participation and understanding, Korea's economic dynamism may become even more strongly pronounced in the future.

Title: Prudent Sovereign Debt Management: A Prerequisite for Financial Stability
Subtitle: The Governor's speech at the 11th IMF Consultations on Managing Sovereign Risk and Public Debt, organized by the IMF and the Ministry of Finance and Strategy of Korea
text: Prudent Sovereign Debt Management: A Prerequisite for Financial Stability Choongsoo Kim* June 22, 2011 Governor The Bank of Korea * This paper was prepared for a speech at the 11th IMF Consultations on Managing Sovereign Risk and Public Debt, organized by the IMF and the Ministry of Finance and Strategy of Korea. The author expresses his thanks to Dr. Hyun Jeong Kim and Dr. Jun Il Kim of the Bank of Korea Economic Research Institute for providing valuable information and comments. Distinguished guests, and ladies and gentlemen, It is my great pleasure to be here today, for this 11th IMF consultation meeting. I would like to thank the International Monetary Fund and the Ministry of Strategy and Finance for inviting me to speak. I understand that this meeting aims to address the most topical issues at presentsovereign risk and financial stability. I hope this meeting can shed light on these critical issues, and deliver consensus on what should be done to face the challenges ahead in the area of sovereign debt management. The global economy has now turned the corner from the Great Recession, but only at the expense of heightened sovereign risk in advanced economies, where sovereign debt has risen sharply since the global crisis hit. To be specific, G7 sovereign debt had climbed to 110 percent of GDP by the end of 2010, from 83 percent in 2007, and is projected to rise still further to over 120 percent of GDP by 2015. Not surprisingly, it is a precipitous fall in revenue that accounts for the brunt of the observed debt increase, although increased spending for fiscal stimulus and financial bailouts has also been a factor. The deteriorating debt dynamics have caused significant market concerns about sovereign risk, and ultimately pushed several periphery countries in Europe to the brink of sovereign default, which they have avoided only thanks to international financial support from the EU and the IMF. More alarming is that debt path projections show sovereign risk in major advanced economies remaining high, if not rising, for a considerable time, with the possibility of escalation to unsustainable levels if economic growth falters or if cross-border contagion creates additional casualties down the road. There is little doubt that this high and rising sovereign debt is a real threat to global financial stability, not to mention real stability. High public debt increases the cost of capital and crowds out private investment, thereby undermining long-term growth potential. And preliminary evidence points to negative effects on growth when sovereign debt is at or above 90 percent of GDP (Reinhart and Rogoff, 2010). On the financial front, government debt is the reference asset against which all private debt securities are priced and arbitraged, and accounts for a significant portion of the assets held by financial institutions. The government debt markets are moreover also the central corridor of the monetary policy transmission channel. In short, sovereign debt sustainability is a prerequisite for both real and financial stability. Against this backdrop, I would like to share with you my views on sovereign debt management, and its implications for monetary policy. To this end, I will focus on two types of risks that sovereign debt management must deal withsolvency or sustainability risk, and liquidity risk. These risks interact with each other, especially in cases where sovereign debt involves a large amount of external debt issued in foreign currencies. I will then touch briefly on the implications of sovereign debt management for monetary policy, before closing. Sustainability risk Let me take up sustainability risk first. The notion of intertemporal solvency is of limited use in operationalizing debt sustainability, as it requires only that the present value of future primary surpluses be no less than the current debt. In theory, therefore, governments can make fiscal solvency problems disappearby promising sufficiently large fiscal adjustments in the future. In reality, however, not all promises work well at all times. As a result, additional restrictions are needed if we wish to define debt sustainability. From the sovereign debt managers point of view, I think the central question is what should be considered a prudent level of sovereign debt. And as Chairman Bernanke (2011) pointed out, this is country specific and difficult to tell precisely. That it is country specific may well explain why some European countries have fallen victim to debt crises but the United States or the United Kingdom has not, at least so far, despite the broadly similar levels of debt among them. The recent study by the IMF (Ostry et al. 2010) sheds new light on how to calculate prudent debt levels, or more precisely how to estimate the debt limit beyond which sovereign debt dynamics become explosive and a debt crisis is thus unavoidable. The study makes two behavioral assumptions, which I find quite sensible. First, the markets are not impressed by promises unsupported by countries past track records of fiscal adjustment. Second, debt management is subject to fiscal fatigue, whereby governments typically behave responsibly to stabilize debt ratios, but do not do so alwaysparticularly when debt gets very largefor political and other reasons. The fiscal fatigue hypothesis turns out to be well supported by the data. This study not only predicts the debt crisis of the peripheral European countries but also offers a good analytical explanation for the suddenness of the crisis. The markets had indeed been rather calm in the months leading up to May 2010, when concerns for Greece surfaced suddenly and escalated rapidly thereafter. Specifically, the CDS premium on Greek debt had remained at 300 basis points on average from January to March 2010, before soaring above 500 basis points in April and 700 in May. In retrospect, it is puzzling why the market price of Greek debt changed so rapidly and suddenly, when its fiscal deficit was revised upward by only a few percentage points of GDP. The study shows that the debt dynamics deteriorate at an increasing rate as debt approaches the debt limit, while also becoming more sensitive to uncertainty concerning fiscal outturns. Several useful lessons can be drawn from these results and what we have witnessed during the euro area periphery debt crisis. First, the prudent level of sovereign debt may be lower than previously thought, even for advanced countries. I expect the markets to be more alert to solvency risk, charging additional risk premiums as they see appropriate. This implies that future primary surpluses will be discounted at higher rates than otherwise, yielding lower present values. It will in addition be increasingly difficult to generate large primary surpluses going forward, in view of population aging and the resultant deceleration in growth. Second, fiscal credibility matters greatly for debt dynamics. And credibility is not something that can be acquired overnight. Rather, it can be earned only by maintaining a good track record of responsible fiscal behavior, and putting good institutions in place. Good institutions mean not only a well-designed policy framework but also effective enforcement. In this connection, it is worth noting that the empirical evidence regarding the role of fiscal rules in stabilizing debt ratios is mixed, and mainly because fiscal rules are not always enforced. For example, the uniform debt target envisaged in the Stability and Growth Pact has been consistently violated by many EU members. Chiles fiscal rule, introduced in 2001, was in contrast a huge success, as it was underpinned by credible enforcement. In Chile, the fiscal target was set for the structural balance, while an independent committee was assigned to forecast copper prices and potential GDP. More important, I believe, is the fact that the Chilean government repeatedly honored the recommended fiscal target. Third, transparency is crucial for avoiding unnecessary penalties imposed by the markets, particularly when debt is high enough to cause market concerns. Frequent and repeated upward revisions of fiscal deficits were one cause of the loss of confidence in the case of the Greek crisis. Last but not least, governments should pay more attention to gross than to net debt, in their debt management. While net debt is a more appropriate measure of solvency or sustainability in conceptual terms, gross debt has mattered more to the market perceptions on debt sustainability. Net debt is often incomparable across countries, due to differences in definitions or in the treatment of asset components. More important is that focusing on net debt may lead to optimism bias, as it fails to take appropriate account of unfunded future liabilities of the social security system. Liquidity risk Now let me turn to liquidity risk. Liquidity risk has been well recognized by emerging market borrowers, but appears less so for advanced borrowers. Unlike emerging market countries, advanced economies have thus far enjoyed the privileges of issuing sovereign debt in their own currencies, with few or no restrictions on market access. Obviously, the ongoing debt crisis of the euro area casts doubt on whether such privileges will remain at their disposals. That said, I would like to highlight the currency denomination and maturity structure of sovereign debt as a key element of liquidity risk management. The currency denomination of their sovereign debt is of paramount importance to borrowers in emerging markets, where currency crises are typically followed by debt crises. And in emerging market countries, in fact, currency, liquidity, and solvency risks are all tightly intertwined. In this regard, policy efforts to issue more sovereign debt in the local currency should yield enormous stability benefits for emerging market borrowers. Underlying the liquidity benefit of local currency debt is the liquidity backing by the central bank through its lender of last resort function. In terms of liquidity risk, therefore, the local currency debt issued by advanced but minor members of a currency union may be closer to the foreign currency debt issued by emerging market borrowers than to the debt issued by advanced countries with their own central banks. Simply speaking, Greece can and did issue debt in its own currency, but it cannot print the euro and its access to ECB credit may be uncertain and limited when most needed. Of course, the recent debt crisis in Greece is more a crisis of insolvency than illiquidity. Nevertheless, the members of a currency union, and particularly the minor ones, do have to pay greater attention to liquidity risk management than their peers with their own central banks. The debt maturity structure is another important element of debt management. Since this issue has been extensively researched, I will make a few observations with regard to the maturity structure of external public debt of emerging market borrowers. Short-term debt is cheaper but riskier than long-term debt. Faced with this tradeoff between riskiness and borrowing cost, emerging market borrowers have over the past two decades or so increased their proportions of shortterm debt. And this revealed preference suggests three possibilitieseither an improved tradeoff in favor of short-term debt, or debtor moral hazard, or both. Setting aside the issue of moral hazard, I would like to highlight the role of foreign reserves in improving the tradeoff. As is well known, the foreign reserves of emerging market countries have been rising over this same period of increasing short-term debt. And a plausible explanation for this joint increase in reserves and short-term debt would be that short-term debt has become more attractive, in terms of its risk-adjusted cost, as the higher level of foreign reserves provides better insurance against liquidity risk. This view implies that the debt maturity structure is endogenous to the foreign reserves, just the opposite of what the existing literature on optimal reserve levels suggests. Regardless of the direction of causality between the foreign reserves and the debt maturity structure, avoiding excessive short-term debt and debt service bunching should be a high priority in debt management. More generally speaking, as Charles Goodhart (2010) has put it, debt management requires high-calibre market tactics to maintain the confidence of market participants. Sovereign debt management and monetary policy Before closing, I would like to make a few remarks on the interaction between monetary and macro-prudential policies, and sovereign debt management or, more broadly, fiscal policy. First, monetary policy affects the debt dynamics in various ways. At present, the highly accommodative monetary policy stances offer significant help in slowing the increase in debt. And in fact, prior to the global crisis the growth-adjusted real interest rate, a key driver of the debt dynamics, was on average negative in all three debt crisis countries in Europe, and positive but very low at less than one half percent in the United States and the United Kingdom. Such favorable conditions enabled these countries to increase their sovereign debt levels at little cost. In view of the rising inflationary pressures in both advanced and emerging countries, however, central banks will likely be forced sooner or later to raise rates. And unless counterbalancing fiscal adjustments are deployed, higher interest rates will surely aggravate the already fragile debt dynamics. An alternative scenario is one of fiscal dominance, whereby monetary policy is subordinated to fiscal objectives even despite rising inflationary pressures. One may think that higher inflation and low nominal interest rates will help to reduce debt ratios. Such help will not last long, however, as higher inflation will lead to higher market interest rates and eventually stagnation in economic growth. This is the worst case scenario in the long run. Second, the global community is currently exploring a new macroprudential framework, that will complement monetary policy but also have implications for sovereign debt management. It involves a long list of regulatory reform measures, including risk-weighted capital charges and liquidity coverage regulations among others. Under the new framework, financial institutions' demand for sovereign debt is likely to increase. And this will be a plus for sovereign debt management, but only if sovereign debt is considered to be as risk-free and liquid as before. These considerations imply that reducing sovereign debt is an urgent need of the day. While some inflation may help temporarily, inflating debt away is not an option. Monetary policy needs to remain focused on price and financial stability. One might worry about the risk of perverse inflation dynamics, similar to those observed in Brazil in the 1980s when monetary tightening resulted in hyperinflation by increasing the fiscal deficit. I personally believe such a risk to be almost non-existent, if monetary tightening for inflation control is accompanied by sustained and credible fiscal consolidation for debt reduction. Concluding remarks Ladies and gentlemen, The global crisis has demonstrated how fiscal credibility and prudence during normal times pay off well during times of crisis or tail-risk events. It has also proven that sovereign debt crises can occur quite suddenly even in advanced economies. The lessons of the Great Depression saved us from Great Depression II, but not from the Great Recession. Moreover, the costs of avoiding Great Depression II have turned out to be high. The increased sovereign risk and mounting debt burdens, if unaddressed for long, will have lasting effects on growth and financial stability. Debt must thus be reduced to a prudent level, sooner rather than later, and fiscal reform must accompany it to make this debt reduction sustainable. Embarking on fiscal consolidation is certainly a very tough decision, especially given the great uncertainty surrounding economic recovery. Unfortunately, no better alternative seems within our reach. Fiscal consolidation will be particularly difficult for countries with poor track records of fiscal responsibility. The markets will be timid and suspicious until seeing some initial progress. But this initial progress will also be the most difficult to achieve. Nevertheless, history is not destiny. Fiscal consolidation will be difficult also for countries with few immediate fiscal concerns but large longer-term fiscal burdens. Korea is a case in point. Korea has been commended for its fiscal prudence with its current debt ratio standing at about 30 percent. And the government plans to achieve a balance in the budgetexcluding social securityby 2014. The Korean population is aging at the fastest rate in the world, however, and the demand for social welfare spending is growing rapidly. I hope this meeting useful not only for countries with high sovereign debt but also for countries like Korea needing to prepare better for the future. I also hope the meeting will be a productive global forum, in which sovereign debt managers share their knowledge and experiences to align their policies, contributing thereby to sustainable and balanced growth of the world economy. Thank you. References Bernanke, Ben S., 2011, "Fiscal Sustainability", Speech at the Annual Conference of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, June 14. Goodhart, C.A.E., 2010, "The Changing Role of Central Banks", BIS Working Paper, No. 326. Ostry, J. D., A. R. Ghosh, Jun I. Kim, and M. S. Qureshi, "Fiscal space", IMF Staff Position Note, SPN/10/11, 2010. Reinhart, Carmen M. and Kenneth S. Rogoff, 2010, "Growth in a Time of Debt", NBER Working Paper, No. 15639.

Title: Financial Contagion and Volatile Capital Flow
Subtitle: Opening Ceremony of the 32nd SEACEN Board of Governors Meeting
text: Financial Contagion and Volatile Capital Flow Choongsoo Kim Governor The Bank of Korea Opening Ceremony of the 32nd SEACEN Board of Governors Meeting November 22, Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia His Excellency Prime Minister Altankhuyag, Honorable Governor Zoljargal, Governors and Delegates of SEACEN member central banks, Ladies and Gentlemen, As the chair of the SEACEN Board of Governors, it is a great honor to deliver the response address at the opening ceremony of the 32nd SEACEN Board of Governors meeting, with Prime Minister Altankhuyag in attendance. On behalf of all participants, I would like to express my deep gratitude to Governor Zoljargal and Bank of Mongolia for their efforts in organizing this meeting and conference. In the course of the Governors Conference, the High-level seminar and the SEACEN-BIS Executive Seminar held this year, we have engaged in in-depth discussions on effective ways of harmonizing monetary and macro-prudential policies amid the increased uncertainty surrounding the external financial sector. We also shared our experience and wisdom on the impact of the Eurozone crisis on Asia and the overall global economy, and the appropriate policy options in response. I would like to thank members and delegates for your enthusiastic participation and continuing efforts in making these achievements possible. Capital Flows and Financial Contagion The global community has still not emerged from the global financial crisis. It is time now to combine our strength, to prevent this crisis that began in Wall Street, and evolved then into the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis, from spilling over into emerging market economies.
